sections.title: Mate
sections.summary: The drink that runs the country

classes.title: What is mate?
classes.summary: A bitter herb, a gourd and an invitation

pages.title: Not a drink. A ritual.
pages.body: **Mate** is hot water poured over **yerba**, the dried, ground leaves of a holly tree from the northeast. You sip it through a metal straw from a small gourd, a **calabaza**, that's *also* called a **mate**. Then it gets refilled and passed on. And you don't *drink* (beber) mate: you **tomás** mate. Someone offers you one? Say **dale** (sure).
pages.fun_fact: By law, mate is Argentina's *infusión nacional*: the national herbal drink.

pages.statement: In Argentina, the word "mate" can mean both the drink and the cup you drink it from.
pages.explain: Exactly. "Pasame el mate" can mean the cup, the drink, or both. Context does the rest.

pages.title: The Guaraní got there first
pages.body: Long before the Spanish showed up, the **Guaraní** people of what's now Paraguay, northeast Argentina and southern Brazil were drinking the leaf. They call the plant **ka'a**. Later, **Jesuit** missions in Guaraní lands learned to *grow* it on plantations instead of picking it wild. Most yerba still comes from that same corner: **Misiones** and **Corrientes**.

pages.prompt: Which people first drank yerba mate?
pages.explain: The Guaraní. The Spanish and the Jesuits came later and turned it into a big business.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it means

pages.scenario: You're new in Buenos Aires. A coworker holds up a gourd and says: "¿Tomás mate?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
pages.explain: **Tomar** is the verb for mate, and the question is almost always an invitation. Say **dale** and you're in. (Yes, *mate* is also checkmate, and a buddy in English. Not today.)

pages.statement: Yerba mate is a kind of green tea from China.
pages.explain: Totally different plant: a South American holly. It does have caffeine, which is why half the country runs on it.

classes.title: The gear
classes.summary: Mate, bombilla, termo, yerba: your starter kit

pages.title: The mate (the cup)
pages.body: The classic one is a dried **calabaza** (gourd). There are also wooden, glass, ceramic and steel ones, and the chunky leather-wrapped **mate camionero**, the "trucker's mate". A new gourd needs work first: to **curar el mate** (cure it), you fill it with wet yerba and leave it a day or so. And never use soap on it. The gourd soaks it up, and so does your next mate.

pages.title: The bombilla
pages.body: The **bombilla** is a metal straw with a filter at the bottom, so you drink the water and not the leaves. Usually steel or alpaca (a nickel-silver alloy), sometimes fancy silver. It goes in once and stays put. It is not a spoon, and it is definitely not a stirring stick.

pages.statement: If the mate is getting clogged, it's fine to stir the yerba with the bombilla.
pages.explain: Moving the bombilla wrecks the setup and clogs it more. If it's blocked, tell whoever's serving. Their mate, their problem.

pages.title: The termo and the yerba
pages.body: The **termo** (thermos) keeps water hot for hours, which is why you see people carrying one under their arm in the park. At home it's the **pava** (kettle). **Yerba** comes **con palo** (with stems, milder) or **sin palo** (just leaves, stronger). First time buying? Grab a con palo pack. And pick a brand carefully: people get *very* loyal about theirs.

pages.prompt: Match the gear to what it does

pages.scenario: At the supermarket you see "yerba con palo" and "yerba sin palo".
pages.prompt: What's the difference?
pages.explain: **Palo** means stick or stem. Stems make it milder and slower to wash out. **Sin palo** hits harder.

pages.prompt: You're making the mate. Yerba and bombilla are in your hands; the hot water is on the stove, out of reach. Ask your friend.
pages.text: Pasame la ___, que el agua ya está.
pages.translation: Pass me the kettle, the water's ready.
pages.explain: The **pava** is the kettle. The other two are already in your hands.

pages.statement: A brand-new calabaza is ready to use straight out of the shop.
pages.explain: First you **curar el mate**: a day or so with wet yerba inside. Skip it and the first mates taste funky, and the gourd can even crack.

example.en: Don't move the straw.

vocabulary.note: Never stir with it.

classes.title: How to cebar
classes.summary: Making mate, step by step, without embarrassing yourself

pages.title: Cebar: the verb that matters
pages.body: **Cebar** means to prepare and serve mate: pour the water, hand it over, get it back, repeat. The person doing it is the **cebador** (or **cebadora**). It's a small job with big status. A good cebador is appreciated; a bad one hears about it, lovingly, all afternoon.

pages.title: The montañita
pages.body: Fill the mate about ¾ with yerba. Cover the mouth with your hand, flip it, shake, and tilt it so the yerba slides to one side. That slope is the **montañita** (little mountain). One common way from here: wet the low side with a splash of warm water, then push the bombilla in right there. Always pour into the low side and keep the top dry.

pages.title: Hot, but never boiling
pages.body: The golden rule: you want **agua caliente** (hot water), around 70 to 80 °C, and you never let it **hervir** (boil). Boiling water will **quemar la yerba** (burn the yerba) and make it bitter and harsh. Old-school trick: turn off the pava when it starts to hum, right before the bubbles come.
pages.fun_fact: Many electric kettles in Argentina have a "mate" setting for exactly this.

pages.scenario: The pava is bubbling hard, full boil. Your friend is waiting with the mate ready.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Let it cool down a bit first
pages.explain: Boiling water burns the yerba. You'll hear "¡la quemaste!" and you'll deserve it.

pages.prompt: Prepare a mate the way you just saw
items: Fill the mate about ¾ with yerba
Cover it, flip it, shake it
Tilt it to make the montañita
Wet the low side with a bit of warm water
Put in the bombilla on the wet side
Pour hot water, not boiling, next to the bombilla
pages.explain: That's one common way. Some cebadores put the bombilla in before any water, and they'll defend it to the death.

pages.title: Who drinks the first one?
pages.body: The first mate is often bitter, a bit foamy and full of dust, so the **cebador** usually drinks it, or spits it out. Hence the saying **el primero es para el zonzo**: the first one's for the fool. After lots of rounds the flavor fades and the mate is **lavado** (washed out). Time for fresh yerba.

pages.statement: When friends share mate, the first one usually goes to the cebador, not to a guest.
pages.explain: Right. The first one is the harsh one, so the cebador takes the hit. It's a small sacrifice, not a privilege.

pages.prompt: The mate has lost all its flavor. What do you say?
pages.translation: Hey, this mate is washed out.
pages.explain: **Lavado** means it's lost its flavor. Time for fresh yerba.

classes.title: The rules of the ronda
classes.summary: Mate etiquette, so nobody gives you the look

pages.title: The ronda
pages.body: When people share mate, there's one mate, one bombilla and one **ronda** (round). The **cebador** fills it and hands it to you, bombilla facing you. You drink *all* of it until it gurgles, then hand it back. Not to your neighbor: back to the cebador, who fills it for the next person. And only the cebador touches the yerba and the bombilla.

pages.scenario: You just finished your mate. The person next to you is looking at it hopefully.
pages.prompt: Who do you give it to?
pages.explain: Always back to the **cebador**. They refill it and pass it on. The mate never skips the cebador.

pages.scenario: Someone hands you a mate and the montañita looks kinda off, the bombilla a bit crooked.
pages.prompt: Should you fix it?
pages.explain: Hands off. Fixing someone's mate is like rearranging their kitchen while they cook.

pages.title: Gracias means "I'm out"
pages.body: This one catches every foreigner. In a ronda, saying **gracias** when you hand the mate back doesn't mean "thanks", it means "thanks, **I'm done**". Say it after your first mate and you won't get another. Want to keep going? Just hand it back, maybe with a smile or a **¡qué rico!** (so good!).

pages.statement: Saying "gracias" as you hand the mate back tells the cebador to skip you from now on.
pages.explain: Classic trap for visitors. **Gracias** = I'm done. Say it only when you want out of the ronda.

pages.title: It's not a microphone
pages.body: Don't hold the mate while you tell a long story. The whole ronda is waiting, and the water is getting cold. Someone will say **"¡No es un micrófono!"** and everyone will laugh at you, kindly. Drink it all, hand it back. And don't complain that it's too hot or too bitter: you're a guest in someone else's mate.

pages.prompt: Your friend is talking and holding the mate forever. What do you say?
pages.translation: Come on, it's not a microphone.
pages.explain: The classic line for someone who hogs the mate.

pages.title: Got a cold? Skip it
pages.body: Don't wipe the bombilla before you drink. Sharing it is the whole point, and many people read wiping as "you think I'm dirty". If you're sick, or you just don't feel like sharing, say **no, gracias** the first time the mate comes your way. Nobody minds, and nobody asks why.

pages.scenario: You've got a cold, and your friends are starting a ronda.
pages.prompt: What's the move?
pages.explain: A friendly **no, gracias** at the first round and you're out, no drama. Everyone will thank you later.

glossary.en: the person who serves the mate

vocabulary.en: said handing it back: I'm done, skip me
vocabulary.note: Only say it when you want out.

vocabulary.en: hurry up and drink (lit. it's not a microphone)

classes.title: Mate every day
classes.summary: Sweet or bitter, cold or cooked, everywhere you go

pages.title: Amargo or dulce?
pages.body: Most people drink it **amargo** (bitter, no sugar). **Mate dulce** has sugar or sweetener added, more common in some provinces and families. It's a friendly rivalry, not a war. Some purists will tease you, though. People also add **yuyos** (herbs) like peperina or burrito, or a bit of orange peel.

pages.scenario: The cebador asks: "¿Amargo o dulce?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
pages.explain: **Amargo** is no sugar, **dulce** is with sugar. Both answers are OK, but amargo gets you more street cred.

pages.title: Mate cocido
pages.body: **Mate cocido** is the lazy (and cozy) version: yerba in a tea bag, or boiled and strained, served in a regular cup. Often with milk and sugar. It's the drink of school breakfasts, the afternoon **merienda** (snack time), and cold winter mornings. No bombilla, no ronda, no rules.

pages.title: Tereré: the cold one
pages.body: **Tereré** is mate with cold water or juice, often with ice and herbs. It's huge in **Paraguay** and in hot provinces like Corrientes, Misiones, Chaco and Formosa. If someone offers you tereré on a scorching day up north, say yes. In Buenos Aires you'll see it on summer days, but the hot mate never really takes a vacation.

pages.prompt: Match the drink to what it is
pairs: yerba in a cup, like tea

pages.statement: Mate cocido is served in a regular cup, with no bombilla.
pages.explain: Right: it's made like tea. No bombilla, no ronda, and nobody will tell you off for saying gracias.

pages.title: Where? Everywhere.
pages.body: In the office, at university, in the park, at the beach, on a road trip (the co-pilot serves). You'll see people walking with the termo under their arm. **Matear** means to drink mate, usually in company, and a **matera** is the bag that carries the whole kit.

pages.scenario: You're the co-pilot on a road trip. The driver says: "Cebame uno."
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Make a mate, hand it over
pages.explain: The co-pilot is the cebador. Keep them coming, and don't burn the driver.

pages.prompt: Inviting a friend over for mate
pages.translation: Want to come over for mate?
pages.explain: **Matear** = to drink mate, usually together. It's a whole social plan.

vocabulary.en: made like tea, in a cup

example.en: Shall we have mate in the park?

classes.title: Mate next door
classes.summary: Uruguay, southern Brazil and a surprise fan in the Middle East

pages.title: Same leaf, different rules
pages.body: Argentina doesn't own mate. **Uruguay**, **Paraguay** (home of the cold **tereré**) and southern **Brazil** drink it every day too, and each one is sure its way is the right way. The champion per person is Uruguay, which drinks even more than Argentina. Take the ferry to **cruzar el charco** (cross "the puddle", the River Plate) and you'll notice the difference in five minutes.

pages.title: Uruguay: the termo lives under the arm
pages.body: In Montevideo people walk to work, to the rambla, to the beach with the **termo bajo el brazo** (thermos under the arm). Uruguay grows almost no yerba: most of it comes from **Brazil**, ground fine and almost **sin palo**. It's more **fuerte** (strong) and bitter than the Argentine stuff, and full of **polvo** (dust).

pages.statement: Most of the yerba Uruguayans drink is grown in Brazil.
pages.explain: The biggest mate drinkers in the world grow almost none of their own. That's why **yerba uruguaya** tastes so different: it's a Brazilian-style fine grind.

pages.scenario: You come back from Montevideo with a pack of yerba uruguaya and use it in your next ronda in Buenos Aires.
pages.prompt: What will your Argentine friends probably say?
pages.explain: Fine-ground, almost no stems, lots of polvo: it hits harder and can clog a bombilla. Some porteños love it, some can't stand it.

pages.prompt: Describe the classic Montevideo look
pages.text: Los uruguayos andan con el termo bajo el ___.
pages.translation: Uruguayans walk around with the thermos under their arm.
pages.explain: **Bajo el brazo** = under the arm. In Buenos Aires you see it too, just less.

pages.title: Brazil: chimarrão
pages.body: In **Rio Grande do Sul**, Brazil's southern state, the gaúchos drink **chimarrão**: bright green, powder-fine yerba in a big gourd called a **cuia**, sipped through a **bomba**. Same ronda, same hot water, different accent. Cowboys on both sides of the border, same habit.

pages.prompt: Match the habit to where you'll see it

pages.title: Mate in the Middle East
pages.body: Syria has been the main buyer of Argentina's exported yerba year after year. The link is people: in the late 1800s and early 1900s many Syrians and Lebanese moved to Argentina, and some went home with the habit. Today mate is especially loved by the **Druze** communities of Syria and Lebanon, gourd, bombilla and all.
pages.fun_fact: Chile is a distant second on the export list.

pages.prompt: Which country buys the most yerba from Argentina?
pages.explain: Syria, by far. Uruguay mostly buys from Brazil, and Chile is a distant second.

example.es: Siempre anda con el termo bajo el brazo.
example.en: He always walks around with the thermos under his arm.
This yerba is really strong.

sections.title: Asado
sections.summary: Fire, meat and a whole Sunday with your people

classes.title: More than a barbecue
classes.summary: Why an asado is a whole afternoon, not a meal

pages.title: It's not just meat
pages.body: An **asado** is grilled meat, sure. But mostly it's an excuse to spend hours together. Sunday lunch with the family, Friday night with friends, a birthday, a work thing — you name it, there's an asado. When someone says **¿hacemos un asado?** (shall we do an asado?), they're really asking: *wanna hang out all day?*
pages.fun_fact: Argentines also say **asado** for a specific cut: the ribs. Context tells you which one.

pages.title: Clear your schedule
pages.body: Nobody does a quick asado. Someone lights the fire late morning, the meat cooks slowly, you eat around two, and then comes the **sobremesa** — sitting at the table long after the food is gone, talking, joking, arguing about football. Getting up at five is totally normal. Leaving right after eating? A bit rude.

pages.statement: At a Sunday asado, still sitting at the table at five in the afternoon is normal.
pages.explain: Completely normal. The **sobremesa** is half the point. Leaving right after the food looks like you only came to eat.

pages.title: The asador
pages.body: Every asado has one **asador**: the person in charge of the fire and the meat. Traditionally it's the dad, the uncle, the friend who "knows". It's a role with a lot of pride attached. While the meat cooks, people hang out next to the grill with a drink to keep the asador company. The grill is where the party starts.

pages.scenario: You arrive at the asado. The fire's going, the meat is on, and the table is still empty.
pages.prompt: Where's everyone?
options: By the grill, drink in hand
pages.explain: Around the **asador**, keeping them company. Grab a drink and join them.

pages.scenario: Your coworker invites you: "¿Hacemos un asado el domingo? Vení a la una." (Come at one.)
pages.prompt: When will you probably eat?
pages.explain: The fire is slow and so is everything else. Show up at one, have a drink by the grill, and eat when the asador says so.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning
pairs: the person in charge of the grill
chatting at the table after eating
an invite to spend the day

example.en: Shall we do an asado on Sunday?

vocabulary.en: long chat at the table after the meal
wanna get together? (lit. shall we do an asado?)

classes.title: Playing with fire
classes.summary: Parrilla, fogón, leña, carbón — and the embers

pages.title: Parrilla or fogón?
pages.body: The **parrilla** is the grill: an iron grate over the embers, often built into the backyard in brick. The **fogón** is an open fire on the ground — think countryside, camping, or a whole lamb on an iron cross leaning over the flames (**asado a la cruz** or **al asador**: two names, same dish). City asados are almost always on a parrilla.
pages.fun_fact: Many Buenos Aires apartments have a small parrilla on the balcony or rooftop. Priorities.

pages.title: The secret is patience
pages.body: Here's the secret: you don't cook over flames. You cook over **brasas** (embers). The asador burns wood or charcoal on the side, then shovels the glowing embers under the grill, little by little. Slow heat, lots of patience. If you see flames licking the meat, something went wrong.

pages.statement: A good asado is cooked over big, tall flames so it's done fast.
pages.explain: It's cooked slowly over **brasas** (embers). Flames burn the outside and leave the inside raw.

pages.title: Leña vs carbón
pages.body: **Leña** is firewood — hardwoods like quebracho or algarrobo. It takes longer but many swear it gives better flavor. **Carbón** (charcoal) lights faster and is easier, so it's what most people use in the city. Which is better? Ask two Argentines and you'll get three opinions.

pages.prompt: Match the fire words

pages.scenario: The asador keeps a fire going off to one side and shovels embers under the grill, a bit at a time.
pages.prompt: Why not just burn the logs right under the meat?
options: It's bad luck at an asado
pages.explain: Flames char the outside and leave the inside raw. Embers give steady, gentle heat.

pages.prompt: The asador wants more heat under the meat. What do they ask for?
pages.text: Poné más ___ debajo de la carne.
pages.translation: Put more embers under the meat.
pages.explain: **Brasas**, always. Ice and water are for the drinks.

vocabulary.note: Also a restaurant that serves grilled meat.

example.es: Poné más brasas debajo del vacío.
example.en: Put more embers under the flank.

glossary.en: whole lamb roasted on an iron cross (also: al asador)

classes.title: What comes off the grill, and when
classes.summary: Picada, sausages, achuras, then the big cuts

pages.title: First, the picada
pages.body: While the fire does its thing, there's a **picada**: a board with cheese, salami, olives, bread, maybe peanuts. It keeps everyone alive for the first couple of hours. Don't fill up on it, though — you've got a long way to go.

pages.title: Then, the sausages
pages.body: The first things off the grill are usually the sausages: **chorizo** (pork-and-beef sausage) and **morcilla** (blood sausage, dark and soft). They get cut up on a board and passed around, often on a piece of bread. Squeeze of lemon optional, second helping expected.

pages.title: The brave stuff
pages.body: Next, the **achuras** (offal). **Chinchulines** are small intestines, grilled until golden and crispy. **Mollejas** are sweetbreads, the thymus gland: crispy outside, creamy inside. Try the mollejas with lemon. Thank me later.
pages.fun_fact: Technically chorizo and morcilla aren't offal, but at the grill plenty of people lump them in with the achuras.

pages.prompt: Match it to what it is

pages.title: Finally, the cuts
pages.body: Then the main event, the **cortes** (cuts): **asado de tira** (short ribs cut across the bone), **vacío** (flank) and **entraña** (skirt steak, juicy and loved). The asador decides the order. Your job is to eat and say **¡qué rico!** (so good!).

pages.prompt: Put a classic asado in order
items: Picada while the fire gets going
Chorizo and morcilla
Vacío, entraña and asado de tira
pages.explain: Every family does it a bit differently, but snacks, then sausages, then the big cuts is the usual rhythm. The achuras come off somewhere in between.

pages.scenario: Someone slices a dark, almost black sausage and hands you a piece on bread: "Probá la morcilla."
pages.prompt: What are you about to eat?
pages.explain: **Morcilla** is blood sausage: soft, rich, a bit sweet. Sounds scary, tastes amazing. Saying **no, gracias** is fine too.

pages.title: How do you like it?
pages.body: The asador might ask how you want your meat. **Jugoso** means juicy, pink inside. **A punto** is medium. **Cocido** is well done. Most Argentines like it a punto or a bit jugoso. Asking for it very rare? You'll get a raised eyebrow.

pages.prompt: Ask for your meat medium
pages.translation: Medium for me, please.
pages.explain: **A punto** = medium. **Jugoso** if you want it pinker, **cocido** if you want it well done.

pages.statement: Vacío and entraña are types of achuras.
pages.explain: They're **cortes** (cuts of beef). Achuras are the offal: chinchulines, mollejas and friends.

example.en: Is the offal ready yet?

example.es: Para mí, a punto, por favor.
example.en: Medium for me, please.

glossary.en: short ribs cut across the bone

classes.title: Choripán, provoleta and the sauces
classes.summary: The sandwich, the grilled cheese and what goes on top

pages.title: The choripán
pages.body: **Choripán** = **chorizo** + **pan** (bread). A grilled sausage, split open in a crusty roll. That's it, and it's perfect. It's the first thing out at many asados, and it's also street food: outside football stadiums, at protests, on the Costanera. Everyone calls it **chori**.

pages.title: The provoleta
pages.body: **Provoleta** is a thick round of provolone-style cheese grilled until crispy outside and melty inside, with oregano and chili flakes on top. It's the classic starter at any parrilla: order one for the table and eat it fast, straight from the little pan, before it turns to rubber.

pages.title: Chimichurri and salsa criolla
pages.body: Two sauces rule. **Chimichurri**: parsley, oregano, garlic, chili flakes, vinegar and oil. **Salsa criolla**: chopped tomato, onion and bell pepper in vinegar and oil. Both go on the choripán and the meat. Where does the name chimichurri come from? Nobody knows for sure, and everyone has a theory.

pages.prompt: Match the thing to what's in it

pages.statement: Of the two classic sauces, salsa criolla is the one with chopped tomato.
pages.explain: Right: tomato, onion and bell pepper. **Chimichurri** is the green one, with parsley, garlic and oregano.

pages.scenario: You're at a football match in Buenos Aires. Outside the stadium, smoke everywhere and people lining up at a street grill.
pages.prompt: What are they most likely selling?
pages.explain: The **chori** is the king of street food at stadiums. Cheap, fast, and you eat it standing up with chimichurri dripping everywhere.

pages.prompt: Your turn at the street grill. Order a sausage sandwich with the green sauce.
pages.translation: A chori with chimichurri, please.
pages.explain: **Un chori con chimichurri**: the most-said sentence outside any stadium on a Sunday.

vocabulary.note: Short: chori.

example.en: Shall I make you a chori?

vocabulary.en: green herb, garlic and vinegar sauce

classes.title: You're invited — now what?
classes.summary: What to bring, what to say, and how not to annoy the asador

pages.title: Never show up empty-handed
pages.body: The host usually buys the meat. You bring something else: **vino** (wine, often a Malbec), **bebida** (drinks: soda, beer, fernet), **postre** (dessert — ice cream is a classic), or **hielo** (ice, and someone always forgets it). Just ask: **¿qué llevo?** (what should I bring?).
pages.fun_fact: With friends, everyone often chips in for the meat. That's **hacer una vaquita**.

pages.scenario: Your friend's family invited you to their Sunday asado. You ask what to bring and they say "nada, vení" (nothing, just come).
pages.prompt: What do you actually do?
options: Show up with nothing, as told
Bring a kilo of steak for yourself
pages.explain: "**Nada, vení**" is being polite. A bottle of wine or some dessert is always welcome. Bringing your own meat can look like you don't trust the host.

pages.prompt: Ask what you should bring
pages.translation: What should I bring to the asado?
pages.explain: **¿Qué llevo?** — the classic question. Argentines use **llevar** (take) from the guest's point of view.

pages.title: The golden rule
pages.body: Don't tell the asador how to cook. Not "it needs more heat", not "in my country we…". And never grab the tongs: the fire and the meat are theirs. Keep them company, bring them a glass of wine, and say **¡huele bárbaro!** (smells amazing!). Want to help? Ask **¿te ayudo en algo?** and do exactly what they say.

pages.scenario: You think the vacío has been on too long. The asador turns and asks: "¿Todo bien?"
pages.prompt: Best answer?
options: Grab the tongs and take it off
pages.explain: Trust the asador. Criticizing the asado is almost a personal insult.

pages.title: The applause
pages.body: When the meat's done and everyone's eaten, someone raises a glass: **¡Un aplauso para el asador!** Everyone claps, even if the meat was a bit dry. The asador cooked, so the others clear the table and wash up. Then nobody gets up: the **sobremesa** (the long chat at the table) has started, and you stay for it.

pages.prompt: Complete the classic toast
pages.translation: A round of applause for the grill master!
pages.explain: Always the **asador**. A **mozo** is a waiter, and nobody applauds the flank.

pages.statement: At an asado, the asador usually gets out of washing up.
pages.explain: They did the cooking. Offering to help with the dishes earns you points, and a second invitation.

pages.prompt: A perfect guest's afternoon
items: Ask ¿qué llevo?
Arrive with wine and ice
Keep the asador company at the grill

classes.title: Asados from the rest of the country
classes.summary: Lamb on a cross, beef in its hide and dinner in a plough disc

pages.title: Patagonian lamb
pages.body: Down south the star isn't beef. It's **cordero patagónico al asador**, also called **asado a la cruz**: a whole lamb opened flat, wired to an iron cross and stuck in the ground, leaning over the fire. Yes, the cross is *also* called an **asador**, like the grill master. It cooks slowly, for hours, until the skin crackles.

pages.scenario: You're walking through El Calafate and see a restaurant window with lambs spread on iron crosses around a fire.
pages.prompt: What are you looking at?
pages.explain: Lamb on the **asador** (the cross), Patagonia's signature. It's slow food in the most literal way: it was probably on the fire before lunch was even a thought.

pages.title: Asado con cuero
pages.body: The big-party version: beef cooked **con cuero**, with its hide still on. The hide works like a pot, holding in the juices and fat. Usually it's a **vaquillona** (young heifer) in huge pieces, over steady embers for **12 hours or more**. It's festival food, made for a crowd.
pages.fun_fact: Travel tip: the town of Viale, in Entre Ríos, throws a national festival for it every year.

pages.statement: In an asado con cuero, the hide is left on to keep the juices in.
pages.explain: Exactly: the hide works like a pot. That's also why it takes forever.

pages.scenario: A town festival poster says: "Vaquillona con cuero, se sirve a las 13 hs."
pages.prompt: When did the asadores probably start cooking?
pages.explain: Twelve hours or more of fire means lighting up the night before and taking turns. Someone always brings a guitar and a termo.

pages.title: The disco
pages.body: Out in the **campo** (countryside), someone took a worn-out **disco de arado** (plough disc), welded on legs and handles, and got a giant wok for the fire. Now it's everywhere: **pollo al disco**, **carne al disco**, onions, peppers, chorizo and a splash of wine, all stewing together. One disco feeds a crowd, and everyone stands around it with a piece of bread.

pages.prompt: Match the dish to how it's cooked
pairs: whole lamb on an iron cross
beef cooked with its hide on
chicken stewed in a plough disc

pages.prompt: Your friend in the campo announces tonight's dinner
pages.translation: Tonight we're making chicken in the disc.
pages.explain: **Al disco** = cooked in the plough disc. **Con cuero** is for beef with the hide, and nobody cooks the plough itself.

classes.title: Dinner at ten
classes.summary: When Argentines eat, and how to behave at the table

pages.title: Four meals, odd hours
pages.body: The **desayuno** (breakfast) is tiny: a **café con leche** and some **tostadas**. The **almuerzo** (lunch) lands around one. Around five comes the **merienda**, a mini-breakfast with mate or coffee. And the **cena** (dinner)? Ten-ish. Book a restaurant for eight and you'll eat alone with the waiters.
pages.fun_fact: Invited to dinner at someone's home? Arriving 15 to 30 minutes late is normal. On the dot is early.

pages.statement: If friends invite you to dinner at their place "a las diez", showing up at twenty past ten is fine.
pages.explain: More than fine. Arriving a bit late to a dinner at someone's home is normal. Right at ten, you might catch the host still cooking.

pages.prompt: Match each meal to when Argentines have it
pages.explain: The merienda is what makes a 10 p.m. dinner survivable. Skip it and you'll be starving by eight.

pages.title: Nobody brings the bill
pages.body: In a restaurant the **mozo** (waiter) will never drop the check on your table uninvited. That would be like kicking you out. You ask for it: **"¿Me traés la cuenta?"**, or just catch their eye and pretend to write in the air. Until then the table is yours, and people stay for a long **sobremesa**, chatting over coffee.

pages.scenario: You've finished eating and you're in a hurry. The waiter walks past without stopping.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: They're waiting for you to ask
The bill comes by itself, later
pages.explain: Bringing the bill unasked is almost rude here. Say **"¿Me traés la cuenta, por favor?"** and it's on its way.

pages.title: Cubierto, propina, vaquita
pages.body: Many menus charge a **cubierto** per person: bread, water, the table setting. It is *not* a tip. The **propina** (tip) goes on top, usually about 10%. With friends, lots of dishes are ordered **para compartir** (to share, in the middle of the table), and the bill is split evenly. Or everyone throws in a share: that's **hacer una vaquita**.

pages.statement: If the bill says "cubierto", the tip is already included.
pages.explain: The **cubierto** pays for bread, water and the setting, and it doesn't necessarily reach the waiter. The **propina** is separate.

pages.scenario: Four friends at a pizzería. Someone looks at the menu and says: "¿Pedimos para compartir?"
pages.prompt: What are they suggesting?
pages.explain: Pizzas, empanadas, a **picada**: all for the middle. Say **dale** and grab a slice.

pages.prompt: The dinner is over and you want to pay.
pages.translation: Excuse me, can you bring me the bill?
pages.explain: **La cuenta** is the bill. Using **traés** (voseo) with the waiter is normal and friendly, not rude.

vocabulary.note: Moza for a woman.

example.en: Can you bring me the bill?
Shall we order something to share?

vocabulary.en: to chip in (everyone pays a share)

example.es: Hagamos una vaquita para las pizzas.
example.en: Let's all chip in for the pizzas.

glossary.en: lingering at the table after a meal

classes.title: Empanadas
classes.summary: Folds, provinces and a rivalry that never ends

pages.title: The national handheld
pages.body: An **empanada** is a half-moon of dough stuffed with filling, baked or fried. Every Argentine has a favorite place, a favorite filling and a grandma who does it better. You order them by the **docena** (dozen) or **media docena** (half dozen), for home, a party or a lazy Sunday night.
pages.fun_fact: The classic fillings: **carne**, **pollo**, **jamón y queso**, **humita** (creamy sweet corn) and **verdura**.

pages.title: The repulgue is a label
pages.body: The folded, braided edge is the **repulgue**. It seals the empanada, and it's also a code: each filling gets its own fold, so you can tell carne from pollo without biting. There's no national standard, though. Every shop and every grandma has its own system, so if it's not written on the box, just ask: **"¿Cuál es cuál?"**

pages.scenario: A dozen empanadas arrive in a box. Six have one kind of braided edge, six have another. Nothing is written on the box.
pages.prompt: What's the best move?
options: Bite one of each to find out
Assume the braided ones are carne
pages.explain: The repulgue codes change from shop to shop. Asking **¿cuál es cuál?** (which is which?) is totally normal. Biting and putting back is not.

pages.title: Salta vs Tucumán
pages.body: The northwest takes this very seriously. The **salteña** is small and juicy, with meat, egg, spring onion and little cubes of **papa** (potato). The **tucumana** says no to potato: knife-cut meat, onion, egg, cumin, and lots of juice. Each province claims it makes the best one, and neither will ever admit otherwise.

pages.title: Cortada a cuchillo
pages.body: On good menus you'll see **carne cortada a cuchillo**: beef chopped by hand instead of ground, so the filling stays juicy. Then the eternal question: **al horno** (baked) or **frita** (fried)? Baked is the everyday one in Buenos Aires; fried is a northern delicacy that stains your shirt. Either way, bite a corner first and let the steam out. They're full of hot juice.

pages.statement: A classic empanada tucumana has potato in it.
pages.explain: Potato is the **salteña** thing. Put potato in a tucumana and someone from Tucumán will politely explain why you're wrong for twenty minutes.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it means

pages.scenario: The first empanada of the night arrives straight from the oven. Your friend grabs it with their hand and bites a corner.
pages.prompt: Why a corner first?
options: It's bad luck to start in the middle
To let the hot juice out first
The corners are the best part
pages.explain: A good juicy empanada is basically soup in a pastry. People eat them with their hands, leaning over the plate, and up north they say a good one drips down to your elbow.

pages.prompt: Calling the empanada place to order for the family
pages.text: Hola, quería una ___ de carne y media de pollo.
pages.translation: Hi, I'd like a dozen beef and a half-dozen chicken.
pages.explain: Empanadas are counted in **docenas**. "**Quería**" (I wanted) is the polite, very Argentine way to order.

example.en: We ordered a dozen and a half.

classes.title: Pizza porteña
classes.summary: Thick, cheesy, eaten standing up, with fainá on top

pages.title: Not Naples, not New York
pages.body: Buenos Aires pizza is its own animal. The classic is **al molde** (in a pan): thick, fluffy dough buried under a scandalous amount of cheese. The thin, crispy style is **a la piedra**. The default order is a **muzza**, short for **muzzarella**: tomato sauce, cheese, a few green olives. Porteños will defend it against any Italian, with arguments and hand gestures.

pages.title: Fugazza and fugazzeta
pages.body: **Fugazza** is dough topped with a mountain of onion and oregano, no tomato. Add cheese and it's a **fugazzeta**. Pizzería **Banchero**, in La Boca, is credited with putting the cheese on. Then came the **fugazzeta rellena**: cheese *inside* the dough, onions on top. Heavy? Completely.

pages.prompt: Match the pizza word to what it is

pages.title: Fainá on top
pages.body: **Fainá** is a thin, flat bread made of chickpea flour, brought by Genoese immigrants (in Genoa it's *farinata*). Here people put a slice of it right on top of their pizza slice. That's a pizza **a caballo** (on horseback). Wash it down with a **moscato**, a sweet cheap wine, and you've got the old porteño trio: **moscato, pizza y fainá**.

pages.statement: In Buenos Aires, putting a slice of fainá on top of your pizza is normal.
pages.explain: Totally normal: it's pizza **a caballo**. In Genoa they'd look at you funny. On Avenida Corrientes nobody blinks.

pages.title: Standing at the counter
pages.body: **Avenida Corrientes** is the pizza street, and **Güerrín** is the famous one: a line out the door, and a choice between sitting down or eating **de parado** (standing up) at the **mostrador** (counter), a **porción** in your hand, before or after the theater. Eating de parado is faster, cheaper, and honestly more fun.

pages.scenario: It's 11 p.m. on Corrientes. The play just ended, there's no free table at Güerrín, and you're hungry.
pages.prompt: What do porteños do?
options: Wait an hour for a table
Eat a porción at the counter
pages.explain: Eating **de parado** at the mostrador is a classic. A **porción de muzza** and maybe a slice of fainá: done in ten minutes.

pages.prompt: Ordering at the counter
pages.text: Una porción de muzza y una de ___, por favor.
pages.translation: A slice of cheese pizza and one of fainá, please.
pages.explain: Pizza and fainá are ordered together all the time. Then you decide if it goes **a caballo**.

pages.scenario: Your friend orders "una fugazzeta rellena" for the table.
pages.prompt: What arrives?
options: Onion pizza, cheese inside the dough
Cheese pizza with ham on top
A pizza folded like an empanada
pages.explain: Cheese stuffed *inside*, a mountain of onion on top. Share it, or skip dinner tomorrow.

example.en: Shall we get a large cheese pizza?

example.es: Comimos de parado en la barra.
example.en: We ate standing at the counter.

vocabulary.en: with fainá on top (lit. on horseback)

vocabulary.note: The moscato-pizza-fainá combo is a bit old-school, but still loved.

classes.title: Nonna's kitchen
classes.summary: Milanesas, Sunday pasta and ñoquis on the 29th

pages.title: The milanesa
pages.body: A thin slice of beef, dipped in egg, coated in **pan rallado** (breadcrumbs), then fried or baked. It came with Italian immigrants and became *the* home-cooked dish; there's chicken too, and **soja** (soy) for vegetarians. **Milanesa con papas fritas** is what kids ask for on their birthday. In a roll it's a **sánguche de milanesa**, and with two fried eggs on top it's a milanesa **a caballo**.

pages.title: The napolitana
pages.body: A **milanesa a la napolitana** has tomato sauce, ham and melted cheese on top. The name comes from **Nápoli**, a restaurant across from the Luna Park stadium in Buenos Aires, around 1940. The legend: a cook burnt a milanesa and hid the damage under ham, cheese and sauce. Others say it was invented on purpose. Either way: 100% porteño.

pages.statement: The milanesa a la napolitana was invented in Naples, Italy.
pages.explain: It was born in Buenos Aires, at a restaurant called **Nápoli**. Order one in Naples and they'll have no idea what you mean.

pages.title: Sunday pasta and the tuco
pages.body: In many families, Sunday lunch means pasta at the grandparents': **ravioles**, **tallarines** (tagliatelle), **ñoquis**, with **tuco**, a tomato sauce simmered for hours, often with a piece of meat. Grandma and grandpa are **nona** and **nono**, straight from Italian. And the **sorrentinos**, big round stuffed pasta? Despite the name, most stories credit a family in **Mar del Plata**.

pages.title: Ñoquis del 29
pages.body: On the **29th** of every month, people eat **ñoquis** (gnocchi) with a banknote under the plate, for luck and money. One explanation: by the end of the month salaries had run out, and potato gnocchi were cheap. That's also why a **ñoqui** is someone on the public payroll who only shows up around the 29th, to get paid.

pages.scenario: It's the 29th. Your host serves ñoquis and slips a bill under your plate before you sit.
pages.prompt: What do you do with the money?
options: Give it back: it's not yours
Leave it there while you eat
Use it to pay for dinner
pages.explain: It stays under the plate during the meal, for luck. Afterwards, many people keep it in their wallet until next month.

pages.statement: Calling a public employee a "ñoqui" means they get paid without really working.
pages.explain: Exactly: they only show up around the 29th, to collect. It's a classic political insult, and nothing to do with pasta except the date.

pages.prompt: Match the dish to what it is
pairs: milanesa with fried eggs on top

pages.prompt: Your friend is vegetarian and the menu has one option for them.
pages.text: Para mí, una milanesa de ___ con puré.
pages.translation: For me, a soy milanesa with mashed potatoes.
pages.explain: **Milanesa de soja** is everywhere, cheap and a vegetarian lifesaver.

example.es: Los domingos comemos en lo de la nona.

classes.title: Stews and corn
classes.summary: Winter pots, patriotic locro and corn in its husk

pages.title: Locro, the patriotic stew
pages.body: **Locro** is a thick stew of white corn, beans, squash and several meats (pork, chorizo, beef). It comes from the Andes, from long before Argentina existed. On **25 de mayo** and **9 de julio**, families, clubs and neighborhoods make huge pots of it. Spoon on the **quiquirimichi**, a red, spicy fat with paprika and chili.

pages.scenario: It's the 25th of May. Your neighbors invite you to the club and ask you to bring a container.
pages.prompt: What are you most likely eating?
pages.explain: Clubs and parishes often sell **locro** by the portion on patriotic dates, and people take it home in their own tupper.

pages.statement: Locro was invented in Buenos Aires by Italian immigrants.
pages.explain: It's Andean, and much older than Argentina. The immigrants brought the pasta; the locro was already here.

pages.title: Carbonada in a pumpkin
pages.body: The **carbonada** is a stew of beef, squash, corn and sweet potato, often with dried peaches for a sweet touch. The showstopper version is served inside a whole baked pumpkin, and you scrape the walls as you eat. On a cold night, any **guiso** (stew) at home will do.

pages.title: Corn in its own wrapper
pages.body: From the northwest come the **choclo** (corn) classics. The star is **humita en chala**: fresh corn grated into a sweet paste, wrapped in the corn's own husk, the **chala**, tied up and boiled. You unwrap it at the table like a present. Same humita you find inside empanadas, just in its natural packaging.

pages.prompt: Match the dish to its description
pairs: corn paste in a corn husk

pages.prompt: Winter just arrived. What's for dinner?
pages.text: Con este frío, se viene un ___.
pages.translation: With this cold, it's stew time.
pages.explain: **Guiso** season. Often in the diminutive: **un guisito**, which somehow makes it cozier.

example.es: Con este frío, se viene un guisito.
example.en: With this cold, it's stew time.
