corn on the cob, sweet corn
sweet corn paste boiled in its wrapper

classes.title: Helado
classes.summary: Italian roots, flavors called gustos, and ice cream by the kilo

pages.title: Helado, all year round
pages.body: Thanks to Italian immigrants, Argentina has some of the best **helado** (ice cream) outside Italy. There are thousands of **heladerías** (gelato shops), and people eat it even in winter. Flavors are called **gustos**. You pick a **cucurucho** (cone) or a **vasito** (small cup): the small ones take two gustos, the bigger ones three or four.

pages.scenario: At the heladería, the guy behind the counter asks: "¿Qué gustos?"
pages.prompt: What does he want to know?
pages.explain: **Gusto** means flavor. "Dulce de leche y limón" is a perfectly good answer.

pages.title: By the kilo, delivered
pages.body: The real move is ordering helado to your door, packed in a foam box: **un cuarto** (a quarter kilo), **medio** (half) or **un kilo**. Late at night, after dinner, for the whole family, even in July. Up to four gustos fit in a kilo, and a kilo is about right for four people.

pages.scenario: Four friends, after dinner at your place. You're ordering helado to the door.
pages.prompt: What size do you ask for?
pages.explain: **Un kilo** for four. Un cuarto is for one person with self-control, and a vasito is for a walk in the park.

pages.title: The flavors to try
pages.body: A porteño favorite is **dulce de leche granizado**: dulce de leche ice cream with chocolate flakes. Then there's **sambayón**, from the Italian *zabaione*: egg yolks, sugar and wine. A grown-up flavor. Order both, and add a fruit one so you can say you ate something healthy.

pages.statement: Sambayón is a flavor made with egg yolks, sugar and wine.
pages.explain: Right, it's the Italian *zabaione* turned into helado. Your abuelo's favorite, probably.

pages.prompt: At the counter, order a cone with the porteño favorite
pages.text: Un cucurucho de dulce de leche ___, por favor.
pages.translation: A cone of dulce de leche with chocolate flakes, please.
pages.explain: **Granizado** = with chocolate flakes. You'll order it again tomorrow.

example.en: Which flavors do you want?
I ordered a quarter kilo of ice cream.

glossary.en: dulce de leche with chocolate flakes

sections.title: Alfajores y dulces
sections.summary: Dulce de leche, kioscos and the snack that runs on sugar

classes.title: Dulce de leche and friends
classes.summary: The spread on everything, and the sweets it hangs out with

pages.title: The brown gold
pages.body: **Dulce de leche** is milk and sugar cooked slowly for hours until it turns thick, brown and caramel-y. We put it on a **tostada** (toast), in cakes, in alfajores, on a spoon straight from the jar at midnight. On everything? **Obvio** (obviously). Just don't call it caramel. Say that to an Argentine and watch their face fall.

pages.title: The legend
pages.body: The story goes like this: 1829, a ranch in Cañuelas. Rosas, the strongman governor, meets his rival Lavalle to sign a truce. A maid is heating milk with sugar, gets distracted by the drama, forgets the pot, and finds it turned into dulce de leche. Cute story. Almost certainly a legend: Uruguay, Chile, France and others claim it too.

pages.statement: Uruguay also claims dulce de leche as its own invention.
pages.explain: It does, loudly. The Cañuelas story is a legend, and similar milk sweets existed in plenty of places. Just enjoy it.

pages.title: Clásico vs repostero
pages.body: At the supermarket you'll see two kinds. **Clásico** (or **familiar**) is soft and spreadable — for toast and the spoon. **Repostero** is thicker and firmer, made for baking: it holds its shape inside alfajores and cakes without dripping everywhere. **Repostería** means pastry-making, hence the name.

pages.scenario: You're making alfajores and the filling keeps oozing out the sides.
pages.prompt: What did you buy wrong?
pages.explain: Repostero is firmer and stays put. Clásico is for the tostada and the spoon.

pages.title: The supporting cast
pages.body: **Chocotorta**: Chocolinas cookies dipped in milk, layered with dulce de leche mixed with cream cheese. No oven, every birthday. **Pastafrola**: a tart with a lattice top, filled with membrillo or **batata** (sweet potato) jam. **Mantecol**: a peanut nougat bar people get weirdly emotional about. **Bon o Bon**: a little chocolate bonbon with peanut cream, a kiosco staple.

pages.prompt: Match the sweet to what it is
pairs: lattice tart with quince or sweet potato jam

pages.prompt: Your friend asks if you want dulce de leche on your toast. Of course you do.
pages.translation: With dulce de leche, obviously.
pages.explain: **Obvio** is how we say "obviously". And for the toast, it's always obvio.

example.es: Le pongo dulce de leche a todo.
example.en: I put dulce de leche on everything.

classes.title: What is an alfajor?
classes.summary: Two cookies, dulce de leche in the middle, and a thousand years of history

pages.title: The national snack
pages.body: An **alfajor** is two soft cookies (**tapas**, literally "lids") stuck together with a **relleno** (filling), usually **dulce de leche**, and often dipped in chocolate. That's it. That's the whole religion. We eat them at the office, on the bus, after football, in the middle of the night. If an Argentine offers you half their alfajor, that's basically friendship.
pages.fun_fact: Industry estimates say Argentines eat around six million alfajores a day. Nobody has counted properly — we were busy eating.

pages.title: Not born here, though
pages.body: Plot twist: the alfajor isn't Argentine by birth. The word comes from Andalusian Arabic, and in Muslim Spain (al-Ándalus) it was a honey, almond and spice sweet. It's still made in Andalucía today. The Spanish brought the name to the Americas, and here it turned into cookies plus dulce de leche.

pages.statement: The alfajor was invented in Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: The name and the idea come from al-Ándalus, Muslim Spain. Argentina just made it its own — and, humbly, perfected it.

pages.title: The family tree
pages.body: Each region has its own. **Alfajor de maicena**: crumbly cornstarch cookies, dulce de leche, edges rolled in **coco rallado** (grated coconut) — the homemade one your abuela makes. **Marplatense**: chocolate-coated, from Mar del Plata, the classic kiosco one. **Santafesino**: crunchy layers with a white sugar glaze. **Cordobés**: soft, glazed, often filled with fruit jam.

pages.prompt: Match the alfajor to what makes it special
pairs: soft and filled with fruit jam
dipped in chocolate, the kiosco classic

pages.title: More is more
pages.body: Then there's the **triple**: three tapas, two layers of dulce de leche. More alfajor per alfajor. The **simple** is the regular two-tapa one. And the **alfajor de fruta** swaps the dulce de leche for **membrillo** (quince paste) or other jams — the cordobés tradition. Ask for one at a kiosco and you'll hear: "¿Simple o triple?"

pages.scenario: At the kiosco you ask for an alfajor. The kiosquero asks: "¿Simple o triple?"
pages.prompt: What's the difference?
options: One alfajor or a pack of three
pages.explain: **Simple** = two tapas, **triple** = three, with double the dulce de leche. Skipped lunch? You know what to say.

pages.prompt: Your friend from Córdoba hands you an alfajor filled with quince paste. What's inside?
pages.translation: It has a quince paste filling.
pages.explain: **Membrillo** is quince paste. **Maicena** is the cornstarch in the cookies, and the **tapa** is the cookie itself.

example.en: Can I have an alfajor?

example.es: Mi abuela hace alfajores de maicena.
example.en: My grandma makes cornstarch alfajores.
Give me a triple, please.

classes.title: Brands, kioscos and the eternal debate
classes.summary: Havanna or Jorgito? Pick a side at the kiosco on the corner

pages.title: The kiosco
pages.body: Every block has one. A **kiosco** is a tiny shop — sometimes just a window — selling candy, drinks, cigarettes, phone credit and, above all, alfajores. Many stay open late; some never close (look for the **24 hs** sign). The bigger ones are **maxikioscos**. The person behind the counter is the **kiosquero**. Just point and say **¿me das…?** (can I have…?).
pages.fun_fact: The **ventanita** kiosco is literally a window in someone's house. Knock, ask, pay, done.

pages.scenario: It's 1am, you're walking home from a party and you desperately want something sweet.
pages.prompt: Where do you go?
pages.explain: The kiosco. Late hours are its whole personality. Look for the light on and the "24 hs" sign.

pages.title: The heavyweights
pages.body: Three names to know. **Havanna**, from Mar del Plata, is the fancy one: the box you bring as a **regalo** (gift). **Jorgito** and **Guaymallén** are the everyday kiosco buy: cheap, humble, legendary. And **Fantoche** is famous for its triple. There are dozens more, and every Argentine has a favorite.

pages.scenario: You're meeting your Argentine partner's family for the first time, and you pass through Mar del Plata on the way.
pages.prompt: What do you bring as a regalo?
pages.explain: A box of Havanna is the classic gift. Guaymallén is beloved, but it's a coins-in-your-pocket snack, not a meet-the-parents gift.

pages.title: The debate that never ends
pages.body: Ask a table of Argentines "which is the best alfajor?" and clear your afternoon. Some swear by Havanna. Others say it's overpriced, and the real deal is a Jorgito or an **alfajor blanco**, covered in white sugar glaze instead of chocolate, like the Guaymallén blanco. There is no right answer. Well — there is, it's yours, and everyone else is wrong.
pages.fun_fact: There's even a Campeonato Mundial del Alfajor, held in Buenos Aires. A "world" championship for our own snack: peak Argentina.

pages.statement: An alfajor blanco is dipped in white chocolate.
pages.explain: It's a white **sugar glaze**, crunchy and sweet. White chocolate is a different, fancier thing.

pages.prompt: At the kiosco, you want two alfajores. Ask for them.
pages.translation: Can I have two alfajores?
pages.explain: **¿Me das…?** with **vos** is the natural, friendly way to ask. The other two would mean "do you owe me" and "do you read me".

vocabulary.en: corner shop for candy, drinks and snacks

example.en: I'm going to the kiosco, want anything?

vocabulary.en: a supersized one, almost a mini-market

vocabulary.note: Read 'veinticuatro horas'.

vocabulary.en: one with a white sugar glaze

example.en: I brought you Havanna as a gift.
Can I have a Jorgito?

classes.title: Facturas: anarchy at the bakery
classes.summary: Medialunas, bolas de fraile and the rebel bakers who named them

pages.title: What are facturas?
pages.body: **Facturas** are the pastries you buy at the **panadería** (bakery), usually by the **docena** (dozen) in a paper bag. They're the official partner of mate. Afternoon at a friend's place? Someone shows up with a dozen facturas. It's the law. (Yes, "factura" also means invoice. Context helps.)

pages.scenario: Your friend texts: "Venite a tomar mate a las 5."
pages.prompt: What do you bring?
pages.explain: Facturas. Mate at 5pm plus a dozen facturas is the most Argentine afternoon there is. Wine is for the asado.

pages.title: Manteca or grasa?
pages.body: The queen is the **medialuna** ("half-moon", a small croissant). Two kinds: **de manteca** (butter) — sweeter, glazed, curved; and **de grasa** (beef fat) — drier, a little salty, usually straight. You order them by name: "media docena de manteca". Debating which is better is another national sport.

pages.statement: A medialuna de grasa is the sweet, glazed one made with butter.
pages.explain: That's the **de manteca**. **Grasa** means fat — beef fat — and those are saltier and less sweet.

pages.title: Rebel bakers
pages.body: In 1887 Buenos Aires bakers, many of them Italian and Spanish anarchists, founded their first union. The story goes that they named pastries to mock the powers of the day: the **vigilante** (police) is long like a cop's baton; **bolas de fraile** ("friar's balls") and **suspiros de monja** ("nun's sighs") poke the Church; **cañoncitos** ("little cannons") and **bombas** the army.
pages.fun_fact: Historians debate how much of this is documented, but it's the story every baker will tell you.

pages.prompt: Match the factura to who it teases

pages.title: Order like a local
pages.body: At the panadería you ask for a mix: **una docena surtida**, a dozen assorted. Or you pick: "Seis medialunas y seis facturas". **Bolas de fraile** are fried dough balls filled with dulce de leche or pastry cream. **Cañoncitos** are puff pastry tubes filled with dulce de leche. Last one left? Be nice: **comela vos** (you eat it).

pages.prompt: You want twelve mixed facturas. Ask the baker.
pages.translation: An assorted dozen, please.
pages.explain: **Surtida** = assorted. The baker picks a bit of everything, and you look like you've lived here for years.

pages.scenario: At the table, only one factura is left. Your friend says "dale, comela vos".
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: They're offering you the last one
They're asking you to split it
They want you to pay for them
pages.explain: **Dale, comela vos** = "Go on, you eat it." The last factura is a sacred and delicate thing. Accept gracefully.

example.en: I'll bring pastries for the mate.
An assorted dozen, please.

classes.title: ¿Qué hay de postre?
classes.summary: Flan, panqueques, arroz con leche and the rest of the abuela's menu

pages.title: The question after lunch
pages.body: Sunday lunch is over, and someone asks the big one: **¿qué hay de postre?** (what's for dessert?). At home or at a **bodegón** (old-school neighborhood restaurant), the answers are homemade classics: **flan**, **budín de pan**, **panqueques**, **arroz con leche**. Too full? The magic words are **un poquito nomás** (just a little bit).

pages.title: Flan mixto
pages.body: **Flan** is egg custard with a caramel top. Here it rarely comes alone: you get it with a fat spoonful of dulce de leche, with **crema** (whipped cream), or with both, which is a flan **mixto**. On menus, **flan casero** means house-made, and it's the thing to order at a bodegón.

pages.scenario: At a bodegón, the mozo asks: "¿El flan con crema, con dulce o mixto?"
pages.prompt: What is "mixto"?
pages.explain: **Mixto** = both toppings. It's the correct answer. The mozo won't say it, but he's proud of you.

pages.prompt: Before ordering, check that the flan is house-made
pages.translation: Is the flan homemade?
pages.explain: **Casero** = homemade. If the answer is yes, order it. If it's no, order it anyway, but with less joy.

pages.title: Panqueques and arroz con leche
pages.body: **Panqueques** here are thin crêpes, rolled around dulce de leche. Some parrillas serve them **quemados**, with sugar burnt crunchy on top. **Arroz con leche** is rice pudding: rice slowly cooked in milk with sugar, lemon peel and cinnamon. Every kid knows the song that starts **"Arroz con leche, me quiero casar…"**

pages.title: Nothing gets wasted
pages.body: **Budín de pan** is bread pudding made from yesterday's bread, milk, eggs and caramel: immigrant thrift turned into dessert. And the cheapest classic is the **postre vigilante**, also just **queso y dulce**: a slice of cheese with **membrillo** (quince paste) or **batata** (sweet-potato paste). Not the bakery pastry: a different cop story, about police ordering it at bodegones because it cost almost nothing.

pages.scenario: The bodegón menu says "postre vigilante".
pages.prompt: What arrives at your table?
options: A long pastry from the bakery
pages.explain: **Queso y dulce**: cheese and fruit paste, one bite of each. Cheap, simple, perfect. The long pastry is the *factura* vigilante.

pages.prompt: Match the dessert to what it is
pairs: custard with dulce de leche and cream
cheese with quince or sweet-potato paste
rice cooked in milk with cinnamon

pages.scenario: You're full after a huge lunch, but the abuela brings out a tray of homemade flan.
pages.prompt: What's the smart move?
pages.explain: Turning down the abuela's flan is a small tragedy. **Un poquito nomás** keeps everyone happy.

example.en: What's for dessert?
Is the flan homemade?

glossary.en: cheese with quince or sweet-potato paste

sections.title: Fútbol
sections.summary: Not a sport here. A religion with a fixture list.

classes.title: ¿De qué cuadro sos?
classes.summary: The five big clubs, the Superclásico and the question you can't dodge

pages.title: The question
pages.body: Meet someone new in Buenos Aires and within ten minutes you'll hear: **¿De qué cuadro sos?** — *Which team are you?* A **cuadro** is a club. It's not small talk: your club is inherited from your dad, your grandpa, your barrio. People change jobs, partners, even countries. Changing clubs? Never. **Cambiar de cuadro** is basically treason.
pages.fun_fact: Plenty of babies are signed up as club members (**socios**) days after being born.

pages.title: Los cinco grandes
pages.body: Five clubs are called **los cinco grandes** — *the big five*: **Boca Juniors**, **River Plate**, **Independiente**, **Racing Club** and **San Lorenzo**. They have the most fans and, historically, the most titles. Everyone else is a *chico* (small club) — though say that to a fan of Vélez or Estudiantes and you'll get a long lecture.

pages.scenario: A taxi driver asks: "¿De qué cuadro sos?" You don't follow football at all.
pages.prompt: What's the smoothest answer?
options: "Boca, obvio." and hope for the best
pages.explain: Turning the question back is gold: he'll happily talk for the whole ride. Faking a team works until he asks for your favorite player, and "football is boring" kills the conversation.

pages.title: El Superclásico
pages.body: **Boca vs River** is the **Superclásico**. A **clásico** is any derby; this one gets the *super*. Boca, in blue and gold, plays at **La Bombonera** (*the chocolate box*), its **cancha** (stadium) in La Boca. River, white with a red sash, plays at **El Monumental** in Núñez. Funny detail: River was also born in La Boca and moved north later. Neighbors first, enemies forever. Golden rule: never wear one team's colors near the other's cancha.
pages.fun_fact: They once met in a Copa Libertadores final so heated that the second leg had to be played in Madrid. River won.

pages.statement: Boca and River were born in different parts of the city.
pages.explain: Both started in La Boca. River only moved north to Núñez later, which is why the rivalry feels like a family feud.

pages.title: Insults with pride
pages.body: Rivals give each other nasty nicknames, and fans end up wearing them proudly. River fans call Boca fans **bosteros** (from **bosta**, *manure* — the story goes it was a dig at the smell by the Riachuelo). Boca fans call River fans **gallinas** (*chickens*, as in cowards), a name that stuck after River blew a big final. San Lorenzo fans are **cuervos** (*crows*), after the priest who founded the club.

pages.statement: If a River fan calls you a "bostero", they think you support Boca.
pages.explain: Exactly. And if you *do* support Boca, the correct reply is a proud smile. Being **bostero** is a badge of honor for them.

pages.title: Avellaneda: two stadiums, one block
pages.body: Just south of the city, in **Avellaneda**, live **Racing** (light blue and white) and **Independiente** (red). Their stadiums are only a few hundred meters apart — you can see one from the other. That's the **clásico de Avellaneda**. Independiente fans are the **Diablos Rojos**, *Red Devils*. Imagine sharing a street with the one team you hate most.

pages.prompt: Match the club to its shirt
pages.explain: Handy on match day: now you know which shirt not to wear in which barrio.

pages.scenario: You're staying in La Boca and a friend lends you a red-and-white River shirt because it's cold. You're about to walk to the kiosk next to the Bombonera on match day.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Wear it, it's just a shirt
Wear it, but say you're a tourist
pages.explain: Never wear the rival's colors in the wrong barrio, especially on match day. Best case: jokes and dirty looks. Worst case: you really don't want to find out.

pages.prompt: Ask your new friend which team they support
pages.translation: Which team are you (a fan of)?
pages.explain: **Cuadro** is the everyday word for club. A **cuadra** is a city block, and the **cancha** is the stadium: useful words, but not here.

example.en: Which team do you support?

vocabulary.note: Boca, River, Independiente, Racing, San Lorenzo.

vocabulary.en: Boca fan (rivals' insult, worn with pride)

vocabulary.note: Don't say it to a River fan unless you're friends.

example.en: Shall we go to the match on Sunday?

classes.title: La hinchada
classes.summary: Chants, drums, the mysterious thing called aguante, and how to actually get in

pages.title: Hincha, not fan
pages.body: A fan is a **hincha**, and all the fans together are **la hinchada**. The story goes that the word comes from a man in Montevideo who inflated (**hinchar**) the balls and shouted so hard he became famous. Whatever the origin: a hincha doesn't *watch* a match. A hincha *plays* it from the stands.
pages.fun_fact: **Hinchar** also means to annoy. "No me hinchés" = "Stop bugging me."

pages.title: Cantitos and the bombo
pages.body: The stands never go quiet. The hinchada sings **cantitos** (chants) for the whole match, often to the tune of old rock or cumbia songs, mixing love for the club with creative insults for the rival. The **bombo**, a big bass drum, keeps the beat, and **trapos** (banners) hang everywhere. The heart of it all is the **popular**: the cheap standing terraces.

pages.statement: In the popular, most people watch the match from their seats.
pages.explain: Seats? In the **popular** people stand, jump, sing and push for the whole match. Clapping politely is for tennis.

pages.title: El aguante
pages.body: **Aguante** comes from **aguantar**, *to endure*. For a hincha it means loyalty that survives everything: rain, losses, even relegation. "**¡Aguante Racing!**" is roughly *Come on, Racing!* You also hear it outside football: "**¡Aguante el asado!**" The team can be losing 3–0 and the hinchada still sings — that's aguante.

pages.prompt: Cheer for your team, rioplatense style
pages.translation: Come on, Boca! (lit. "endurance, Boca!")
pages.explain: **¡Aguante…!** + anything you love. *¡Basta, Boca!* means "enough, Boca!", and *¡Cuidado, Boca!* is a warning.

pages.title: So you want to go to a match
pages.body: Here's the catch: at the big clubs, most tickets go to **socios** (paying club members), and they sell out fast. Most visitors go with an official tour package: ticket, transport and a guide who knows which gate is yours. Skip the guys selling tickets outside the stadium, since fakes are common. And leave anything in rival colors at the hotel.

pages.scenario: You want to see Boca at La Bombonera, but the club's website says tickets are for socios only.
pages.prompt: What's your best bet?
options: Buy from a guy outside the stadium
Show up and ask at the gate
pages.explain: It costs more, but you get a real ticket and someone who knows the way in. Street tickets are often fake, and the gate won't sell you one.

pages.title: The dark side: barras bravas
pages.body: Every big club has a **barra brava** (or just **la barra**): the organized hardcore group that leads the chants and carries the drums. Many are also tangled up in violence and shady business — ticket resale, parking, politics. After years of deaths, visiting fans were banned. Talk of bringing them back comes up again and again, but at most league games you'll still see only one hinchada.

pages.scenario: At the stadium, a guy from the barra walks past and tells your section to stand up and sing.
pages.prompt: What's the smart move?
options: Explain that you paid for your seat
Stand up and at least pretend to sing
Tell him to sit down himself
pages.explain: You're a guest in their church. Stand, clap, hum along. Arguing with the barra, or telling them off, is never a good plan.

pages.prompt: Match the word to the thing
pages.explain: **Trapo** literally means *rag*. For the barras, losing your trapo to a rival is the ultimate humiliation.

pages.statement: When a team gets relegated, its hinchada usually keeps filling the stadium in the lower division.
pages.explain: That's aguante: the bad times are exactly when it counts. Relegated big clubs often sell out their stadiums a division below.

vocabulary.en: a club's whole crowd in the stands

example.en: Come on Independiente!

vocabulary.note: Often just "la barra".

example.en: Stop bugging me.

classes.title: Talk like a hincha
classes.summary: Golazos, gambetas, caños and the Sunday picado

pages.title: Potrero and picado
pages.body: Argentines say their football was born in the **potrero** — a dirt lot where kids play with a ball, a couple of stones as goalposts and zero rules. A casual game with friends is a **picado**. "¿Armamos un picado?" = *Shall we get a game together?* Today it's usually **fútbol 5** on synthetic grass, then beers.
pages.fun_fact: Calling a player "**de potrero**" is a big compliment: street-smart, creative, fearless.

pages.title: Gambeta and caño
pages.body: A **gambeta** is a dribble, the twisty, dancing kind Maradona and Messi made famous. A **caño** is a nutmeg: the ball between the defender's legs. Getting a caño in a picado means your friends will remind you for weeks. And a **golazo** is a stunning goal. The **-azo** ending makes anything bigger: **golazo**, **partidazo**.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning

pages.scenario: In a picado, you slip the ball between the legs of your friend Nacho and run past him. Everyone screams.
pages.prompt: What did you just do?
pages.explain: **¡Caño!** No goal yet, and the picado is the whole game. Nacho will now be teased until the next one. Maybe longer.

pages.title: El DT and the hachero
pages.body: The coach is **el DT** (*de-té*), short for **director técnico**. Every Argentine is secretly a DT: they all know who should play. Lionel Scaloni, the DT who won in Qatar, even gave the team its nickname: **la Scaloneta**. And the defender who kicks everything in sight, ball or ankles? A **hachero**, an *axe man*.

pages.statement: In Argentina, "el DT" is the team's doctor.
pages.explain: **DT** = **director técnico**, the coach. The doctor is just *el médico*, and nobody at the bar has opinions about him.

pages.title: Hacer la previa
pages.body: Before any big match you **hacer la previa**: meet up earlier to eat, drink, sing and get in the mood. The previa can last longer than the match itself. After the game, there's analysis at the bar until late. And on Monday comes the **gastada**: the teasing from rival fans if you lost. You take it, and you pay it back when you win. Watching football alone? Suspicious behavior.

pages.prompt: Invite your friends to meet up before the Superclásico
pages.translation: Shall we do the pre-match hangout at my place?
pages.explain: The **previa** is the before. The **gastada** is Monday's teasing, and the **cancha** is where the match is played.

pages.statement: Calling a player "de potrero" is a dig: it means he never learned to play properly.
pages.explain: It's a big compliment: street-smart, creative, fearless. For Argentines, the potrero is where the best ones learned.

pages.scenario: Your team lost 4–0. Your Argentine friend's phone keeps buzzing with memes from rival fans.
pages.prompt: What's the local tradition here?
options: Mute the group and hide for a week
Take it, and pay it back when you win
Tell them it's only a game, relax
pages.explain: The **gastada** is part of the deal. You take it, you keep a list, and you pay it back with interest. "It's only a game" is the one answer nobody here accepts.

example.en: Shall we get a game together?

vocabulary.en: dirt lot where kids play football
to hang out before an event

example.es: Hacemos la previa en lo de Juan.
example.en: We're meeting at Juan's place first.

glossary.en: the national team, after coach Scaloni

classes.title: The table, the drop and the VAR
classes.summary: Promedios, irse a la B and everything you'll hear on TV

pages.title: Fixture, fecha, tabla
pages.body: The season calendar is the **fixture** (say *fíxtur*), and each round is a **fecha**. After every fecha people check the **tabla** (league table): three points for a win, one for an **empate** (draw). A 5–0 is a **goleada** (thrashing). On Monday, the office talks about nothing else.

pages.title: The nightmare: el descenso
pages.body: The worst thing that can happen to a club is the **descenso** (relegation), or **irse a la B**, going down to the B. The dream of the smaller clubs is the **ascenso** (promotion). Even giants fall: four of the big five have gone down, River most painfully, in 2011. **Boca** never has, and Boca fans never let anyone forget it.

pages.statement: Of the big five, Boca is the only club that has never gone down.
pages.explain: San Lorenzo, Racing, River and Independiente all went down at some point. It's Boca's favorite chant against every one of them.

pages.title: Promedios
pages.body: Here's a very Argentine twist: relegation isn't only about this season. Part of it depends on the **promedio**, your points per match averaged over the last three seasons. One great year can't save a struggling club, and one bad year rarely sinks a big one. Critics have long said that's exactly the point: to protect the big clubs. The rules change often; the promedios keep coming back.

pages.scenario: Your team is fifth this season, but your friend is still nervous about "los promedios".
pages.prompt: Why?
options: The VAR can take points away
pages.explain: Promedios drag the past along with you. A club that just came up is especially at risk: it has only a few matches to average, so every loss hurts.

pages.title: ¿Fue penal?
pages.body: Every tight call now goes to **el VAR** (say *el var*), and the debate lasts days: **¿fue penal?** (was it a penalty?), **¿estaba en offside?** Old-timers still say **orsai**, the way their grandparents pronounced offside. Some say the VAR killed the goal scream, since you wait before celebrating. Others say the ref was robbing us anyway, so at least now it's on camera.

pages.prompt: Match the TV word to its meaning
Your friend is worried before the last match of the season.
pages.text: Si perdemos, nos vamos a la ___.
pages.translation: If we lose, we go down.
pages.explain: **Irse a la B** = get relegated. Said with real fear, even when the second division isn't literally called 'B' anymore. *La A* would be going up.

pages.statement: If an old-timer yells "¡orsai!" at the TV, he wants a penalty.
pages.explain: **Orsai** is offside, said the way his grandparents said it. For a penalty he'd yell **¡penal!**, and then argue about it until Thursday.

example.es: ¿Contra quién jugamos en la próxima fecha?
example.en: Who do we play in the next round?

vocabulary.en: to go down to the second division (lit. "go to the B")

example.es: Si perdemos, nos vamos a la B.
example.en: If we lose, we go down.

vocabulary.note: Old-fashioned; today most people say offside.

classes.title: Diego, 1986 and the pioneers
classes.summary: A World Cup with a shadow, the Hand of God, and the women who beat England first

pages.title: La Selección
pages.body: When Argentina plays, the whole country stops. The national team is **la Selección**, or **la Albiceleste** (*the white and sky-blue*). Club rivalries freeze for ninety minutes: a Boca fan and a River fan hug when Argentina scores. The team has won three **Mundiales** (World Cups): **1978**, **1986** and **2022**.

pages.title: 1978: a cup with a shadow
pages.body: Argentina hosted and won the **1978** Mundial. But the country was under a military dictatorship that used the cup as propaganda while people were disappearing. The players are respected; the cup itself still makes many Argentines uneasy, and some results remain under suspicion that was never proven. If it comes up, listen more than you talk.

pages.statement: Most Argentines remember the 1978 win as a purely happy moment.
pages.explain: The dictatorship makes 1978 a sore, debated topic. Plenty of people feel torn about celebrating it. Tread gently.

pages.title: Diego
pages.body: **Diego Armando Maradona** grew up poor in Villa Fiorito and became the greatest idol the country has ever had. He wore the **10**, so he's **el Diez**, or simply **el Diego**. You'll see his face on murals all over the city. Some fans even joke about the *Iglesia Maradoniana*, a fan "church" with its own Christmas on his birthday.

pages.title: Mexico 1986 vs England
pages.body: Mexico, **1986**: a quarter-final against England, four years after the **Malvinas** (Falklands) war. Diego punches the ball in and the goal stands: **la Mano de Dios**, *the Hand of God*. Many call it **viveza criolla**, street-smart cunning. Minutes later he dribbles past half the English team: **el Gol del Siglo**, *the Goal of the Century*. Argentina then beat West Germany in the final.
pages.fun_fact: Radio commentator Víctor Hugo Morales screamed "¡Barrilete cósmico!" — *cosmic kite* — and it became legend.

pages.scenario: An English friend at an asado says: "Maradona cheated, that's it." Everyone goes quiet.
pages.prompt: How do most Argentines see the Mano de Dios?
options: A shameful moment they'd rather forget
Viveza criolla, with a bit of revenge
A clean goal the referee got right
pages.explain: For many it's cheeky cunning and a symbolic revenge after Malvinas. Plenty of people also admit it was a handball. Expect a passionate debate, not agreement.

pages.prompt: What's the famous handball called?
pages.translation: The Hand of God
pages.explain: **Mano** = hand. It's feminine even though it ends in -o: *la mano*. A foot (*pie*) or a head (*cabeza*) would have been legal.

pages.statement: Argentina won the 1986 Mundial by beating West Germany in the final.
pages.explain: 3–2 at the Azteca. Jorge Burruchaga scored the winner, after a pass from — who else — Diego.

pages.title: Same stadium, fifteen years earlier
pages.body: Diego wasn't the first Argentine to shine against England at Mexico City's **Estadio Azteca**. In 1971, at an unofficial women's World Cup, Argentina's women beat England there, and **Elba Selva** scored all four goals. That match day, 21 August, is now the **Día de la Futbolista**, the Day of the Woman Footballer.

pages.statement: At that 1971 match in Mexico, England's women beat Argentina.
pages.explain: Argentina won 4–1, all four by Elba Selva — fifteen years before Diego's famous goals against England at the same stadium.

pages.prompt: Tell your friend what 21 August is
pages.text: Hoy es el Día de la ___.
pages.translation: Today is the Day of the (Woman) Footballer.
pages.explain: **Futbolista** works for men and women; **la futbolista** is a woman who plays.

vocabulary.en: the Hand of God (1986 handball goal)

example.en: We won the '86 World Cup.

example.es: Es futbolista y juega en Boca.
example.en: She's a footballer and plays for Boca.

classes.title: Messi and Qatar
classes.summary: Heartbreak in Brazil, glory in Qatar

pages.title: The quiet kid from Rosario
pages.body: **Lionel Messi** grew up in **Rosario** and left for Barcelona as a kid. For years some Argentines grumbled that he didn't sing the anthem and only shone in Spain. He grew up a **Newell's** fan, and he's **la Pulga** (*the flea*) for being small. That grumbling is now very, very dead.

pages.title: So close
pages.body: The **2014** World Cup final, in Brazil: Germany scored late in extra time and won 1–0. Messi, named best player of the tournament, walked past the trophy he couldn't touch, and that photo still hurts here. Two more lost Copa América finals followed, and Messi briefly quit **la Selección**, the national team.

pages.statement: After those lost finals, Messi quit the national team for a while.
pages.explain: Briefly. Half the country begged him to come back, and he did. Good call.

pages.title: Qatar 2022
pages.body: The final against France was madness: Argentina up 2–0, France levels, Messi scores in extra time, France levels again. Then **penales** (penalties). **Dibu Martínez**, the **arquero** (*goalkeeper*), saves one, and **Gonzalo Montiel** scores the last. Messi finally lifts the cup.
pages.fun_fact: The celebration in Buenos Aires drew millions of people — the Obelisco disappeared under a sea of shirts.

pages.statement: In the Qatar final, France came back from two goals down.
pages.explain: Twice, in fact: from 2–0 and again from 3–2. Many Argentines say they didn't breathe for about three hours.

pages.title: Muchachos
pages.body: The soundtrack of Qatar was a cantito: **"Muchachos, ahora nos volvimos a ilusionar"** — *Guys, now we've got our hopes up again*. Fans wrote it to the tune of a song by the band La Mosca. It name-checks Malvinas, Diego and Leo. Sing it at any party and the whole room joins in.

pages.prompt: Start the Qatar song and see who joins in
pages.translation: Guys, now we've got our hopes up again.
pages.explain: **Ilusionarse** = to get your hopes up. *Enojar* (get angry) and *dormir* (sleep) would make a very different World Cup.

pages.title: Cábala and mufa
pages.body: Argentines take luck seriously. A **cábala** is your lucky ritual: same seat, same socks, same mate. If the team wins, you change NOTHING. And the friend who always seems to be watching when we lose? He's **mufa**, a jinx. During a final, he may be politely sent to watch from the kitchen.

pages.scenario: Final, Argentina winning. Your friend's cousin walks in late, and France scores twice. Everyone turns to look at him.
pages.prompt: What is everyone thinking?
pages.explain: He's the jinx. Next match he watches from the kitchen — and keeping him there becomes the new cábala.

pages.prompt: Your friend is scared to change his lucky socks. He says:
pages.translation: I'm not washing them, it's my lucky ritual.
pages.explain: **Cábala**: the lucky ritual. The opposite is **mufa**, bad luck, or the person who brings it.

example.en: Dibu is the best goalkeeper.

classes.title: Beyond Buenos Aires
classes.summary: Rosario, Córdoba and La Plata, where the local derby beats Boca-River

pages.title: Not everything is Boca-River
pages.body: Porteños forget it, but some of the fiercest rivalries are outside the capital. Argentines call the rest of the country **el interior**, and in cities like **Rosario**, **Córdoba** and **La Plata** the local **clásico** (derby) matters far more than the Superclásico. Ask a **rosarino** (someone from Rosario) about Boca and River and you'll get a shrug. Ask about Newell's and Central and cancel your plans.

pages.title: Rosario: leprosos vs canallas
pages.body: It's **Rosario Central** against **Newell's Old Boys**. The story goes that both were invited to a charity match for a leprosy clinic. Newell's said yes and became the **leprosos** (lepers); Central said no and became the **canallas** (scoundrels). Both wear the insults with pride. Even the national team splits: Messi grew up a Newell's kid, while Di María is pure Central.

pages.statement: Messi and Di María are both from Rosario, but from rival clubs.
pages.explain: Same city, opposite sides: Messi played in **Newell's** youth teams, Di María came up at **Central** and went back to play there. Rosario family dinners have survived worse.

pages.scenario: Your first night in Rosario. A new friend pours you a beer and asks: "¿Sos leproso o canalla?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
pages.explain: It's the Rosario version of **¿de qué cuadro sos?** If you don't have a team, say so with a smile. Picking one at random can cost you friends.

pages.title: Córdoba and La Plata
pages.body: In **Córdoba**, the big one is **Belgrano** against **Talleres**, and Belgrano fans are the **piratas** (pirates). In **La Plata**, it's **Estudiantes** against **Gimnasia**: Estudiantes fans are **pinchas**, Gimnasia fans are **triperos**. Same rule everywhere: the local derby comes first, and Boca-River is something they watch on TV.

pages.scenario: A taxi driver proudly tells you he's a **pincha** and that the triperos had a terrible season.
pages.prompt: Which city are you most likely in?
pages.explain: Pinchas (Estudiantes) and triperos (Gimnasia) are La Plata's two tribes. In Rosario it'd be leprosos and canallas; in Córdoba, piratas and Talleres.

pages.statement: Most rosarinos care more about Boca-River than about their own clásico.
pages.explain: Newell's-Central is the one that stops the city. Boca-River gets a shrug, at most.

glossary.en: the rest of the country (outside Buenos Aires)
which team are you (a fan of)?

sections.title: Tango
sections.summary: The sad, sexy music of the Río de la Plata, and how not to embarrass yourself at a milonga

classes.title: Born on the edge of town
classes.summary: Two cities, one port, and a German squeezebox

pages.title: From the arrabal
pages.body: Tango was born in the late 1800s in the **arrabal**, the rough outskirts of the city: crowded tenements called **conventillos**, corner bars, the port. It was the music of immigrants, sailors, workers and **compadritos** (local tough guys with a knife and a nice hat). Polite society found it scandalous, until tango became a craze in **Paris**. Suddenly the rich loved it.

pages.title: Buenos Aires AND Montevideo
pages.body: Careful here: tango isn't only **porteño** (from Buenos Aires). It's **rioplatense**: it grew up on both sides of the **Río de la Plata**, in Buenos Aires and in **Montevideo**. Uruguayans will remind you, with love and zero patience. The most famous tango of all, **La Cumparsita**, was written by a Uruguayan and premiered in a Montevideo café.
pages.fun_fact: Argentina and Uruguay went to UNESCO together, and tango became Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

pages.scenario: You're in Montevideo and you say: "I love Argentine tango!" Your Uruguayan friend raises an eyebrow.
pages.prompt: What's the safer thing to say?
pages.explain: **Rioplatense** covers both cities. It's even how UNESCO put it. Your friend will lower the eyebrow.

pages.title: Men danced with men
pages.body: Around 1900 there were way more men than women in the city, because most immigrants were young single guys. So men often practiced tango **with each other**, on the street corner or in the patio, to the sound of an **organito** (a street barrel organ). Getting good mattered: you had to be decent before anyone would dance with you.

pages.statement: Tango started as elegant ballroom music for the rich in Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: The opposite. It was born among the poor and the rough, and the upper class only embraced it after Paris did. Nothing like European approval to change a porteño's mind.

pages.title: A squeezebox from Germany
pages.body: The sound of tango is the **bandoneón**, and it's German. The name comes from **Heinrich Band**, who sold them, supposedly so small churches with no organ could have music. Sailors and immigrants brought it to the Río de la Plata; nobody's sure who brought the first one. From church hymns to brothel music in one boat trip.

pages.title: The fueye
pages.body: Tangueros call the bandoneón **el fueye**, from *fuelle* (bellows). It's famously hard: dozens of buttons, and each one plays a *different note* depending on whether you open or close it. Old German-made ones are still the most wanted, and a good one costs a small fortune.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it is
pairs: the rough outskirts of the city

pages.prompt: Why is the bandoneón so hard to play?
options: It's as heavy as a piano
It only plays in one key
pages.explain: Same button, different note depending on whether the bellows open or close. Now imagine doing that at tango speed.

example.en: My grandpa was a huge tango fan.

classes.title: At the milonga
classes.summary: The unwritten rules of the dance floor, and tango today

pages.title: What's a milonga?

word.en: a dance night, and a rhythm

pages.body: A **milonga** is a tango dance night: a hall, tables around a wooden floor, music from a DJ or a live orquesta, and people of every age dancing until late. (It's also a faster, bouncier rhythm related to tango, so yes, you can dance a milonga at the milonga.) There are milongas every night of the week in Buenos Aires.

pages.title: The cabeceo
pages.body: Nobody walks up and asks "¿bailamos?" at a traditional milonga. You use the **mirada** (look) and the **cabeceo** (a small nod). You catch someone's eye from across the room and nod. If they nod back, you go get them. If they look away, no one got rejected in public. The regulars, the **milongueros**, are masters at it.

pages.scenario: At a milonga, you catch someone's eye and nod. They look down at their shoes.
pages.prompt: What happened?
options: They didn't see you, walk over and ask
They said no, politely. Try someone else.
They want you to nod again, harder
pages.explain: Looking away is the polite **no**. Walking over anyway puts them on the spot, and that's exactly what the **cabeceo** exists to avoid.

pages.title: Tandas and cortinas
pages.body: The music comes in **tandas**: sets of 3 or 4 songs of the same style and usually the same orquesta. Between tandas, the DJ plays a **cortina** (curtain), a short bit of non-tango music. That's the signal: everyone leaves the floor and changes partners. Many milongas end the night with **La Cumparsita**.

pages.title: Gracias = I'm done
pages.body: Here's the trap. You dance the whole tanda with your partner. If you say **gracias** after the first song, it doesn't mean "thanks", it means "thanks, **that's enough**". Your partner will walk you back to your table. Want to keep going? Just smile and wait for the next song.

pages.statement: At a milonga, it's polite to say "gracias" after every song.
pages.explain: **Gracias** ends the tanda. Say it after one song and you just dumped your partner, politely but clearly.

pages.title: The ronda
pages.body: Couples move around the floor in a **ronda**, counterclockwise, like cars on a track. These are the **códigos** (unwritten rules) of the floor: no passing, no stopping to chat, no big kicks that hit the couple behind you. And never **teach on the floor**: correcting your partner mid-dance is a big no. Save it for class, or better, for never.

pages.prompt: A tanda at the milonga, in order
items: Catch someone's eye and nod (cabeceo)
Meet on the floor and join the ronda
Dance the whole tanda together
The cortina plays: say gracias, back to your table

pages.title: Show or milonga?
pages.body: Tourists often see tango at a **cena show**: dinner, sequins, flying legs, a rose in someone's mouth. Porteños call it **tango for export**. It's real skill, but it's stage tango. At a milonga, the dance is small, close and improvised. Each August the city hosts the **Mundial de Tango**, with a stage category and a **pista** (social floor) one.

pages.scenario: You want to see how porteños actually dance tango, not a show.
pages.prompt: Where do you go?
options: A dinner show with a set menu
A neighborhood milonga, just to watch
pages.explain: At a **milonga** you can sit, have a drink and watch. Nobody minds, as long as you stay off the floor until you know the **códigos**.

classes.title: Gardel
classes.summary: The voice, the smile, and the question of where he was born

pages.title: El Zorzal
pages.body: **Carlos Gardel** is *the* tango **cantor** (singer), and the country's first pop **ídolo**. Slicked-back hair, a smile that sold records, a voice people still call perfect. They call him **el Zorzal criollo** (the local songbird) and **el Morocho del Abasto**: the dark-haired guy from Abasto, the market barrio where he grew up. His house there is now a museum.

pages.title: Toulouse or Tacuarembó?
pages.body: Where was he born? Most researchers say **Toulouse, France**: son of a single mother who brought him to Buenos Aires as a toddler. But Gardel himself once signed papers saying he was born in **Tacuarembó, Uruguay**. Many Uruguayans believe that version, and new documents keep reopening the fight. Argentines just say he's porteño, since that's where he grew up.

pages.statement: Gardel himself once signed papers saying he was born in Uruguay.
pages.explain: He did, and Tacuarembó has never let it go. Toulouse has the French birth record. Everyone claims him.

pages.title: Cada día canta mejor
pages.body: In 1935, at the peak of his fame, Gardel died in a plane crash in **Medellín**, Colombia, during a tour. The country went into mourning, and the myth started right there. Hence the classic line about him: **cada día canta mejor**, "he sings better every day". It's the perfect joke: he's been dead for ages and he keeps improving.

pages.scenario: Your friend's uncle, a Gardel fanatic, says: "Gardel murió en el 35, pero cada día canta mejor."
pages.prompt: What's he saying?
options: A new singer sounds just like him
pages.explain: It's affection and a joke at the same time. For tangueros, Gardel isn't a dead singer, he's a permanent presence.

pages.title: A pucho for Gardel
pages.body: At his tomb in **Chacarita** cemetery, fans put a lit **pucho** (cigarette) between the fingers of his bronze statue. Legend says if it burns all the way, your wish comes true. He's so present that when someone won't stop whining, porteños say **andá a cantarle a Gardel**: go sing it to Gardel, meaning go tell someone who cares.

pages.scenario: Your roommate has been complaining about the same ex for an hour.
pages.prompt: What can you say, cheekily?
pages.explain: **Andá a cantarle a Gardel** is a cheeky brush-off: take your sad song somewhere else. Cheeky, not rude, so save it for friends.

pages.title: Día Nacional del Tango
pages.body: Argentina celebrates the **Día Nacional del Tango** on **December 11**, Gardel's birthday. If you're in Buenos Aires that week, keep an eye out for free concerts and open-air milongas around the city. A perfect excuse to try your first cabeceo.

classes.title: Big bands and a rebel
classes.summary: The golden age of the orquestas, and the man they called tango's assassin

pages.title: The golden age
pages.body: In the **1940s**, tango was pop music. Every club, radio station and neighborhood dance had an **orquesta típica**: bandoneones, violins, piano and double bass, often with a singer. People followed bandleaders like football teams. Friday night meant going to hear *your* orquesta, and arguing about it on the way home.

pages.title: Hear the difference
pages.body: Tango DJs still build whole nights around a few orquestas. **Juan D'Arienzo**, **el Rey del Compás** (the King of the Beat): punchy and rhythmic, pure energy. **Carlos Di Sarli**: smooth and elegant. **Osvaldo Pugliese**: dark, dramatic, deep. And **Aníbal Troilo**, **Pichuco**, maybe the most loved **bandoneonista** (bandoneón player) ever.

pages.prompt: Match the bandleader to how he sounds

pages.title: A red carnation on the piano
pages.body: Pugliese was a member of the Communist Party and was jailed more than once for it. When he couldn't show up, his orquesta played anyway, with a **clavel rojo** (red carnation) on the empty piano. Everyone in the room got the message. As an old man he packed the **Teatro Colón**, just where his mom always said he would end up.

pages.statement: When Pugliese was in prison, his orquesta cancelled all its shows.
pages.explain: They kept playing, with a red carnation on the piano instead of him. A silent protest everyone understood.

pages.title: Piazzolla breaks the rules
pages.body: **Astor Piazzolla**, from Mar del Plata, played bandoneón in Troilo's orquesta as a young man. Then he went to Paris to study classical music with **Nadia Boulanger**, who told him to stop hiding tango and build on it. He came back and mixed tango with jazz and classical: **tango nuevo**. Think **Libertango** and **Adiós Nonino**.

pages.title: "That's not tango!"
pages.body: The traditionalists hated it. Piazzolla got called **el asesino del tango** (tango's assassin), and "**eso no es tango**" followed him for years. He answered that it was *música contemporánea de Buenos Aires*. Today he's one of the most played Argentine composers in the world, and the fight is still tango's oldest **grieta** (divide), at family dinners included.

pages.scenario: At a family dinner, the grandpa says Piazzolla ruined tango. The grandson says Piazzolla saved it.
pages.prompt: What's the grandpa's line?
pages.explain: **Eso no es tango** is the purist's battle cry. The grandson's side is Piazzolla's own answer: *música contemporánea de Buenos Aires*.

pages.scenario: You're in a café and the radio plays **Libertango**.
pages.prompt: What are you hearing?
pages.explain: **Libertango** is pure Piazzolla: tango mixed with jazz and classical, made to be *listened* to — which is exactly what bugged the dancers.

example.es: Este tango tiene un compás bárbaro para bailar.
example.en: This tango has a great beat for dancing.

example.es: En mi familia hay grieta con Piazzolla.
example.en: My family is split over Piazzolla.

classes.title: What tango sings about
classes.summary: Mom, the barrio, the woman who left, and a world gone wrong

pages.title: Three minutes of heartbreak
pages.body: Tango **letras** (lyrics) have favorite subjects. **La mina que se fue**, the woman who left (and it's always her fault). **La vieja**, mom, a saint. **El barrio**, the neighborhood as it used to be. And **nostalgia** for everything. Tango poet **Discépolo** put it best: **el tango es un pensamiento triste que se baila**, a sad thought you can dance to.

pages.title: Old slang in the lyrics
pages.body: Early lyrics are full of **lunfardo**, Buenos Aires street slang. Some of it you'll only hear in old tangos now: **percanta** is a woman, **bulín** a bachelor pad, **garufa** a night out partying. Those words survived only because tango kept singing them.

pages.prompt: Match the tango word

pages.title: Mi Buenos Aires querido
pages.body: Gardel and his lyricist **Le Pera** wrote **Mi Buenos Aires querido**: a man far away, dreaming of seeing the city again. It's pure **extrañar**, missing home. The famous line: **"cuando yo te vuelva a ver, no habrá más penas ni olvido"** (when I see you again, there'll be no more sorrow or forgetting). Every Argentine living abroad has cried to it at least once.

pages.title: Volver
pages.body: **Volver** (to return), also Gardel and Le Pera, is about coming back older to a city and a love you left. It has maybe the most quoted line in tango: **"que veinte años no es nada"** (twenty years is nothing). People say it at reunions, birthdays, anywhere time has passed and everyone pretends it hasn't.

pages.prompt: You run into an old school friend after ages. What do you say, quoting Volver?
pages.translation: Unbelievable! Twenty years is nothing.
pages.explain: Straight out of **Volver**. Every Argentine will get the reference, and probably start humming.

pages.title: Cambalache: the angry one
pages.body: **Cambalache**, by Discépolo, isn't about love. It says the 20th century is a mess where "lo mismo un burro que un gran profesor" (a donkey and a great professor, same thing): **"el mundo fue y será una porquería"** (the world was and will be garbage). A military government later banned it from the radio for years. It still sounds like this morning's news.
pages.fun_fact: A **cambalache** is a junk shop where everything is thrown together. People still say "¡esto es un cambalache!" about a total mess.

pages.statement: For a few years, Cambalache was banned from Argentine radio.
pages.explain: The military government of the 1940s went after it, and Perón later lifted the ban. Being banned only made it more famous.

pages.scenario: A friend looks at the chaos at a government office and sighs: "Esto es un cambalache."
pages.prompt: What do they mean?
pages.explain: Thanks to Discépolo, **cambalache** means a mess where nothing makes sense and nobody plays fair. The tango turned a shop into a worldview.

sections.title: Música
sections.summary: Rock nacional, folklore, cumbia, trap, and crowds louder than the band

classes.title: Rock nacional
classes.summary: Rock in Spanish, born in a café bathroom and raised under a dictatorship

pages.title: Born in a bathroom
pages.body: In 1967, **Los Gatos** released the **tema** (song) **"La balsa"** (*The raft*). Legend says it was finished in the bathroom of **La Perla del Once**, a 24-hour café, to dodge the waiters who kept kicking the musicians out for being loud. It was a hit, proof that rock sung in Spanish could sell. Before that, rock here meant singing in English. **Rock nacional** was born.

pages.statement: "Rock nacional" means rock with patriotic lyrics.
pages.explain: It means rock made here and sung in Spanish. The big idea was simple and radical: you can rock in *castellano*.

pages.title: El Flaco and Charly
pages.body: Two names you must know. **Luis Alberto Spinetta**, **el Flaco** (*the skinny one*), wrote poetic, dreamy songs, starting with his band **Almendra**. **Charly García** started as a teenager in the duo **Sui Generis** and became the wild genius of Argentine rock: brilliant, unpredictable, loved.
pages.fun_fact: Charly once jumped from a ninth-floor hotel window into the pool below. And survived.

pages.statement: Charly García once jumped from a hotel window into a pool, and survived.
pages.explain: It happened in Mendoza, and he walked away. Charly stories like this are part of the legend, and people tell them with affection.

pages.title: Singing in code
pages.body: During the 1976–83 dictatorship, rock was watched, censored and harassed. So musicians wrote in metaphors. Charly's band **Serú Girán** filled stadiums with songs that said things *without saying them*. For many kids, a rock concert was the only place they could feel free together.

pages.title: The Malvinas paradox
pages.body: During the 1982 Malvinas war, the military government pushed radios to stop playing music **en inglés**. The same regime that had harassed rockers suddenly needed Spanish songs to fill the airwaves. Rock nacional exploded. Many musicians used the moment to ask for peace, at a huge festival in Buenos Aires.

pages.scenario: It's the middle of the Malvinas war. You turn on the radio in Buenos Aires.
pages.prompt: What are you most likely to hear?
options: The Beatles and Queen, as usual
pages.explain: English-language music was pulled off the air during the war, so local rock and folklore took over. Plenty of bands went from underground to mainstream almost overnight.

pages.title: Gracias totales
pages.body: In the 80s came **Soda Stereo**, led by Gustavo **Cerati**, and took Argentine rock across all of Latin America. At their farewell show at River's stadium, Cerati closed with a line everyone still quotes: **"¡Gracias… totales!"**. Today people say it, half joking, to thank someone *big time*.
pages.fun_fact: Fito Páez's **El amor después del amor**, with guests like Spinetta, Charly, Cerati and Mercedes Sosa, is the best-selling **disco** (album) in Argentine rock history.

pages.prompt: A friend lends you their car for the weekend. How do you thank them, Cerati style?
pages.translation: Thanks… totally!
pages.explain: **Gracias totales** is Cerati's goodbye. Say it and every Argentine gets the reference.

vocabulary.note: Argentines say tema more than canción in casual talk.

example.en: Put on that Soda song.

vocabulary.note: Playful, a bit over the top. Everyone gets the reference.
Also a very common nickname for any thin guy.

example.es: Ese disco lo escuché mil veces.
example.en: I've listened to that album a thousand times.

classes.title: Folklore, peñas and pañuelos
classes.summary: Guitars, handkerchiefs and the voice of La Negra

pages.title: Folklore is not old stuff
pages.body: In Argentina **folklore** is a living music scene, not a museum. It's the music of the provinces: guitars, the **bombo legüero** (a deep drum made of wood and hide), violins and voices. It has many rhythms, like **zamba**, **chacarera** and **chamamé**, and young people still sing it at parties, especially in the north.

pages.title: La Negra
pages.body: **Mercedes Sosa**, from Tucumán, was **La Negra**, a nickname of affection. During the dictatorship she was arrested on stage, mid-concert, and went into exile in Europe. When she came back, still under the dictatorship, she packed theater after theater in Buenos Aires. Her version of **"Gracias a la vida"** still makes whole rooms cry.

pages.statement: In Argentina, "Negra" can be a nickname said with love.
pages.explain: It was Mercedes Sosa's nickname, used with affection. **Negro/negra** is a very common nickname for friends and family, though, like everywhere, tone and context matter a lot.

pages.title: The peña
pages.body: A **peña** is a folklore night: long tables, **empanadas** and **locro**, wine, and live music. There's no "audience". When a zamba or chacarera starts, people get up and dance between the tables, then sit back down and keep eating. A spontaneous version with friends and a guitar is a **guitarreada**.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it is
pairs: folklore night with food and dancing

pages.title: Zamba vs chacarera
pages.body: **Zamba** (not the Brazilian samba!) is slow and romantic. Two dancers circle each other, never touching, waving a **pañuelo** (handkerchief), in a kind of flirting. **Chacarera**, tied to Santiago del Estero, is fast and happy: finger snaps, the man's **zapateo** (stomping footwork) and the woman's **zarandeo** (swirling her skirt).

pages.scenario: At a peña, the music goes slow and the couples on the floor pull out white handkerchiefs.
pages.prompt: What are they dancing?
pages.explain: The **pañuelo** is the trademark of the zamba. Slow, circling, never touching. If people are stomping and snapping, that's a chacarera.

pages.title: Nine moons in Cosquín
pages.body: Every late **January**, the small town of **Cosquín**, in the Córdoba hills, hosts the **Festival Nacional de Folklore**: nine nights, **las nueve lunas**. Every night opens with the famous shout **"¡Aquí Cosquín!"**, on a main stage named after the great folk guitarist **Atahualpa Yupanqui**. Go for the big shows, stay for the peñas all over town until sunrise.

pages.prompt: You're at a peña and someone invites you to get up and dance a chacarera. You say yes:
pages.translation: Sure! But I don't know how to stomp.

classes.title: Cumbia and cuarteto
classes.summary: The bailanta, a cumbia saint, and the tunga tunga from Córdoba

pages.title: The bailanta
pages.body: Rock fills stadiums, but **cumbia** fills the dance floor. Born in Colombia, it became deeply Argentine in the dance halls of the suburbs, the **bailantas**. At any wedding or birthday, at some point the DJ puts on cumbia and even your serious uncle turns out to be a secret **cumbiero** (cumbia lover). You don't have to like it. You just have to dance.

pages.title: Gilda, the cumbia saint
pages.body: **Gilda** was a kindergarten teacher who became a cumbia star in her 30s, in a scene run by men. When a song catches on, Argentines say it **pegó**, from **pegar** (to stick), and her **"No me arrepiento de este amor"** pegó everywhere. In 1996 her tour bus crashed on **Ruta 12**, in Entre Ríos. People started asking her for miracles at a shrine by the road, and she became a **santa popular** (folk saint).

pages.statement: At the crash site on Ruta 12 there's a shrine to Gilda where people still leave offerings and ask for favors.
pages.explain: People ask for health, work or love, and leave thanks. On key dates thousands visit. The Church never made her a saint; the people did.

pages.title: Cumbia villera
pages.body: In the late 90s, with the economy collapsing, a rawer style was born in the poor neighborhoods: **cumbia villera**. Its big name is **Pablo Lescano** and his band **Damas Gratis**. The lyrics talk about the street, partying and the police. Critics say they glorify drugs and treat women badly. Fans say it's the honest voice of the barrio. Both debates are still alive.

pages.title: Cuarteto: Córdoba's heartbeat
pages.body: **Cuarteto** was born in **Córdoba**, and you'll know it by the bouncy piano beat everyone calls **tunga tunga**. Its king is **La Mona Jiménez**, who has played packed weekly **bailes** (dances) for decades. UNESCO recently added cuarteto to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

pages.scenario: You're at a wedding in Córdoba. At 3 a.m. the DJ switches to a fast beat with a bouncy piano, and everyone runs to the dance floor.
pages.prompt: What's probably playing?
pages.explain: In Córdoba, the late-night party is cuarteto. That bouncy piano is the **tunga tunga**. Refusing to dance is not really an option.

pages.title: El Potro
pages.body: **Rodrigo Bueno**, **el Potro** (*the colt*), took cuarteto from Córdoba to Buenos Aires and filled the **Luna Park** again and again. He died young, in a car crash after a show, and became a legend overnight. His songs, like **"Soy cordobés"** and **"Lo mejor del amor"**, are still party must-haves.

pages.prompt: Match the name to the story
Your friend is inviting you to a night of cumbia dancing:
pages.translation: Shall we go to the bailanta tonight?
pages.explain: The **bailanta** is the cumbia dance hall. A **peña** is folklore, and the **cancha** is the football stadium.

classes.title: Trap, RKT and Bizarrap
classes.summary: From freestyle battles in a park to the biggest stages in the world

pages.title: It started in a park
pages.body: For years, on Sunday afternoons, kids met at **Parque Rivadavia**, in Caballito, for **El Quinto Escalón** (*the fifth step*): free rap **batallas** (battles) on the park's steps. Rappers improvised rhymes against each other, **tirar freestyle**, and the crowd picked the winner. Names like **Duki**, **Trueno** and **Wos** came out of there. Today they fill stadiums.

pages.statement: Most of Argentina's big trap stars came up through expensive music schools.
pages.explain: Many of them started in free freestyle battles in parks and plazas, recorded on phones and shared on YouTube. The street was the school.

pages.title: The man in the cap
pages.body: **Bizarrap** is a producer who never shows his face: always a cap and dark glasses. In his **BZRP Music Sessions**, a guest raps or sings over his beat, filmed in a small studio. A **sesión** can launch a career overnight, and his one with **Shakira** broke YouTube records. If you listen to one thing before your trip, make it a Biza session.

pages.scenario: Your Argentine friend says: "¿Viste la nueva sesión de Biza?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
options: If you heard Bizarrap's new session
If you saw Bizarrap in person
If you watched a new TV series
pages.explain: **Biza** is short for Bizarrap, and nobody has *seen* him, not really. When a new session drops, half the country listens that same day.

pages.title: The new stars
pages.body: **Duki** is the king of the scene. **María Becerra** **la rompió** (killed it, from **romperla**) at River's stadium, twice. **Tini**, once a Disney star, fills stadiums with pop, and **Nicki Nicole**, from Rosario, mixes trap and R&B. When a song is a banger, it's a **temazo**: the **-azo** ending makes anything bigger and better.

pages.prompt: You just heard María Becerra's new song and you loved it.
pages.translation: What a banger! I can't stop listening to it.
pages.explain: **Temazo** = a great song. A **trapo** is a rag, and a **parque** is a park: nothing to listen to on repeat.

pages.title: RKT and the turreo
pages.body: **RKT** was born in the late 2000s, from DJs at a club called **Rescate** in San Martín, Buenos Aires province. It's reggaetón plus cumbia villera, with huge bass. **L-Gante** made it explode with the viral **"L-Gante RKT"**. RKT parties are called **turreo**. Critics call the lyrics crude; fans say it's the sound of their barrio.

pages.prompt: Match the artist to the story
pairs: came up in park freestyle battles
producer who never shows his face

pages.statement: If someone says a singer "la rompió", they mean she broke something on stage.
pages.explain: **La rompió** = she killed it, she was amazing. "María la rompió en River" is a compliment.

example.en: Come on, drop a freestyle.
The new session is out.

example.en: Duki killed it.
What a tune!

classes.title: Live: pogo, bengalas and misas
classes.summary: Why foreign bands leave Argentina a little shaken

pages.title: Recital, not concierto
pages.body: In Argentina you buy **entradas** (tickets) for a **recital** or a **show**; **concierto** sounds a bit formal. At a big one, **campo** is the standing area on the pitch, **platea** is seats. The **telonero** is the opening act. And the crowd does not just listen: it sings *every* word, often louder than the band.

pages.scenario: Your friend texts you: "Tengo dos entradas para campo, ¿venís?"
pages.prompt: Where will you be?
options: In a seat up in the stands
Standing on the pitch, near the stage
pages.explain: **Campo** is the standing area on the field. Closer to the band, and closer to the pogo.

pages.title: Olé, olé, olé
pages.body: Between songs, the crowd sings a football-style chant with the artist's name: **"Olé, olé, olé, olé… Charly, Charly!"**. Foreigners get it too, and the Rolling Stones even named a documentary *Olé, Olé, Olé!*. Argentina has so many Stones fans they have a name: **rollingas**. And when the band walks off before the encore: **¡otro, otro!** (one more!).

pages.prompt: The band walks off before the encore. What does the whole stadium shout?
pages.translation: One more, one more!
pages.explain: **¡Otro, otro!** is the Argentine way to ask for an encore. *Chau* would send them home, and *campo* is where you're standing.

pages.prompt: A typical Argentine recital night, in order
items: The telonero plays while the crowd fills up
The band comes out and everyone sings every word
The band walks off, the crowd chants "¡otro, otro!"
They come back for the encore

pages.title: Misas ricoteras
pages.body: **Patricio Rey y sus Redonditos de Ricota**, **los Redondos**, led by the **Indio Solari**, never did much press. Their shows were called **misas** (masses) by fans, who traveled across the country for them. In the 90s, barrio rock like theirs, La Renga or Los Piojos, got the name **rock chabón**, with football-style banners, chants and **bengalas** (flares).
pages.fun_fact: Fans call the Redondos song "Ji ji ji" "the biggest pogo in the world".

pages.title: The pogo
pages.body: The **pogo** is jumping and bumping into each other in a big mass, usually near the stage. It looks like chaos, but there's an unwritten rule: **si alguien se cae, se lo levanta** (if someone falls, you pick them up). If you're not up for it, stay on the edges. **Pogear** is the verb.

pages.scenario: You're in the middle of the pogo at a rock show. The guy next to you trips and falls.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Keep jumping, it's part of the pogo
Stop and help pick him up right away
Wait until the song ends to help
pages.explain: The first rule of the pogo: whoever falls gets picked up, fast. People around you will do the same. Rough, but with a code.

pages.title: Bengalas and Cromañón
pages.body: The flares had a dark side. In 2004, at a Callejeros show at **República Cromañón**, a small club in Once, a **bengala** set the ceiling on fire. The venue was overcrowded and an emergency exit was locked. **194 people died**, most of them young. It changed live music forever: much stricter controls, and a flare indoors is now unthinkable.

pages.statement: Since Cromañón, lighting a bengala inside a club in Argentina is seen as totally unacceptable.
pages.explain: Cromañón is a deep wound, and the families still hold memorials every December 30. You'll still see flares at some big outdoor shows, but inside a venue? Never.

example.en: Are you going to the gig on Saturday?

sections.title: Cómo hablamos

classes.title: Vos, not tú
classes.summary: The little pronoun that makes you sound Argentine

pages.title: Goodbye, tú
pages.body: Your textbook taught you **tú**. Forget it here. In Argentina, "you" (informal) is **vos**: **vos sos** (you are), **vos tenés** (you have), **¿vos querés?** (do you want?). Say *tú tienes* in Buenos Aires and people will understand you perfectly, and instantly clock you as someone who learned Spanish from a book, or from Netflix.
pages.fun_fact: Uruguay and Paraguay use vos too, and so do parts of Central America.

pages.title: Just move the stress
pages.body: Good news: most vos forms are easy. In the present, take the infinitive, drop the **-r**, add **-s** and stress the end: **hablar → hablás**, **tener → tenés**, **querer → querés**. And the vowel inside never changes: **tenés**, never *tienés*. Commands just drop the **-r**: **¡vení!** (come!), **¡mirá!** (look!), **¡decime!** (tell me!). The one weird one: **ser → vos sos**.

pages.prompt: Match the tú form to its vos twin
pages.explain: Same verb, no vowel drama: *tienes* becomes **tenés**, *quieres* becomes **querés**. That's why kids here pick up verbs so fast.

pages.title: Why vos survived here
pages.body: Vos is old Spanish. In colonial times, **tú** took over in the rich centers, **Lima** and **Mexico City**, where viceroys and their courts kept up with Madrid's fashions. The Río de la Plata was a far-off, poor corner of the empire. Nobody bothered to update our pronoun, so vos just stayed. Funny twist: schools here kept teaching **tú** for decades anyway.

pages.statement: For decades, Argentine schools taught tú instead of vos.
pages.explain: Even though nobody spoke it at home. Only in **1982** did the Academia Argentina de Letras accept vos as correct, educated Spanish, and classrooms slowly switched.

pages.title: No vosotros, no usted
pages.body: Plural "you" is always **ustedes**. **Vosotros** is for Spain; here it only lives in the national anthem and old prayers. And **usted**? You'll hardly hear it. Everyone gets **vos**: the waiter, the doctor, your friend's grandmother. Being polite comes from softer words instead: **disculpá**, **¿me podrías…?**, **por favor**.

pages.scenario: You're at a kiosco. The guy behind the counter is about your age. You want to ask if he has change.
pages.prompt: What sounds most natural?
pages.explain: **¿Tenés cambio?** Short, vos, done. Also notice you don't even need to say *vos*: the **-és** ending already tells everyone who you mean.

pages.prompt: Your friend is late and texts you. What do you answer?
pages.translation: Sure, come whenever, no rush, I'll wait for you.
pages.explain: **Vení** is the vos command. *Ven* is tú, *venid* is vosotros: both sound foreign here.

pages.scenario: You're visiting your friend's grandmother, 85, for the first time. She offers you tea.
pages.prompt: How do you ask her if she wants help in the kitchen?
pages.explain: **¿Querés que te ayude?** Even with an 85-year-old grandma, vos is normal here; a warm tone does the polite part. *¿Quiere que la ayude?* is usted and sounds stiff, *¿Queréis…?* is Spain.

example.en: And what are you up to?
Where are you from?
Do you want a coffee?
Tell me the truth.
