classes.title: Sho, che and the melody
classes.summary: The sound, the word and the tune that give a porteño away

pages.title: Sho me shamo
pages.body: The quickest way to spot a porteño: **y** and **ll** sound like English **"sh"**. **Yo** is "sho". **Calle** (street) is "cashe". **Pollo** (chicken) is "posho". **Lluvia** (rain) is "shuvia". **Me llamo** is "me shamo". The rest of the Spanish-speaking world calls it "the Argentine thing", and it's also heard across the river in Montevideo.

pages.title: Grandma says zh, you say sh
pages.body: It used to be softer: a buzzing **zh**, like the *s* in *measure*. Over the second half of the 20th century, younger porteños pushed it to a crisp **sh**, like *shoe*. Studies show young people, and especially women, lead the change. So a grandma in Palermo might say "zho" and her granddaughter "sho". Both are 100% porteño.

pages.statement: You'll hear "sho" across the river in Montevideo too.
pages.explain: Montevideo shares the sound. Meanwhile, parts of Argentina, like the northeast, often keep a softer *y*. The sh is a Río de la Plata thing more than an Argentine one.

pages.prompt: Which word would a porteño say with a "sh" sound?
pages.explain: **Calle** → "cashe". The double **ll** is the giveaway. *Casa* and *plaza* have no y or ll, so no sh.

pages.title: Che!
pages.body: **Che** is how you get someone's attention: "hey", "dude", "listen". **Che, ¿me pasás la sal?** It's so typical of us that Ernesto Guevara's Cuban comrades nicknamed him **Che** because he said it all the time. Its partner in crime goes at the end of a sentence: **¿viste?**, *you know?* **Hacía un frío, ¿viste?**

pages.scenario: You're walking with a friend and see an old classmate across the avenue.
pages.prompt: What's the most porteño way to call him?
pages.explain: **¡Che!** *Oye* sounds Spanish or Caribbean, and *oiga* is for a stranger you're about to complain to.

pages.title: Where does che come from?
pages.body: Nobody knows for sure, and people love arguing about it. One theory: **Guaraní**, where *che* means "I" or "my". Another: **Mapudungun** (the Mapuche language), where it means "people". A third: the **Valencian** "hey". Pick your favorite and defend it over a mate. One word we're sure about: **chau**, the everyday goodbye, comes from Italian *ciao*.

pages.title: Spanish with an Italian tune
pages.body: Foreigners often say porteños sound Italian, and there's science behind it. Researchers compared Buenos Aires intonation with other languages and found it's closer to **Neapolitan** Italian than to Spanish from Spain. The melody likely came with the huge wave of Italian immigrants around 1900. Before that, the city probably sounded more like Spain.

pages.statement: The Italian-sounding melody of Buenos Aires Spanish has been there since colonial times.
pages.explain: It's relatively recent. Researchers link it to the early 20th century, when Italians poured into the city. Their accents faded, but the tune stuck.

pages.prompt: You're telling a friend why you were late. Finish it like a porteño.
pages.text: Y nada, se me hizo tarde, ¿___?
pages.translation: So yeah, I ran late, you know?
pages.explain: **¿Viste?** at the end = you know? **Chau** is goodbye, and **che** goes at the start, to get attention.

example.en: Hey, do you have the time?

vocabulary.note: From the Italian ciao.
Said "cashe" in Buenos Aires.

example.en: I'm Sofía, and you?
It was so cold, you know?

glossary.en: Hey, can you pass me the salt?

classes.title: Lunfardo
classes.summary: The street slang born in the conventillos

pages.title: A language made of immigrants
pages.body: Around 1900, Buenos Aires was packed with newcomers, mostly Italians and Spaniards, living side by side in **conventillos** (tenements). Out of that mix came **lunfardo**: a street vocabulary built from Italian dialects, Spanish slang, Portuguese and whatever else was lying around. The name itself probably comes from **lombardo**, someone from Lombardy, which back then had become slang for "thief".

pages.title: Police first, poets later
pages.body: The first people who wrote lunfardo down, in the late 1800s, were **police officers and journalists**, convinced it was the secret code of thieves. Turned out half the city talked like that. Then **tango** took it to the radio, and lyrics sung by **Carlos Gardel** spread it everywhere. After that, there was no stopping it.
pages.fun_fact: Yes, slang has its own academy here: the **Academia Porteña del Lunfardo**. Its members take it very seriously.

pages.statement: The first people to write lunfardo down thought it was a secret code of thieves.
pages.explain: Police officers and journalists did. Then it turned out bakers, clerks and grandmas talked like that too.

pages.title: Money and people
pages.body: Starter pack, part one. **Guita** is money. A **mango** is a single peso, so **no tengo un mango** = I'm broke. A **pibe** is a kid or a young guy (a girl is a **piba**), and grown adults are pibes too. A **mina** is a woman: very common, but a bit macho, so hear it more than you say it.

pages.title: Work, food and laziness
pages.body: Part two. The **laburo** is your job, from Italian *lavoro*: **me voy al laburo**. To eat is **morfar**: **¿qué morfamos?** And **fiaca** is that heavy, can't-be-bothered laziness that hits after a big lunch: **¡qué fiaca!**

pages.prompt: Match the lunfardo to its meaning

pages.title: Bondi: a word that took the tram
pages.body: In Brazil, trams are called **bonde**, from English **bond**. The story goes that early tram tickets were sold as "bonds". The word traveled south, and in Buenos Aires the tram became the **bondi**. When trams disappeared, the name jumped onto the **colectivo** (city bus). So every time you say "me tomo el bondi", you're quoting an English word by way of Brazilian Portuguese.

pages.scenario: A friend texts: "Estoy sin un mango, ¿morfamos en casa?"
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: They're broke, so dinner at home
They lost their keys, so meet at home
pages.explain: **Sin un mango** = without a peso. **Morfar** = to eat. Bring a bottle of wine and you're the hero.

pages.title: The art of chamuyo
pages.body: **Chamuyo** is smooth talk: half truth, half invention, all charm. It comes from the Caló (Spanish Romani) *chamullar*, to talk. You **chamuyás** a date, a cop or your boss. Someone who does it too well is a **chamuyero**. And if someone's story sounds too good, just say **eso es puro chamuyo**: that's pure baloney.

pages.prompt: Your friend claims he almost got signed by Boca. What do you say?
pages.translation: Come on, that's pure baloney.
pages.explain: **Chamuyo** = sweet-talking nonsense. The other two would just mean "pure work" or "pure bus".

pages.statement: Today lunfardo is mostly an old tango thing.
pages.explain: Some words aged (you'll only hear **percanta**, woman, in old tangos), but **guita**, **laburo**, **pibe** and **bondi** are everyday Spanish here, from kids to newsreaders.

example.en: I don't have enough money.

example.en: I'm broke.

vocabulary.note: Piba for a girl. Used for adults too.
Very casual. Better to hear it than to say it.

example.en: I'm off to work.
I'm taking the bus.

classes.title: Vesre, re and posta
classes.summary: Words backwards, words turned up, and the truth

pages.title: Al vesre
pages.body: Porteños like to flip words around. Swap the syllables of **revés** (backwards) and you get **vesre**: the name of the game is itself vesre. **Café** becomes **feca**, **mujer** becomes **jermu**, **tango** becomes **gotán**, **pagar** (to pay) becomes **garpar**, and **hotel** becomes **telo**. Remember that last one; it matters. Vesre grew up with lunfardo, on the streets and in tango lyrics.

pages.prompt: Flip them back: match the vesre to the original
pages.explain: Some are old-fashioned now (**gotán**, **jermu**), but **garpar** (to pay) and **telo** are used every day.

pages.title: Careful with telo
pages.body: A **telo** is not just any hotel. It's a **hotel alojamiento**: rooms by the hour, discreet entrance, for couples who want privacy. With so many people living with their parents into their twenties, telos are a normal, even cheerful, part of city life. For your holiday hotel, just say **hotel**.

pages.scenario: At a party you tell a new friend: "Me estoy quedando en un telo re lindo en Palermo." Everyone bursts out laughing.
pages.prompt: Why?
options: You said you're in a love hotel
pages.explain: **Telo** = love hotel, rented by the hour. For your stay, say **hotel**, or **hostel** if you're a backpacker. Great story for the rest of the night, though.

pages.title: Re: the volume knob
pages.body: Want to say "very"? Stick **re** in front: **re lindo** (really nice), **re lejos** (super far), **re bien**. Need more? **Recontra**: **recontra cansado**, dead tired. It even works alone as an answer: **—¿Te gustó? —¡Re!** (Did you like it? Totally!) Once you start, you'll never say *muy* again.

pages.prompt: Your friend asks how the concert was. It was amazing.
pages.translation: It was really good!
pages.explain: **Re bueno** is the natural way. *Feca* is coffee, and *telo*… let's not go there.

pages.prompt: From calm to over-the-top: order these
items: Es lindo.
Es re lindo.
Es recontra lindo.
pages.explain: **Re** turns it up, and **recontra** is for when you really, really mean it.

pages.title: Posta
pages.body: **Posta** means "for real". **¿Posta?** = Really? Seriously? **Te lo digo posta** = I'm telling you straight. **La posta** is the real info, the inside story. The word comes from Italian.

pages.statement: If a friend answers your news with "¿Posta?", they're asking if it's true or just joking.
pages.explain: **¿Posta?** = Seriously? It's the Argentine *¿en serio?*, usually with raised eyebrows.

example.en: Shall we grab a coffee?

vocabulary.note: Playful. Café is still the normal word.

example.en: Who's paying?
It's really far.
Are you really leaving?

vocabulary.en: the inside info, the true story

classes.title: Hands and texts
classes.summary: Gestures you'll see and shortcuts you'll read

pages.title: Talking with your hands
pages.body: Porteños don't just speak, they perform. Hands go up, fingers pinch, wrists shake. Part of it is the Italian heritage, part of it is plain passion. Watch two friends arguing about football from across the street: you'll get the gist without hearing a word. Learn a few gestures and you'll understand half the conversation before your Spanish catches up.

pages.title: The montoncito
pages.body: Fingertips pinched together pointing up, wrist bobbing up and down: that's the **montoncito** (little pile). It means **¿qué te pasa?** or **¿qué querés?**, "what's your problem?", from friendly to threatening depending on the face. Now keep the wrist still and open and close the fingers: that one means someone's scared (**tiene miedo**).
pages.fun_fact: The gesture even has its own emoji: 🤌, officially "pinched fingers".

pages.scenario: Someone cuts in front of you in the bondi line. The lady behind you looks at him, fingers pinched, shaking her wrist.
pages.prompt: What is she telling him?
pages.explain: The bobbing **montoncito** = **¿qué te pasa?** Here, pure indignation. He'll probably move.

pages.title: Three more to know
pages.body: Open hand, palm down, rocking side to side: **más o menos**, so-so. Back of your fingers brushed forward under your chin: **ni idea**, no clue. Index finger pulling down your lower eyelid: **¡ojo!**, careful, keep an eye out. Throw in a shrug and you can survive a whole conversation.

pages.prompt: Match the gesture to what it means
pairs: Flat hand rocking side to side
Back of fingers flicked under the chin
Finger pulling down the lower eyelid

pages.title: The group chat
pages.body: In a WhatsApp group you'll see: **q onda** (what's up, from **¿qué onda?**), **bue** (well, OK… with a sigh), **ntp** (**no te preocupes**, don't worry), **tqm** (**te quiero mucho**, love you), **xq** (**porque**, because), **dsp** (**después**, later). And a strict rule: nobody writes a full sentence when three letters will do.

pages.prompt: Decode the texts

pages.title: Two you'll text all day
pages.body: Two phrases you'll type (and hear) all the time. **Ni ahí** = no way, not even close: **¿Te gusta el reggaetón? —Ni ahí.** **Nada que ver** = that's not it at all, totally unrelated: **¿Estás enojado? —No, nada que ver.** Add a little eye roll and you'll sound like you grew up in Caballito.

pages.prompt: A friend asks if you're mad that she canceled. You're really not.
pages.translation: No, not at all, don't worry.
pages.explain: **Nada que ver** = that's not it at all. Add **tranqui** (relax) and she'll believe you.

pages.scenario: You suggest going for a run at 7 a.m. on Sunday. Your friend replies: "bue".
pages.prompt: How excited are they?
pages.explain: **Bue** is **bueno** with a sigh: fine, whatever, if we must. Expect them to show up late.

vocabulary.en: what's wrong with you?, what's your problem?

example.es: Ojo con el celular en el subte.
example.en: Watch your phone on the subway.

pages.title: Idioms, Argentine style
pages.body: A **dicho** is a saying or expression. Argentines talk in them constantly, and they rarely mean what the words say. Learn the words alone and you'll understand every word of a sentence, and still miss the point. So let's learn the phrases whole, the way a porteño says them.
pages.fun_fact: Many of these are also used in Uruguay: it's the Río de la Plata, not just Buenos Aires.

pages.title: The penny drops
pages.body: **Me cayó la ficha** = 'the penny dropped', 'I finally got it'. It comes from old public phones that ran on **fichas** (tokens): the call only went through when the token fell. The opposite: **no le cae la ficha** = 'he still doesn't get it'.

pages.title: In the oven
pages.body: **Estar al horno** = 'to be in the oven', i.e. in big trouble. Exam tomorrow, nothing studied? **Estoy al horno.** Your team loses 3–0 at half time? **Estamos al horno.** When things are hopeless but it's also a little funny, add **con papas**: **al horno con papas**, like a roast with potatoes.

pages.scenario: Your friend explains a joke for the third time. Suddenly you laugh.
pages.prompt: What do you say?
pages.explain: **Me cayó la ficha** = 'Now I get it!'. The token finally dropped. **No me cae la ficha** would mean you still don't get it.

pages.title: Pulling your hair
pages.body: **Tomar el pelo** = 'to pull someone's leg' (literally 'to take the hair'). **¿Me estás tomando el pelo?** = 'Are you kidding me?'. And when someone needs to get their act together: **ponete las pilas** = 'put your batteries in', i.e. wake up, get going.

pages.prompt: Your roommate has been on the couch all week and exams start Monday.
pages.translation: Hey, get your act together.
pages.explain: **Ponerse las pilas** = recharge and get to work.

pages.title: Drags and vibes
pages.body: **¡Qué garrón!** = 'What a drag!': a cancelled plan, a rainy Saturday, a two-hour line at the bank. The opposite feeling is **buena onda** (good vibes, nice): **Tu hermana es re buena onda** = 'Your sister is really nice'. And **mala onda** is bad vibes, or a person who's unfriendly.

pages.prompt: Match the expression to its meaning

pages.statement: A new coworker never says hi and grumbles at everyone. Your Argentine friends could fairly call him mala onda.
pages.explain: Unfriendly, sour, bad vibes: that's **mala onda**. And a coworker who brings facturas on Friday? **Re buena onda**.

classes.title: Más perdido que turco en la neblina
classes.summary: The comparisons Argentines use to exaggerate everything

pages.title: More X than Y
pages.body: Why say 'very lost' when you can say **más perdido que turco en la neblina**: 'more lost than a Turk in the fog'? Argentines love these **más … que …** comparisons. They're vivid, a bit absurd, and everyone knows them by heart. Use one at the right moment and you'll get a laugh and a look of respect.
pages.fun_fact: 'Turco' was the loose name given to immigrants from the Ottoman Empire: Syrians, Lebanese, Armenians and more. It's old-fashioned, and a bit of a stereotype.

pages.title: Lost, long and boring
pages.body: **Más perdido que turco en la neblina**: totally lost, or clueless. **Más largo que esperanza de pobre**: 'longer than a poor man's hope', for a line, a meeting or a week that never ends. **Más aburrido que chupar un clavo**: 'more boring than sucking a nail'.

pages.scenario: A tourist has been walking in circles around the same plaza for an hour, holding his map upside down.
pages.prompt: How would a porteño describe him?
options: Más perdido que turco en la neblina
Más largo que esperanza de pobre
Más aburrido que chupar un clavo
pages.explain: Lost and clueless = **más perdido que turco en la neblina**. Works for directions, and for anyone who has no idea what's going on.

pages.title: Fakes and pests
pages.body: **Más trucho que billete de tres pesos**: 'faker than a three-peso bill' (**trucho** = fake, dodgy). **Más pesado que collar de melones**: 'heavier than a necklace of melons', for someone who's a real pain. And a happy one: **más contento que perro con dos colas**, 'happier than a dog with two tails'.

pages.prompt: A guy on the street is selling 'original' Messi shirts for almost nothing.
pages.text: Esa camiseta es más trucha que billete de tres ___.
pages.translation: That shirt is as fake as a three-peso bill.
pages.explain: There's no such thing as a three-peso bill, so it's obviously **trucho**.

pages.title: Round and round
pages.body: Someone who can't make a simple decision **tiene más vueltas que una calesita**: 'has more turns than a merry-go-round'. And someone who thinks they're irresistible **se cree la última Coca-Cola del desierto**: 'thinks they're the last Coke in the desert'.

pages.title: What's a refrán?
pages.body: A **refrán** is a proverb: a short, fixed sentence with a lesson inside. Most came from Spain and are known all over the Spanish-speaking world. What's local is how you'll hear them: your abuela quotes one before you finish telling her your problem, and people often say just the first half and let you finish it.

pages.title: Burned by milk
pages.body: The English 'once bitten, twice shy' becomes **el que se quema con leche ve una vaca y llora**: 'whoever gets burned by milk cries when they see a cow'. Another classic: **no hay mal que por bien no venga**, 'every cloud has a silver lining' (there's no bad thing that doesn't bring something good).

pages.title: Birds and gift horses
pages.body: **Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando**: 'a bird in the hand is worth a hundred flying' (in English, only two in the bush). And **a caballo regalado no se le miran los dientes**: 'don't look a gift horse in the mouth'. Your abuela will use it when you complain about a present.

pages.scenario: After a terrible breakup, your friend refuses to even go on a first date.
pages.prompt: Which refrán fits?
options: El que se quema con leche ve una vaca y llora
Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando
A caballo regalado no se le miran los dientes
pages.explain: Burned once, now scared of everything that looks similar.

pages.scenario: You grumble that your aunt's gift is a sweater two sizes too big. Your abuela sighs: "Y bueno, a caballo regalado…", and waits for you.
pages.prompt: How does it end?
options: no se le miran los dientes
pages.explain: **A caballo regalado no se le miran los dientes**: it was a gift, so don't complain. Saying just the first half is the most common way to use it.

pages.title: Said and done
pages.body: **Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho**: 'from saying to doing is a long way'. Easy to promise, hard to deliver. It's the refrán for the friend who starts the gym every Monday, the plumber who's coming 'tomorrow', and every New Year's resolution.

pages.prompt: Your friend promises, again, that he'll start the gym on Monday.
pages.text: Del dicho al ___ hay mucho trecho.
pages.translation: Easier said than done.
pages.explain: **Dicho** (said) and **hecho** (done) rhyme with **trecho** (a stretch of road). That's why it sticks.

pages.title: A country in sayings
pages.body: Some sayings aren't just proverbs: they're a worldview. Crisis after crisis, Argentines built a set of maxims that are part resignation, part humour, part survival guide. Hear them and you'll understand a lot about how people here think. Take them with a pinch of salt: they're often said with a wink.

pages.title: Crying and cheating
pages.body: **El que no llora no mama**: 'the baby who doesn't cry doesn't get fed', if you don't complain, you get nothing. **Hecha la ley, hecha la trampa**: 'as soon as a law is made, so is the way around it'. Both are said with a shrug, about bureaucracy, taxes and life in general.

pages.scenario: The bank keeps ignoring your complaint. Your Argentine friend tells you to call every day and make noise.
pages.prompt: Which saying is she following?
options: El que no llora no mama
Hecha la ley, hecha la trampa
pages.explain: Squeaky wheel gets the grease. Complain, insist, and you'll get it.

pages.title: The vivo and the gil
pages.body: In Argentine slang, a **vivo** is the sharp one, always finding the angle, and a **gil** is the sucker who gets fooled. A famously cynical maxim: **el vivo vive del gil, y el gil de su trabajo**, 'the sharp one lives off the sucker, and the sucker off his work'. That habit of getting ahead by cutting corners has a name: **viveza criolla**.

pages.scenario: A guy walks past the whole line at the bakery, smiles, and gets served first. Nobody says a word.
pages.prompt: In the maxim, who's the gil?
pages.explain: He's playing the **vivo**; the people who waited and said nothing are the **giles**. Pure **viveza criolla**.

pages.title: Joke or confession?
pages.body: Argentines argue about **viveza criolla** at every sobremesa. Critics say it wears down trust: if everyone expects the other guy to cheat, nobody plays fair. Others push back: most people here are honest and tired of the label. Its opposite, and the one people are proud of, is **la gauchada**: a favor done for free.
pages.fun_fact: Plenty of Argentines blame viveza criolla for the country's problems. It's a joke and a confession at the same time.

pages.statement: Plenty of Argentines criticise viveza criolla, even while they joke about it.
pages.explain: It's cynical and self-critical at once. Admiring the **vivo** out loud would make most people wince.

pages.title: Wire and hope
pages.body: **Atado con alambre**: 'tied up with wire', anything held together by a quick, improvised fix. A car, a plan, sometimes the whole economy. And for hard times: **siempre que llovió, paró**, 'every time it rained, it stopped'. When luck saves the day at the last second, someone will say **Dios es argentino**: God is Argentine.

pages.prompt: Your friend is devastated after losing her job. You want to comfort her.
pages.translation: Relax, it always stops raining eventually.
pages.explain: Hard times pass. It's one of the kindest things you can say.

classes.title: Boludo, the word that does everything
classes.summary: Greeting, insult, punctuation: one word, many jobs

pages.title: Welcome to the puteadas
pages.body: Grab a mate. In Argentina a **puteada** is a swear or an insult, and **putear** is to swear at someone (or at the universe). Argentines swear a lot, and often with love. This section teaches you to *understand* them, and, more importantly, when *not* to use them.

pages.title: Boludo

word.tag: Say it only once friends say it to you

pages.body: **Boludo** (**boluda** for a woman) literally means 'big-balled', i.e. an idiot. But between friends it softened into 'dude' or 'mate'. **¿Qué hacés, boludo?** is just 'What's up, man?'. Same word, said slowly with a stare, is still an insult: 'you idiot'. Some people toss it casually at anyone, even at work. Tone and relationship decide everything.
pages.fun_fact: Some porteños use it so often it's basically a comma: 'Fui al súper, boludo, y no había nada, boludo.'

pages.scenario: Your friend Nico sees you at the bar, grins and shouts: '¡Boludo! ¿Qué hacés acá?'
pages.prompt: Is Nico insulting you?
options: No, he's happy to see you
pages.explain: Warm tone plus a friend = **boludo** means 'dude'. He's just surprised to see you there.

pages.scenario: Your brand-new boss, on your first day, says: 'Che, boludo, pasame eso.'
pages.prompt: Is he insulting you?
pages.explain: Some people use **boludo** with anyone. It's very casual for a boss, and never the formal option. Don't say it back until you know him well.

pages.title: Pelotudo: the upgrade
pages.body: **Pelotudo** comes from **pelotas** (balls, again) and means 'idiot' too, but stronger. It's rarely affectionate. **¡Qué pelotudo!** = 'What an idiot!'. A silly or trivial thing is a **boludez** or **pelotudez**: 'Es una boludez' = 'It's nothing / it's a dumb little thing'.

pages.statement: Pelotudo is the friendly, softer version of boludo.
pages.explain: It's the other way around. **Boludo** can be friendly; **pelotudo** almost always stings.

pages.prompt: Your friend apologizes for spilling a bit of mate. How do you say 'Don't worry, it's nothing'?
pages.translation: Relax, it's nothing.
pages.explain: **Boludez** = a trivial thing. Friendly and harmless.

pages.title: The tourist rule
pages.body: Your accent changes how it lands. From a local friend, **boludo** is warm; from a stranger with an accent, it can sound like an insult. So: understand it everywhere, but say it only once your friends say it to you. Never to a waiter, a driver or someone you just met. **Pelotudo**: understand it, never say it. **Boludez**: safe anywhere.

pages.scenario: A stranger bumps into you on the subte and you say '¡Boludo!' with a frown.
pages.prompt: How will he hear it?
pages.explain: No friendship, angry tone: it's an insult. The word didn't change; the context did.

classes.title: Gil, forro, chanta: the cast of characters
classes.summary: The people Argentines love to complain about

pages.title: The gil
pages.body: A **gil** is a sucker: naive, easy to fool. It's an old lunfardo word from tango days, when the **gil** was the one who got scammed and the **vivo** was the sharp guy. **No seas gil** = 'Don't be a sucker'. Rude, but mild.
pages.fun_fact: Tango lyrics are full of giles who got their heart broken.

pages.title: The chanta
pages.body: A **chanta** is a bullshitter: someone who brags, promises and never delivers. The plumber who says 'mañana vengo' for three weeks? **Chanta**. The guy who claims he played in the Primera? **Chanta**. Among friends it's a tease, not a war.

pages.title: The forro
pages.body: **Forro** literally means 'lining' and is also slang for condom. Called at a person, it means a jerk: someone mean, disloyal or selfish. **Sos un forro** = 'You're such a jerk'. It hurts more than **boludo** because it's about character, not brains.

pages.prompt: Match the character to who they are

pages.scenario: A taxi driver charges you triple because you're a tourist, and you paid.
pages.prompt: What would your Argentine friend call you, lovingly?
pages.explain: You got fooled, so you're the **gil**. The taxi driver is the **chanta** (or the **forro**).

pages.title: The pests
pages.body: Someone who won't stop bugging you is a **hinchapelotas** or **rompebolas**: literally 'ball-swelling' and 'ball-breaking'. Pain in the neck. **Pajero** literally means 'wanker'; among friends it usually means lazy or useless: **No seas pajero, ayudame** = 'Don't be lazy, help me'. Crude, so keep it among friends.

pages.statement: Calling your friend a 'hinchapelotas' because he texts you 40 times a day is a fair use of the word.
pages.explain: Exactly the right use. Between friends it's a jokey complaint, not a war.

pages.prompt: Your roommate is on the couch while you carry all the groceries.
pages.translation: Don't be lazy, help me!
pages.explain: **Pajero** here = lazy. A **chanta** lies, a **gil** gets fooled.

pages.scenario: Your friend tells the whole group your secret, just to get a laugh at your expense.
pages.prompt: Which word fits him best?
pages.explain: He didn't brag or break a promise, so he's not a **chanta**. This is mean and disloyal: that's a **forro**. Now you know why it stings.

pages.title: Your cheat sheet
pages.body: Safe to joke with friends: **gil**, **chanta**. Friends only, and only once they use them with you: **hinchapelotas**, **rompebolas**, **pajero**. Understand it, never say it: **forro**. With a stranger, none of them. When in doubt, laugh and keep quiet: you'll sound more local than any puteada.

That plumber is all talk.
You're such a jerk.

classes.title: La puta madre: pure frustration
classes.summary: The exclamations for when everything goes wrong

pages.title: Swearing at the universe

word.tag: Friends only, never at a person

pages.body: Stub your toe, miss the bus, see the inflation numbers: **¡La puta madre!** Nobody's mother is involved; it's just 'Damn it!'. It goes up in levels: **la puta que lo parió** ('the whore who gave birth to it') and the maximum, **la re puta que lo parió**. The **re** means 'really, super'.
pages.fun_fact: People shorten it to just 'La puta…' with a long, tired sigh.

pages.title: The heavy one
pages.body: **¡La concha de tu madre!** is very vulgar (**concha** is vulgar slang for female genitals). Shouted at nobody, after dropping your phone in the toilet, it's frustration. Aimed at a person, it's a serious insult. Fun variant: **la concha de la lora** ('the parrot's...'), pure frustration, no target.

pages.statement: When someone shouts '¡La puta madre!' after missing the bus, they're insulting someone's mother.
pages.explain: It's an exclamation, like 'Damn it!'. No mothers were harmed.

pages.title: Andá a cagar
pages.body: **¡Andá a cagar!**, literally 'go take a shit', means 'get lost'. But between friends it's often disbelief: 'No way!' or 'Shut up!'. The tone tells you which one: said laughing, it's amazement; said cold, with a door closing, it's goodbye.

pages.scenario: You tell your friend you met Messi at the airport. She laughs and says: '¡Andá a cagar!'
pages.prompt: What does she mean?
pages.explain: Laughing + amazing news = disbelief. Same words, said cold, would mean 'get lost'.

pages.title: I couldn't care less
pages.body: **Me chupa un huevo** ('it sucks me an egg', with egg = testicle) means 'I don't give a damn'. Crude, so close friends only. When you really, really don't care, there's a deluxe version: **me chupa un huevo y la mitad del otro**, 'one egg and half of the other'.

pages.prompt: Your friend asks if you care who wins the reality show. You really don't.
pages.translation: I don't give a damn.
pages.explain: **Me chupa un huevo** = I couldn't care less. Crude, so friends only.

pages.title: The family-friendly versions
pages.body: Around kids or grandparents? Swap in a euphemism. **¡Miércoles!** ('Wednesday!') stands in for **mierda** (shit). **¡Pucha!** or **¡La pucha!** replaces **la puta**. **Me importa un pito** ('I don't care a whistle') is the tamer cousin of the egg one. Same frustration, no scandal.

pages.explain: The euphemism is softest, and the **re** takes the classic to the maximum.

pages.explain: Euphemisms sound like the real thing, so everyone knows what you meant, but nobody's offended.

classes.title: Reading the room
classes.summary: The stadium, the traffic, and your girlfriend's grandma

pages.title: At the cancha
pages.body: The football stadium (**la cancha**) is where swearing becomes a sport. The referee (**el referí**) gets **¡Cobrá, la concha de tu madre!** ('Make the call!'), and a slow striker hears **¡Dale, pelotudo!**. Warning: many stadium chants include slurs about gays, other nationalities and so on. Cheer, swear at the ref, but skip the slurs, even if the whole stand is singing them.
pages.fun_fact: The ref is insulted so often that some fans say it's part of the ticket price.

pages.scenario: Your first match. The whole stand starts a chant you don't understand, and your neighbor nudges you to join in.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
pages.explain: Lots of chants are homophobic or racist, and there's growing pushback against them. Clapping and jumping get you in the mood; the words can wait until you know what they say.

pages.title: Behind the wheel
pages.body: Buenos Aires traffic turns saints into sailors. The light turns green and someone honks: **¡Dale, boludo!** ('Come on, idiot!'). Somebody cuts you off: **¡Aprendé a manejar!** ('Learn to drive!') or **¿Quién te dio el registro?** ('Who gave you a license?'). Usually it's just venting. Hand gestures can escalate things, so keep yours on the wheel.

pages.prompt: The light turned green five seconds ago and the car in front hasn't moved.
pages.translation: Come on, idiot!
pages.explain: Classic traffic venting. Said to a stranger in a car, **boludo** is an insult, but a very routine one.

pages.title: The abuela test
pages.body: Before you swear, ask: would I say this in front of my girlfriend's grandma? With close friends, **boludo**, **la puta madre** and **andá a cagar** are totally normal. With your boss, your in-laws, a cop or a stranger? Go polite: **¡pucha!**, **¡miércoles!** Swearing badly makes you sound rude; swearing well makes you sound local.

pages.scenario: Sunday lunch with your girlfriend's family. You burn your tongue on the ravioles.
pages.prompt: What do you say?
pages.explain: **La pucha** says 'ouch, darn' without making the abuela drop her fork.

pages.scenario: You're watching the match at a bar with your friends and your team misses a penalty.
pages.prompt: Which reaction sounds most like your friends?
options: Swear at the friend next to you
pages.explain: At a bar with friends during football, swearing at the universe is expected. Swearing *at* a friend is another story, and 'Oh dear' would get you strange looks.

classes.title: Hello, with a kiss
classes.summary: One kiss, everybody, every time

pages.title: One kiss. Just one.
pages.body: In Argentina you say hi with **un beso**: one kiss, **cachete** a **cachete** (cheek to cheek), usually on the right side. Not two like in Spain, not three. Friends, family, your friend's cousin you just met, the new guy at work: all get **un beso**. And yes, men too: friends, brothers, fathers and sons, often with a pat on the back.

pages.statement: Two Argentine guys who are friends will usually greet each other with a kiss.
pages.explain: A kiss plus a pat on the back is the classic combo, especially among younger men. A handshake between two friends would feel oddly stiff.

pages.title: Saludar a todos
pages.body: Arrive at a party with twelve people and you **saludás a todos**: you go around and kiss every single one, even the ones you don't know. A general "¡hola!" from the door comes across as unfriendly. And you do it again when you leave, a kiss and a **chau** for each one. Budget five minutes for it, both ways.

pages.scenario: You get to a friend's birthday. Fifteen people are already sitting around the table, most of them strangers.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Wave at everyone from the door and sit down
Go around and give each person a kiss
Shake hands with the men, kiss the women
pages.explain: Around the table, one by one, a kiss each. Say your name if they don't know you: "Hola, soy Sam". It's slow, and nobody minds.

pages.title: When it's a handshake
pages.body: The kiss rules social life, but not everything. A very formal first meeting, a job interview in a big company, an older official: often a handshake first. Watch what the other person does and copy them. A lot of the time the second meeting is already a kiss. When in doubt, lean in slowly and let them decide.

pages.title: ¿Todo bien?
pages.body: The greeting that follows the kiss is not a real question. **¿Todo bien?** (all good?), **¿Cómo andás?** (how's it going?), **¿Qué hacés?** (literally "what are you doing?", really just "hi"). The answer is short: **Todo bien, ¿vos?** Nobody expects a report on your week. That comes later, with a mate.

pages.prompt: A friend kisses you hello and says "¿Todo bien?". Answer the Argentine way.
pages.translation: All good, you?
pages.explain: Argentines use **vos**, not *tú*. And bouncing the question back is the polite part.

pages.scenario: A neighbor you barely know passes you in the hallway and says: "¿Qué hacés?"
pages.prompt: What is she asking?
options: What you're doing right now, in detail
pages.explain: **¿Qué hacés?** is a hello. "Bien, ¿vos?" is plenty. Explaining that you're taking out the trash is optional.

pairs: Greet every person in the room

vocabulary.note: Also how people sign off a message: "Beso" or "Besos".

example.en: Go say hi to your aunt.

vocabulary.note: A greeting, not a real question.

classes.title: Argentine time
classes.summary: Late arrivals, loose plans and goodbyes that never end

pages.title: Nine means nine thirty
pages.body: Invited to a dinner **a las nueve**? Nobody expects you at nine. Showing up 20 or 30 minutes late to a party or a dinner at someone's house is normal, even polite: the host is probably still setting the table. Arriving early is the real faux pas. But that's social life only: work, classes and the doctor run on the clock.

pages.statement: Arriving 30 minutes late to a work meeting or a university class is fine, just like with a party.
pages.explain: The flexible clock is for social life. Meetings, classes, the doctor, a flight: be on time, or at least text. Ten minutes is forgiven; thirty is a problem.

pages.title: Ya salgo
pages.body: Learn to decode the texts. **Ya salgo** (I'm leaving now) often means "I'm about to get in the shower". **Estoy saliendo** (I'm heading out) means "soon, ish". **Llego en cinco** (I'll be there in five) means fifteen. Nobody is lying, exactly. It's more like a shared estimate everyone knows how to read.

pages.scenario: Your friend texts "ya salgo" at 21:00. You live 20 minutes apart.
pages.prompt: When do you realistically expect her?
pages.explain: **Ya salgo** has a little padding built in. Order a drink, relax.

pages.title: Traé algo para tomar
pages.body: Never show up empty-handed. The host will say **no traigas nada** (don't bring anything). Bring something anyway. Often they'll ask directly: **traé algo para tomar** (bring something to drink): wine, beer, a soda. Other safe bets: something sweet for dessert, or a tub of **helado** from the heladería, sold by weight, a kilo being the classic. And note: to drink is **tomar** here; *beber* sounds like a textbook.

pages.prompt: Your friend is hosting and you ask what to bring. She answers:
pages.text: Traé algo para ___, que la comida la pongo yo.
pages.translation: Bring something to drink, I've got the food covered.
pages.explain: "Algo para tomar" means drinks, from wine to Coca-Cola. The food is covered, so **comer** is out.

pages.title: Juntada and vamos viendo
pages.body: A **juntada** is any get-together with friends. Plans for one live in a WhatsApp group, full of **audios** (voice notes), some long enough to be a podcast. The key phrase: **vamos viendo** (let's see how it goes). It means the plan is alive but nothing is fixed. Don't book a table for eight based on a "vamos viendo".
pages.fun_fact: Leaving someone on read is **clavar el visto**, literally "nailing the seen".

pages.title: The endless goodbye
pages.body: Leaving takes a while. You announce **bueno, me voy yendo** (well, I'm getting going), then someone serves another round, then you kiss everyone goodbye, then you chat at the door for twenty minutes. Slipping out without saying goodbye is **irse a la francesa** (leaving French-style), and people notice.

pages.scenario: You said "bueno, me voy yendo" ten minutes ago. Now the host pours you another glass.
pages.prompt: What's the Argentine move?
options: Take it: the goodbye just started
pages.explain: Totally normal. Then the kisses, then the chat at the door. From announcement to exit, half an hour is normal. Slipping out is **irse a la francesa**, and people notice.

pages.prompt: Match the phrase to what it really means

example.es: El sábado hay juntada en lo de Caro.
example.en: There's a get-together at Caro's on Saturday.
—Are you coming Friday? —We'll see.
I'll send you a voice note.
He left me on read.

vocabulary.en: time for me to go (the start of a long goodbye)

classes.title: Going out
classes.summary: The previa, the boliche and breakfast at sunrise

pages.title: The night starts late
pages.body: If you're used to going out at nine, recalibrate. The **boliche** (nightclub) opens around one, and **salir a bailar** (going out dancing) really starts at two or three. Going home at six, with the sun coming up, is a normal Saturday, not a wild one. There's a verb for it: **trasnochar**, staying up all night.

pages.title: La previa
pages.body: Before the boliche comes **la previa**: friends meet at someone's place to drink, eat something and warm up. It's cheaper than drinking at the club, and honestly it's often the best part of the night. It usually starts around midnight. Ask **¿dónde es la previa?** (where's the pregame?) and you're part of the plan.
pages.fun_fact: Football fans use the same word for the hours before a match.

pages.scenario: Your friends say: "Previa en lo de Tomi, después vamos al boliche." You show up at Tomi's at 21:00.
pages.prompt: What do you find?
options: Tomi in his pajamas, eating dinner
Everyone already leaving for the club
pages.explain: At nine the night hasn't started. The previa gets going around midnight, and you might leave for the boliche at two.

pages.statement: For plenty of porteños, the previa is the best part of the night.
pages.explain: Cheaper drinks, your own music, and you can actually hear your friends. The boliche is the excuse; the previa is the party.

pages.title: The after
pages.body: For some, six a.m. isn't the end. An **after** is a party that keeps going after the boliche closes, at a house or a place that opens in the morning. Everyone else goes for **un café con medialunas** (coffee and croissants) and heads home to sleep until lunch. Sunday afternoon exists mainly for recovery, often with a mate.

pages.prompt: A classic Saturday night, in order
items: La previa at a friend's place
Walk into the boliche
Dance until the sun comes up
Café con medialunas
pages.explain: The previa from midnight, the boliche around two, dancing until close to six, then coffee as the bars open. That last stop is a porteño classic.

pages.prompt: It's Saturday, and you want to know where your friends are meeting before the club.
pages.translation: Where's the pregame?
pages.explain: The **previa** comes before. The **sobremesa** is the long chat after a meal, and the **cancha** is the football ground.

pages.prompt: Match the night word to its meaning

example.en: Which club are we going to?
We'll do pregame at my place.

classes.title: No filter
classes.summary: Money talk, body comments, and the gauchada

pages.title: Money is not a secret
pages.body: After decades of inflation, prices are everyone's favorite topic. **¿Cuánto pagaste?** (how much did you pay?) is a normal question about your phone, your rent, your shoes. Friends may even ask **¿cuánto ganás?** (how much do you earn?). It's not rude here, it's comparing notes to survive.

pages.scenario: At a party, someone you met ten minutes ago asks how much you pay in rent.
pages.prompt: How should you take it?
options: As small talk: answer if you like
As a hint she needs a loan
pages.explain: Normal here. Answer, dodge with a joke, or ask back: comparing prices is how people keep up with inflation.

pages.title: Estás más gordito
pages.body: Your aunt sees you after the holidays and says **estás más gordito** (you've put on a little weight). It's said with affection, like "you're looking well fed". Couples call each other **gordo** or **gorda** as a pet name, whatever their size. And **flaco** (skinny) is how you call out to a guy you don't know: **¡Flaco, se te cayó esto!**

pages.scenario: Your friend's grandmother pinches your cheek and says: "¡Ay, estás más gordito!"
pages.prompt: What's the best reaction?
pages.explain: It's a warm comment, not a diet review. Laugh it off. She'll probably serve you a second plate anyway. Younger people are more careful with body comments, though.

pages.statement: When an Argentine partner calls you "gorda", they're usually commenting on your weight.
pages.explain: **Gordo/gorda** is one of the most common pet names in the country, like *honey*.

pages.title: La gauchada
pages.body: Argentines love to complain about **viveza criolla**, getting ahead by cutting corners. Its opposite is **la gauchada**: a favor done for free, just because. Lending the neighbor your drill, driving a friend to the airport at dawn, a stranger helping you push your car. **¿Me hacés una gauchada?** (can you do me a favor?) is one of the nicest questions in the language.

pages.scenario: Your coworker asks: "¿Me hacés una gauchada? Mañana necesito que me cubras una hora."
pages.prompt: What kind of thing is she asking for?
pages.explain: A **gauchada** is a favor. The word comes from **gaucho**, the countryside horseman, famous for helping strangers on the road.

pages.prompt: Match the phrase to its meaning
pairs: You've put on a bit of weight (said kindly)
Hey, you! (to a guy you don't know)

example.en: Honey, can you bring bread?
Hey man, do you have the time?
Can you do me a favor?

glossary.note: Said with affection, not as an insult.

classes.title: Christmas in summer
classes.summary: Cider, vitel toné and fireworks at midnight

pages.title: Santa in shorts weather
pages.body: In Argentina Christmas falls in summer. It can be scorching, and Papá Noel is still in his wool coat. Families put up the **arbolito** (Christmas tree) on **8 December**, a public holiday. The big night is not the 25th: it's **Nochebuena**, the night of the 24th, with a long dinner, often outside, that ends well after midnight.

pages.title: The Christmas table
pages.body: The food is mostly cold, because of the heat. The star is **vitel toné**: thin slices of veal in a creamy tuna sauce, an Italian import. Then **pan dulce** (a panettone-style sweet bread), **turrón** (nougat), **garrapiñada** (candied peanuts) and **sidra** (sparkling cider). Yes, there's often an asado too.

pages.prompt: Match the Christmas food to what it is

pages.title: Twelve o'clock
pages.body: At midnight on the 24th everyone stands up for the **brindis** (toast), with **sidra** or champagne, and says **¡Feliz Navidad!** The sky explodes with **fuegos artificiales** (fireworks) from every backyard and balcony. Then the presents: in most homes they're opened right then, not on the morning of the 25th. The 25th is for leftovers and naps.
pages.fun_fact: Many families play **amigo invisible** (Secret Santa) so nobody has to buy twenty gifts.

pages.statement: In most Argentine homes, the presents wait until the morning of the 25th.
pages.explain: Most open them right after the midnight brindis, with the fireworks going off. The morning of the 25th is very quiet.

pages.title: Año Nuevo, then the beach
pages.body: New Year's Eve repeats the formula: dinner, a toast at midnight, fireworks. After **las fiestas** (the holidays), the city empties: January is holiday month, and everyone who can heads for the beach. Downtown, some office workers still throw paper out of the windows on their last working day of the year.
pages.fun_fact: On 6 January, kids leave their shoes out with grass and water for the camels of the **Reyes Magos** (Three Kings).

pages.prompt: It's midnight on the 31st. Your host grabs the sidra and calls everyone to the table.
pages.translation: Time for the toast, it's midnight!
pages.explain: Midnight = **brindis**, then **¡Feliz Año Nuevo!** and a kiss for everyone at the table.

pages.scenario: You're invited to Nochebuena with your partner's family. It's 34 °C.
pages.prompt: What's most likely on the table?
options: Hot turkey with gravy and roast potatoes
Vitel toné, cold salads and pan dulce
Only sweets, dinner is on the 25th
pages.explain: Cold food rules in the heat. Vitel toné, **ensalada rusa** (potato salad) and pan dulce are the classics. Some families still roast something, heat or no heat.

example.en: We put up the tree on the 8th.

example.es: ¡Vamos al brindis, que son las doce!
example.en: Time for the toast, it's midnight!
Where are you spending the holidays?

classes.title: The calendar
classes.summary: Friends' Day, spring, Carnaval, long weekends and birthdays

pages.title: Día del Amigo
pages.body: On **20 de julio** Argentina celebrates **Día del Amigo**, Friends' Day. The idea came from an Argentine who watched the Moon landing on that date and thought the whole world should celebrate friendship. Today restaurants are packed, your phone won't stop buzzing, and you're expected to text your friends: **¡Feliz Día del Amigo!**
pages.fun_fact: In the 2000s so many texts were sent that the phone networks reportedly collapsed.

pages.scenario: It's 20 July. Your Argentine coworker texts you first thing in the morning.
pages.prompt: What does she write?
pages.explain: **¡Feliz Día del Amigo!** Text back the same, and if there's a dinner, go: it's the busiest restaurant night of the winter.

pages.title: Spring and students
pages.body: **21 de septiembre** is a double party: the first day of spring and the **Día del Estudiante**. Students get the day off and fill the parks with picnics, guitars and music. Want a quiet walk in the park? Not on that day.

pages.statement: If you're in a big park on 21 September, expect it to be packed with students.
pages.explain: Picnics, music and very loud teenagers. It's a lovely chaos, and very porteño.

pages.title: Carnaval and long weekends
pages.body: **Carnaval** Monday and Tuesday are public holidays, with **murgas** (street bands in costumes, drums and dance) and foam sprays. Argentines also love a **finde largo** (long weekend): the government adds **feriados puente**, bridge days that join a holiday to the weekend. On a long weekend, buses and hotels fill up fast, so book early.

pages.scenario: Your friend says: "El jueves es feriado y el viernes es puente. ¿Nos vamos a la costa?"
pages.prompt: What is she proposing?
options: A four-day trip to the beach
Working Friday to make up for it
pages.explain: A **puente** turns a Thursday holiday into a four-day weekend. Argentines plan trips around them months in advance.

pages.title: Que los cumplas feliz
pages.body: The birthday song here goes **Que los cumplas feliz** (may you have a happy birthday), to the usual tune. Then the **tirón de orejas**: friends pull your ears, one tug for each year. And never wish someone **feliz cumple** before the day. It's **yeta**: bad luck. The story goes that even Pope Francis, a porteño, warned a crowd who greeted him early.

pages.scenario: Your friend's birthday is tomorrow. You won't see her, so you want to text her today.
pages.prompt: What should you do?
pages.explain: Early wishes are **yeta**. Wait until the day. At midnight is ideal: the first message wins.

pages.prompt: Match the celebration to what people do
pairs: Text all your friends, then dinner
Picnics and guitars in the park

pages.prompt: The candles are out, and your friends are reaching for your ears.
pages.translation: Now, the ear pull!
pages.explain: One tug for every year. Birthdays over 40 get long.

example.en: Happy birthday!

example.en: Don't wish me early, it's bad luck.

sections.title: Buenos Aires
sections.summary: Barrios, bondis, cafés and the city that never goes to bed

classes.title: Porteños and everyone else
classes.summary: Capital, Provincia, el interior, and what they say about each other

pages.title: People of the port
pages.body: People from the city of Buenos Aires, not the suburbs around it, are **porteños**, from **puerto** (port). For centuries the city was the country's gate to the world: ships, goods and millions of immigrants all came in through here. That's why porteños grew up looking at Europe across the water, and why the rest of the country sometimes says they forget there's a whole Argentina behind them.

pages.title: Capital is not Provincia
pages.body: Here's the tricky part. The city, **CABA**, is *not* part of the **Provincia de Buenos Aires**, which wraps around it. The avenue **General Paz** and the **Riachuelo** river mark the border. Cross it and you're in the **conurbano**, the huge ring of suburbs where millions more live. People out there don't say CABA: they just call the city **Capital**.
pages.fun_fact: Fun detail: the capital of the Provincia isn't Buenos Aires at all. It's **La Plata**.

pages.statement: Someone who lives in the conurbano, just outside the General Paz, is a porteño.
pages.explain: Porteños are from the city itself. The conurbano is the Provincia, and people there will tell you so.

pages.scenario: A friend from Quilmes, just outside the city, says: "Mañana voy a Capital a hacer unos trámites."
pages.prompt: Where is she going?
options: Into the city of Buenos Aires
To La Plata, the provincial capital
pages.explain: From the conurbano, **Capital** (or **Capi**) is the city itself. La Plata is the provincial capital, but nobody calls it that.

pages.title: And then, el interior
pages.body: Porteños tend to call everywhere outside the metro area **el interior**. People from Córdoba, Mendoza or Salta don't always love that: it makes the whole country sound like a backyard. Their famous comeback: **"Dios está en todas partes, pero atiende en Buenos Aires"**. God is everywhere, but he keeps office hours in Buenos Aires: a dig at how much power sits in the city.

pages.prompt: Who's most likely to say "Dios está en todas partes, pero atiende en Buenos Aires"?
pages.explain: It's a complaint from the provinces: everything important gets decided in Buenos Aires, and everyone else has to go and ask.

pages.title: The stereotypes, both ways
pages.body: The rest of the country says porteños are **agrandados** (full of themselves), talk too fast and think the world ends at the General Paz. Porteños joke that people in the provinces live slower, take the **siesta** seriously and never hurry. Both sides exaggerate, and both sides laugh. Just don't tell someone from Córdoba they sound "like a porteño".
pages.fun_fact: Abroad, anyone from the whole metro area often just says "soy de Buenos Aires". At home, the difference matters.

pages.scenario: You're in Mendoza and a local asks where you've been. You say: "Estuve en Buenos Aires y ahora estoy conociendo el interior." He raises an eyebrow.
pages.prompt: What happened?
pages.explain: Nothing terrible, but **el interior** is the porteño view of the map. Outside Buenos Aires, people prefer you just name the province: "estoy recorriendo Mendoza".

classes.title: A city of barrios
classes.summary: Where to go, when, and what to watch for, barrio by barrio

pages.title: La Boca and Caminito
pages.body: **La Boca** sits where the Riachuelo meets the river. Its dockworkers built houses of wood and **chapa** (corrugated metal), painted, the story goes, with leftover paint from the shipyards. Its most famous street, **Caminito**, is named after a tango. Go by day, take your photos, and stick to Caminito and the streets right around it.

pages.statement: In La Boca, it's smart to stay around Caminito rather than wander off on your own.
pages.explain: The colorful tourist strip is small, and the streets beyond it are rougher. Locals will tell you the same, especially after dark.

pages.title: San Telmo on Sundays
pages.body: **San Telmo** is the old colonial south: **adoquines** (cobblestones), balconies, antique shops. Every Sunday, **Plaza Dorrego** and calle **Defensa** fill up with the **Feria de San Telmo**: old soda siphons, vinyl, silverware, tango dancers on the **esquina** (corner), and a lot of people **mirando nomás** (just looking). Saying it out loud gets any seller off your back.

pages.prompt: Suggest a Sunday plan
pages.text: ¿Vamos el domingo a la ___ de San Telmo?
pages.translation: Shall we go to the San Telmo market on Sunday?
pages.explain: A **feria** is a street market. There are ferias all over the city, but San Telmo's is the classic one.

pages.title: Palermo, the barrio that keeps splitting
pages.body: **Palermo** is the biggest barrio, so people keep inventing sub-barrios. **Palermo Soho** is bars, design shops and brunch. **Palermo Hollywood** got its name when TV channels and production companies moved in. Real estate agents have added more (Palermo Chico, Palermo Botánico...). Joke among porteños: soon everything will be "Palermo something".

pages.title: Recoleta: a city of the dead
pages.body: The **Cementerio de la Recoleta** is a maze of marble **bóvedas** (family vaults), with presidents, writers and lots of cats. Most visitors come for **Evita**, who rests in the Duarte family vault. Everyone also stops at the tomb of **Rufina Cambaceres**, a girl said to have been buried alive. Historians doubt it, but the legend wins.

pages.title: Once and Barrio Chino
pages.body: **Once** means 'eleven', from the **Once de Septiembre** train station, and it isn't even an official barrio. It's the busy wholesale district: go there for cheap fabric, and anything sold in bulk. And in **Belgrano**, a few blocks of calle Arribeños are **Barrio Chino**, Chinatown, for dumplings and a supermarket full of surprises.

pages.scenario: A friend says: "Voy a Once a comprar tela, es mucho más barato."
pages.prompt: What will she find there?
pages.explain: Once is the wholesale district. Antiques are San Telmo; brunch is Palermo.

pages.prompt: Match the barrio to what you go there for

example.es: Los domingos hay feria en la plaza.
example.en: There's a market in the square on Sundays.
—Can I help you? —No thanks, just looking.

classes.title: Bondi, subte, tacho
classes.summary: How to get around without getting lost (or run over)

pages.title: Getting on the bondi
pages.body: The city bus is the **colectivo**, but everyone calls it **bondi**. It only stops if you ask: at the **parada** (stop), stick your arm out when your line comes, or it'll fly right past. Fares go by distance, so tell the **chofer** (driver) where you're going, then tap your **SUBE** card. Many lines also take a contactless bank card.
pages.fun_fact: The colectivo is a porteño invention: taxi drivers short on customers started taking several passengers at once, along a fixed route.

pages.statement: If you don't stick your arm out, the bondi may drive right past your stop.
pages.explain: Standing at the parada isn't enough. Arm out, eye contact with the chofer, and it stops.

pages.title: Getting off, and the cola
pages.body: To get off, press the **timbre** (bell) before your stop and use the back door. Not sure where to get off? Ask the chofer **¿Me deja en…?** (will you drop me at…?). And at the parada, people line up along the wall: that's **la cola**, and it's sacred. Cut it and you'll hear **¡Hay cola, eh!**
pages.fun_fact: **Bondi** comes from Brazil, where trams were called **bonde**. In Buenos Aires it meant the tram first, then jumped to the bus.

pages.prompt: Take a colectivo, step by step
items: Wait at the parada for your line
Stick your arm out when it comes
Tell the chofer where you're going
Tap your SUBE card
Press the timbre before your stop
pages.explain: Skip the arm and it won't stop. Skip the timbre and you'll ride to the next one.

pages.scenario: You get to the stop. Six people are standing in a neat line along the wall. The bus pulls up right in front of you.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Get on, you're closest to the door
Go to the end of the line
Ask the driver to wait for you
pages.explain: The **cola** is sacred. Cut it and the whole line will let you know.

pages.title: The subte and the tachos
pages.body: The **subte** (metro) is the oldest in Latin America, older than Madrid's. It has six lines, A to E plus H, each with its own color. Taxis are painted **black and yellow**, and in slang a taxi is a **tacho**.
pages.fun_fact: The same SUBE card works on colectivos, subte and trains.

pages.prompt: Match the word to the ride
You're on the bus and want to check you're going the right way. You ask the chofer:
pages.translation: Will you drop me at Plaza Italia? (Does this go to Plaza Italia?)
pages.explain: **¿Me deja en...?** is the classic question to the chofer. Most will answer quickly, and some will even tell you when it's your stop.

classes.title: Obelisco, Colón and a pink house
classes.summary: The landmarks, and what you actually do at each one

pages.title: The Obelisco: almost torn down
pages.body: The **Obelisco** went up in about a month, and plenty of porteños hated it. The city council once even voted to demolish it, and the mayor vetoed the decision. Today it's the city's meeting point: when Argentina wins a World Cup, or when people want to protest, this is where everyone goes.

pages.title: The widest avenue in the world?
pages.body: The Obelisco stands on **Avenida 9 de Julio**. Porteños will proudly tell you it's **la avenida más ancha del mundo**, the widest avenue in the world. Brazilians argue for Brasília. Whoever's right, crossing it on foot usually takes more than one green light: you wait on the islands in the middle.

pages.scenario: You start crossing 9 de Julio the moment the light turns green.
pages.prompt: What happens?
options: Cars stop to let you pass
pages.explain: More than one light is normal. Wait on the island, and don't try to beat the traffic.

pages.title: Why is the Casa Rosada pink?
pages.body: The president's office on **Plaza de Mayo** is the **Casa Rosada**, or just **la Rosada**. The popular story: President **Sarmiento** had it painted pink to mix the red and white of two old rival factions. Many historians give a messier answer: walls back then were painted with lime mixed with **cow's blood**, which helped against the **humedad** (damp).

pages.prompt: What's the practical explanation many historians give for the pink?
options: Lime paint mixed with cow's blood
The sunset reflected off the river
pages.explain: Lime plus blood was a common mix. The red-plus-white story is nicer, so that's the one you'll hear on tours.

pages.title: Teatro Colón
pages.body: Singers and conductors rank the **Teatro Colón** among the best opera houses in the world for its sound. You don't need a gala ticket to see it: there are daily guided tours, and cheap seats way up high in the **paraíso**, the top gallery.

pages.title: Café Tortoni and the cafés notables
pages.body: The **Café Tortoni**, on Avenida de Mayo, is the oldest café in the city, a **bar notable**: one of the historic cafés the city protects. Porteño café rule: order a **cortado**, sit for two hours, read, argue. Nobody will rush you, and the **mozo** won't bring **la cuenta** (the check) until you ask: **¿Me traés la cuenta?**

pages.scenario: You've been at a café for an hour and a half with one cortado. You're ready to leave, but the mozo hasn't brought the check.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: Here, you ask for the check
You're meant to pay at the bar
pages.explain: Bringing the check unasked feels like kicking you out. Catch the mozo's eye and say **"¿Me traés la cuenta?"**.

pairs: cross it in two green lights

pages.text: Un ___ y dos medialunas, por favor.
pages.translation: A cortado and two medialunas, please.
pages.explain: A **cortado** is espresso "cut" with a bit of milk. With **medialunas** it's the classic café order.

classes.title: Five things you'll notice in your first week
classes.summary: Therapy talk, dog packs, midnight pizza, and a phone in your pocket

pages.title: The ciudad de la furia
pages.body: A famous Soda Stereo song calls Buenos Aires **la ciudad de la furia**, the city of fury, and the name stuck: fast, loud, horns honking, everyone in a hurry. Most of that fury is noise, not danger. Here are five things you'll notice in your first week, and what to do about each one.

pages.title: 1. Everyone has a psicólogo
pages.body: Buenos Aires has more psychologists per person than almost anywhere. **Hacer terapia** (being in therapy) is no secret: **"Lo hablo con mi psicóloga"** is a normal thing to say at dinner. Don't be surprised when a new friend quotes theirs.

pages.statement: If a new friend mentions her psicóloga over dinner, she's sharing something unusually private.
pages.explain: It's everyday talk. People quote their therapist the way others quote their horoscope.

pages.title: 2. Dogs by the pack
pages.body: Walk around Palermo or Recoleta and you'll meet a **paseaperros** (dog walker) being dragged along by a whole pack of dogs, all on leashes, all different sizes. The pack gets the sidewalk: step aside and let it pass.

pages.title: 3. The street that never sleeps
pages.body: Avenida **Corrientes** is the city's Broadway: theaters, bookshops open late, and pizza at midnight. People call it **la calle que nunca duerme**. The classic plan: a play, then a slice standing at the counter. Not far away, on avenida Santa Fe, **El Ateneo Grand Splendid** is an old theater turned bookshop, with a café on the stage.

pages.scenario: The play on Corrientes ends at 11 p.m. Your porteño friends say: "¿Vamos a comer una pizza?"
pages.prompt: What's the plan?
pages.explain: On Corrientes, the night is just starting. Pizza after the theater is the whole point.

pages.title: 4. The motochorro
pages.body: The thief to know is the **motochorro**, who grabs a phone from the back of a motorbike. Keep your **celu** (phone) off café tables by the street, and your backpack in front on a crowded bondi. Porteños aren't paranoid: **estar atento** (staying alert) is just a habit here. Make it yours.

pages.scenario: You're at a café table on the sidewalk. You put your phone next to your cup. Your porteño friend moves it into your bag.
pages.prompt: Why?
options: Phones on the table are rude
It's an easy grab from the street
pages.explain: Nobody's paranoid, just **atento**. Phone in your pocket and you'll be fine.

pages.title: 5. ¡Ojo!
pages.body: The word you'll hear most in your first week: **¡Ojo!**, literally 'eye!', meaning watch out. **¡Ojo con el celu!** (careful with your phone). **¡Ojo con la mochila!** (watch your backpack). **¡Ojo, que viene el bondi!** (look out, bus coming). Learn it: you'll use it too.

pages.prompt: Warn a friend who's holding his phone at the curb
pages.text: ___ con el celu, que pasan motochorros.
pages.translation: Careful with your phone, there are bike thieves around.
pages.explain: **¡Ojo!** = watch out. It's the most useful warning word in the city.

example.en: I've been in therapy for five years.

example.en: Watch your backpack on the metro!

sections.title: Las provincias
sections.summary: Argentina beyond Buenos Aires, from the salt flats to the end of the world

classes.title: Buenos Aires is not Argentina
classes.summary: A huge country, 24 districts and one big word: el interior

pages.title: Bigger than you think
pages.body: Argentina is huge: roughly five times France. From **La Quiaca**, on the Bolivian border, to **Ushuaia**, at the bottom of the map, you get high deserts, jungle, vineyards, the pampa and glaciers. The legendary **ruta 40** (Route 40) runs along the Andes almost the whole way. Pack a jacket *and* sunscreen, and never plan to "pop over" anywhere.

pages.title: 23 plus one
pages.body: The country has **23 provincias** plus the **Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires** (**CABA**), the capital, which is *not* a province. The confusing part: there's also a **provincia de Buenos Aires**, the biggest one, wrapped around the city. And its capital isn't Buenos Aires at all, it's **La Plata**, about an hour south.

pages.statement: The city of Buenos Aires is the capital of the province of Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: The city is its own district, CABA. The province's capital is **La Plata**. Plenty of Argentines mix this up too, don't worry.

pages.title: El interior
pages.body: In Buenos Aires, anything outside the city and its suburbs is **el interior**. The metro area holds about a third of all Argentines, so the capital tends to think it *is* the country. Someone from the provinces is a **provinciano**, and for many of them the big city is just **Capital**. They have opinions about it. Many who move there **extrañan** (miss) home forever.

pages.scenario: You meet a girl in Palermo. She tells you she's from Salta and just moved to Buenos Aires for university.
pages.prompt: Which reply goes down best?
pages.explain: Asking what she misses gets you twenty minutes about empanadas, family and the mountains. Calling her porteña is a quick way to get corrected: provincial identity runs deep.

pages.title: The map in five pieces
pages.body: Argentines split the country into regions. The **Noroeste** (Salta, Jujuy): the Andes and salt flats. The **Litoral** (Misiones, Corrientes, Santa Fe): huge rivers and Iguazú. **Cuyo** (Mendoza): wine. The **Centro** (Buenos Aires, Córdoba): the flat pampa. And **Patagonia**, down south: lakes and glaciers. Each has its own accent, its own food and its own jokes about the others.
pages.fun_fact: What you call people changes with every province: a **salteño**, a **mendocino**, a **cordobés**, a **tucumano**. There's no single rule; you just learn them.

pages.prompt: You want to see this. Which region do you head for?
Match the place to what you call someone from there
pages.explain: -eño, -ino, -és, -ano: you just learn them. Getting it right earns you instant points.

pages.prompt: A friend in Buenos Aires tells you his sister left the city for good.
pages.text: Mi hermana se fue a vivir al ___.
pages.translation: My sister moved out to the provinces.
pages.explain: **Al interior** means anywhere in the provinces. **Al exterior** would mean abroad, and **al centro** is just downtown.

example.en: What province are you from?

vocabulary.en: everywhere outside BA, as the capital sees it
vocabulary.note: Said mostly from Buenos Aires. Some provincianos find it a bit porteño-centric.

example.en: I really miss my mum.
We're taking Route 40.

classes.title: The Noroeste: Andes, coca and Pachamama
classes.summary: Salta, Jujuy and the most Andean corner of the country

pages.title: Another Argentina
pages.body: Fly two hours north of Buenos Aires and you land in the Andes. **Salta** (nicknamed **Salta la linda**, Salta the pretty) and **Jujuy** feel closer to Bolivia and Peru than to Palermo: adobe villages, llamas, **ponchos**, quinoa, and Quechua words in everyday Spanish. The **Quebrada de Humahuaca**, a long **quebrada** (gorge) in Jujuy, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

pages.title: The hill of seven colors
pages.body: In the little town of **Purmamarca**, the **Cerro de los Siete Colores** looks hand-painted: stripes of red, purple, ochre and green, from different minerals laid down over millions of years. Further up, at around 3,450 m, the **Salinas Grandes** are a blinding white salt flat. Everyone takes the same fake-perspective photo. You will too.

pages.statement: The Cerro de los Siete Colores gets its brightest stripes from paint touched up for tourists.
pages.explain: It's all geology: layers of different minerals. The paint-brush look is completely natural.

pages.title: Coquear
pages.body: In the northwest, lots of people **coquean**: they tuck coca leaves into their cheek and keep a wad, the **acullico**, there for hours. It fights **la altura** (altitude), cold and tiredness. It's no scandal: national law says chewing coca leaves in their natural state is **not** drug use. A few leaves in your cheek are a world away from cocaine, which is very much illegal.
pages.fun_fact: The odd bit: the leaves are legal to chew, but importing them isn't. Most come across the Bolivian border anyway.

pages.scenario: On a bus to Humahuaca, the man next to you has a bulging cheek and offers you some leaves from a little bag.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
pages.explain: Coca leaf is shared like mate up there. Taking a few helps with the altitude. You can also just say **no, gracias**: nobody will be offended.

pages.title: Feeding the Earth
pages.body: Every **1 de agosto** the Andes celebrate the **Pachamama**, Mother Earth. Families dig a hole, the **boca**, and "feed" it with food, coca, **chicha** (corn beer) and wine, to thank her and ask for a good year. The ritual is the **corpachada**. Meanwhile, all over Argentina, people knock back **caña con ruda** (cane liquor steeped with rue) that morning to keep winter's bad luck away.

pages.statement: On August 1st, many Argentines, even in Buenos Aires, drink a shot of caña con ruda.
pages.explain: On an empty stomach, in one, three or seven sips. The tradition is Guaraní in origin but has spread everywhere.

pages.title: Zambas and carnavalito
pages.body: Salta is the home turf of the **zamba**, a slow, elegant folk dance where couples circle each other waving white **pañuelos** (handkerchiefs). Jujuy dances the **carnavalito**, in a line, to flutes and charangos. And Jujuy's **carnaval** starts with the **desentierro del diablo**: a cloth devil gets dug up from a pile of stones, and the whole town parties until he's buried again.
pages.fun_fact: They say the red poncho with black stripes of Salta mourns General Güemes, the local independence hero.

pages.translation: On August 1st we feed the Pachamama.
pages.explain: **Darle de comer** means to feed. That's literally the idea of the corpachada.

example.en: Chew some coca, it helps with the altitude.

classes.title: Cuyo: wine, water and the siesta
classes.summary: Mendoza, Malbec and the highest mountain outside Asia

pages.title: An oasis in the desert
pages.body: **Cuyo** (Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis) is dry: the name is usually said to mean "land of sands". Mendoza lives on snowmelt from the Andes, channelled through **acequias**, open ditches along every street that water the trees. The system goes back to the **Huarpe** people, before the Spanish. Walk around at night and mind your step: falling into one is a rite of passage.

pages.title: Malbec country
pages.body: Mendoza makes most of Argentina's wine, and most of its **Malbec**. The grape came from France and found its real home here, in sun, altitude and dry air. A **bodega** is a winery, and touring them by bike is a local classic. At dinner, just order **un tinto** (a red): odds are it's a Malbec.

pages.statement: Malbec is originally a French grape that did better in Mendoza than back home.
pages.explain: It comes from southwest France, struggled there after frost and disease, and boomed in Mendoza. Argentines are not modest about this.

pages.title: La Vendimia
pages.body: The grape harvest, the **vendimia**, ends with the **Fiesta Nacional de la Vendimia**. It peaks in early March, with parades, a giant open-air show in an amphitheater in the foothills, and the crowning of the **Reina de la Vendimia**. It's Mendoza's biggest night by far. If you're around, go, and book your bed early: hotels fill up fast.

pages.title: El Aconcagua
pages.body: Right behind Mendoza stands the **Aconcagua**, at almost 7,000 m the highest mountain outside Asia, and the roof of the Americas. Thousands try to summit it each season; plenty turn back because of altitude and wind. You don't need to climb it: from the road to Chile you can see its snowy face from the Horcones lagoon.

pages.statement: The Aconcagua, near Mendoza, is the highest mountain in the Americas.
pages.explain: Almost 7,000 m, the highest point of both the western and southern hemispheres. It's entirely inside Argentina, near the Chilean border.

pages.title: La siesta is real
pages.body: In Buenos Aires, **dormir la siesta** (napping after lunch) is a weekend luxury. In Cuyo and much of the interior it's a schedule. Shops work **horario cortado** (split hours): closed in the early afternoon, open again around five. In summer the streets go silent. Call someone at 3 p.m. and you'll get a sleepy voice, or no answer.

pages.scenario: It's 3 p.m. on a hot January weekday in San Juan. You need to buy a charger and the shop is shut.
pages.prompt: What's the most likely explanation?
options: The shop went out of business
pages.explain: Come back around five or six. The horario cortado is normal in many provinces.

pages.prompt: A mendocino invites you out for the afternoon.
pages.translation: Shall we tour the wineries by bike?
pages.explain: **Bodega** is a winery (in other contexts, a storeroom). Pedal slowly: the tasting is at every stop.

pages.scenario: You're walking back to your hostel in Mendoza after a long dinner with plenty of tinto.
pages.prompt: What should you watch out for?
pages.explain: The acequias run along the curb, open and unlit. They're real irrigation channels, and without them the city's trees would die. Locals will laugh, kindly, when you fall in.

example.es: Mañana vamos a una bodega en Luján de Cuyo.
example.en: Tomorrow we're going to a winery in Luján de Cuyo.

example.es: No me llames a las tres, que duermo la siesta.
example.en: Don't call me at three, I'm napping.
