classes.title: Córdoba: fernet, cuarteto and the tonada
classes.summary: The province that talks slower, parties harder and jokes about everything

pages.title: La tonada
pages.body: You'll hear a cordobés before you see one. The **tonada** (or **cantito**) stretches the syllable *before* the stressed one: **"capiiital"**, **"cordoobés"**, with a little sing-song on top. Some linguists think it's a trace of the **Comechingón** languages spoken there before Spanish. Porteños love imitating it. Cordobeses love telling them they do it badly.

pages.title: La Docta
pages.body: Córdoba's nickname is **La Docta**, "the learned one". Its university, founded by the Jesuits, is the oldest in the country, and for a long time it was the only one. Today the city is full of students from all over Argentina. The old Jesuit block downtown, the **Manzana Jesuítica**, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

pages.title: Fernet con coca
pages.body: **Fernet** is a bitter Italian herbal liqueur. Argentina drinks most of the world's supply, and Córdoba drinks around **a third** of the country's. Mixed with Coca-Cola, lots of ice, and a proper foam on top, **fernet con coca** is the drink of every party. Some cordobeses pour it into a cut-off plastic bottle: the classic **fernet en bidón**.
pages.fun_fact: Argentines also call it a **fernando**. Nobody knows who Fernando was.

pages.scenario: At a party in Córdoba someone hands you a big glass of something dark and fizzy with a thick foam.
pages.prompt: What is it almost certainly?
pages.explain: The unofficial provincial drink. It's bitter the first time and addictive by the third. Pace yourself: fernet is strong stuff, the Coke just hides it.

pages.title: Cuarteto
pages.body: Córdoba's party music is **cuarteto**: a bouncy, piano-driven beat locals call **tunga-tunga**, made for packed dance halls. On a Saturday night, go to a **baile** (a cuarteto dance) and, if you can, see **La Mona Jiménez**, its king, live. Nobody cares if you know the steps. Grab a hand, follow the crowd round the floor, and bounce.

pages.statement: If a cordobés invites you to a baile on Saturday night, expect to dance cuarteto.
pages.explain: The baile is where cuarteto lives: big halls, late nights, everyone dancing. Wear comfortable shoes.

pages.title: Culiado
pages.body: Cordobeses are famous for their humor: fast, cheeky, and full of **jodas** (teasing). Their signature word is **culiado** (said **culiao**). It's vulgar in origin, and still an insult if you say it angrily, but between friends it's closer to "mate" or "dude": "¿Qué hacés, culiao?" The story goes that even Paul McCartney greeted a Córdoba crowd with it.

pages.scenario: You've just met a group of cordobeses. One of them says to another, laughing: "¡Qué hacés, culiao!"
pages.prompt: Should you greet them the same way?
options: Not yet, wait until you're friends
pages.explain: Between friends it's affection. From a gringo they just met, it can land badly. Tone and trust are everything. Wait until they call *you* culiao.

pages.translation: Bring ice, we're making fernet and coke.
pages.explain: Fernet without ice is a crime in Córdoba. Somebody always forgets the ice anyway.

classes.title: The Litoral: rivers, falls and chamamé
classes.summary: Iguazú, Guaraní, Rosario and a very loud yell

pages.title: A coast with no sea
pages.body: The **Litoral** (Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Misiones…) means "coast", but none of it touches the ocean. The coasts are **río** banks: the huge **río Paraná** and **río Uruguay**. Up in the northeast the air is humid, **Misiones** grows the yerba for your mate in bright red soil (**tierra colorada**), and **siesta**, **tereré** and fishing are serious business.

pages.title: Iguazú
pages.body: On the border with Brazil, the **Cataratas del Iguazú** are hundreds of waterfalls, about 80% of them on the Argentine side. The star is the **Garganta del Diablo** (Devil's Throat), a horseshoe of thundering water you reach on a walkway. The story goes that when **Eleanor Roosevelt** saw it, she sighed: **"Poor Niagara!"** Nobody has found proof she said it, but everyone repeats it.

pages.statement: Most of the Iguazú waterfalls are on the Brazilian side.
pages.explain: About 80% of the falls are in Argentina. Brazilians like to point out that their side has the better panoramic view. Do both if you can.

pages.title: Guaraní is still here
pages.body: The northeast is Guaraní land, and you can hear it. In **Corrientes**, Guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish. Everyday speech is full of Guaraní words: **gurí** / **gurisa** (boy / girl), **mitaí** (child), **ñandú** (rhea). Many correntinos pepper their Spanish with it without even noticing.

pages.title: Chamamé and the sapucai
pages.body: The Litoral's music is **chamamé**: accordion, guitar and couples dancing tightly embraced. Every January, **Corrientes** hosts the **Fiesta Nacional del Chamamé**. At the best moment of a song, someone lets out a **sapucai**: a long, high, piercing yell of joy (or grief, or bravery).

pages.scenario: You're at a chamamé dance in Corrientes. Suddenly a man next to you throws his head back and lets out a long, piercing scream.
pages.prompt: What's happening?
pages.explain: The **sapucai** (from Guaraní) is how chamamé fans express emotion. Nobody will expect you to do one. But if you try, go loud.

pages.title: Rosario
pages.body: **Rosario**, in Santa Fe, is Argentina's third city and a river town through and through. Walk the riverside, see the giant **Monumento a la Bandera** (where Belgrano first raised the flag), and order a **liso**: a draft beer in a straight glass. The **rosarinos** will remind you that Messi was born here. So was Che Guevara, who got his nickname in Cuba for saying **che** (hey!) all the time.

pages.statement: Che Guevara's nickname comes from the Argentine way of saying "hey".
pages.explain: Born in Rosario, he kept saying **che**, and his Cuban comrades turned it into his name. It's still the most Argentine word there is.

pages.prompt: Match the place to what you go there for
Grandma in Corrientes uses a Guaraní word for the neighbor's boy. Which one?
pages.translation: That kid is really cheeky.
pages.explain: **Gurí** is what the Litoral and Uruguay call a boy. A **ñandú** is a rhea, and a **sapucai** is a yell. In Buenos Aires you'd hear **pibe**.

example.en: Have you been to the Iguazú Falls?

vocabulary.note: Guaraní origin. In Buenos Aires they say pibe / piba.

vocabulary.en: long cry of emotion in chamamé
accordion folk music of the Litoral

example.en: Two draft beers, please.

classes.title: Patagonia: ice, wind and Welsh tea
classes.summary: Glaciers, whales, chocolate and the end of the world

pages.title: Big and empty
pages.body: **Patagonia** (Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego) covers more than a quarter of Argentina, but only about 1 in 20 Argentines live there. It's steppe, lakes, the Andes and a **viento** (wind) that never stops. You'll spot the tourists: they're the ones chasing their hats.

pages.title: The Perito Moreno
pages.body: Near **El Calafate**, the **glaciar Perito Moreno** ends in a towering wall of ice. Every few years it pushes across the lake, builds an ice bridge, and the bridge collapses on live TV. For decades it was famous for being stable while other glaciers shrank. Bad news: studies now show it has been retreating since around 2020.
pages.fun_fact: Legend says whoever eats a **calafate** berry will come back to Patagonia.

pages.statement: The Perito Moreno glacier is still stable today.
pages.explain: That used to be true. Recent studies show it started retreating around 2020, and the loss is speeding up.

pages.title: Te galés
pages.body: In 1865, a ship dropped about 150 **Welsh** settlers in what's now **Puerto Madryn**. They wanted a place to keep their language and chapels. They founded towns in the Chubut valley, like **Gaiman**, where today you can have a **té galés**: pots of tea, scones, jams and the **torta negra**, a dense fruit cake built to last through winter.

pages.statement: Gaiman's tea houses go back to English settlers who came for the sheep farms.
pages.explain: They were **Welsh**, and they came to keep their language alive. Some families in the valley still speak it. Go hungry: a té galés is a meal, not a snack.

pages.title: Bariloche and the viaje de egresados
pages.body: **Bariloche** looks like the Alps: lakes, wooden chalets, ski slopes and **chocolate** shops on every corner. It's also where Argentine teens go on their **viaje de egresados**, the end-of-high-school trip, with tour-company **coordinadores** trying to keep them alive and sober. Almost every adult has stories. Few will tell you all of them.

pages.scenario: Your Argentine coworker, 35, shows you a photo of a bunch of teens in matching jackets in the snow.
pages.prompt: What's the photo almost certainly from?
pages.explain: The group jacket, the snow, the embarrassing haircuts: classic Bariloche trip. Ask about it and enjoy the story (the censored version).

pages.title: Whales and the end of the world
pages.body: From about June to December, **ballenas** (southern right whales) come to **Península Valdés** to mate and give birth, sometimes a few meters from the shore. Way further south, **Ushuaia** calls itself **el fin del mundo**, the end of the world. Its little **Tren del Fin del Mundo** was once used to take prisoners from the old jail out to cut wood.

pages.title: Cordero al asador
pages.body: Patagonia's great feast is **cordero patagónico al asador**: a whole lamb opened flat on an iron cross, stuck in the ground leaning over the fire, and cooked slowly for hours. The sheep graze wild on the steppe, so the meat tastes different. It's the southern cousin of the asado, and the waiting, with wine and conversation, is part of the plan.

pages.prompt: Match the place to what you go there for
Your host in El Calafate tells you what's for dinner.
pages.translation: Today we're roasting lamb on the cross.
pages.explain: **Cordero al asador**: bring an appetite and patience. It takes hours.

example.es: En el viaje de egresados no dormí nada.
example.en: I didn't sleep at all on my school trip.
We roasted a lamb on a cross over the fire.
What a wind, seriously!

sections.title: Íconos e inventos
sections.summary: Mafalda, Borges, the birome and a Pope who paid his club dues

classes.title: Mafalda and her gang
classes.summary: The six-year-old who worried about the whole world

pages.title: The girl who hated soup
pages.body: **Mafalda** is a **nena** (little girl) with a big bow and bigger questions: world peace, the Beatles, and why grown-ups run things so badly. **Quino**, a cartoonist from Mendoza, first drew her for an ad for **Mansfield** appliances, so her name had to start with M like the brand. The ad never ran, so she got her own **tira** (comic strip) instead. Her mortal enemy? **La sopa**. She hates soup more than war, almost.
pages.fun_fact: Quino died in 2020, one day after Mafalda's birthday.

pages.statement: Mafalda's name starts with M because of a brand of home appliances.
pages.explain: Quino needed a name that echoed **Mansfield**. The campaign never ran, but the girl stayed, and a year later she had her own strip.

pages.title: The gang
pages.body: **Felipe**: dreamy, shy, allergic to homework. **Manolito**: son of a Spanish **almacenero** (corner-shop owner), obsessed with money. **Susanita**: dreams only of a husband and kids, and is a proper **chusma** (gossip). **Miguelito**: a little philosopher in his own head. **Libertad**: tiny, with big political ideas. Plus **Guille**, Mafalda's baby brother. Every Argentine knows a Susanita or a Manolito.

pages.prompt: Match the character to their thing
pairs: works at his dad's almacén, loves money
wants to get married and have kids
the tiny one with big ideas

pages.scenario: Your friend's kid pushes away her bowl of soup at dinner and crosses her arms.
pages.prompt: What's the classic Argentine joke to make?
pages.explain: Mafalda vs. soup is *the* running gag. In the strips, soup stands for everything you're forced to swallow, and a lot of readers saw politics in that bowl.

pages.title: A statue on a bench
pages.body: Quino lived in **San Telmo**, at the **esquina** (corner) of **Chile and Defensa**, and that's where Mafalda lives in the strip too. Today a statue of her sits on a bench right there, and there's always a line of people waiting for a photo next to her. Susanita and Manolito got statues nearby later, because of course they'd want in.

pages.prompt: At Manolito's family shop. What's it called?
pages.text: Manolito atiende el ___ de su papá.
pages.translation: Manolito works at his dad's corner shop.
pages.explain: An **almacén** is the old-school neighborhood grocery store. A few still survive, with a Manolito behind the counter.

pages.statement: Mafalda's statue sits outside the Casa Rosada, on Plaza de Mayo.
pages.explain: She's in **San Telmo**, on her own corner, Chile and Defensa. Go early if you want the bench to yourself. She's also famous far beyond Argentina: Spain, Italy and all of Latin America love her.

example.es: Me encanta esa tira de Mafalda.
example.en: I love that Mafalda strip.
I hate soup, like Mafalda.
Don't be such a gossip, Susanita.

classes.title: Comics, cartoons and snow
classes.summary: Patoruzú, Clemente, El Eternauta and the first animated film ever

pages.title: Patoruzú, the rich cacique
pages.body: **Patoruzú** is a Tehuelche **cacique** (chief) from Patagonia, created by **Dante Quinterno** in the 1920s. He's strong, owns an enormous ranch, and gets fleeced by his city-slicker godfather **Isidoro Cañones**, a lazy porteño playboy. For decades kids read his magazine. Today many see him as a stereotype of indigenous people, and the style feels old-fashioned, but everyone over 40 knows his name.

pages.title: Before Disney: El Apóstol
pages.body: Argentines call cartoons **dibujitos**, and this country made the first feature-length one. In **1917** the Italian-Argentine **Quirino Cristiani** released **El Apóstol**, long before *Snow White*. It mocked President Yrigoyen, who flies up to Olympus and sets Buenos Aires on fire to clean up corruption. Sadly, the only copy later burned in a studio fire.

pages.statement: You can still watch El Apóstol, the first animated feature, today.
pages.explain: The only copy burned, so it's a lost film. All that survives is a handful of stills and the story.

pages.title: Clemente and the papelitos
pages.body: **Clemente** is a striped bird with no wings, drawn by **Caloi**. During the **1978 World Cup**, held under the dictatorship, a famous radio commentator asked fans not to **tirar papelitos** (throw paper confetti), so the country wouldn't look messy. Clemente said the opposite: **"¡Tiren papelitos, muchachos!"** The stadiums ended up covered in paper. The bird won, and it felt a little rebellious.

pages.scenario: You're at a big match in Argentina. The team runs out onto the pitch.
pages.prompt: What rains down from the stands?
pages.explain: **Tirar papelitos** is still a thing in Argentine stadiums. Clemente would approve.

pages.title: El Eternauta: deadly snow
pages.body: In **1957** writer **Héctor Germán Oesterheld** and artist **Francisco Solano López** started **El Eternauta**: a toxic **nevada** (snowfall) covers Buenos Aires, and anyone it touches dies. Juan Salvo and his friends survive by working together. The hero isn't one man, it's the group: **nadie se salva solo**. In 2025 Netflix made it a hit **serie** (TV series) starring **Ricardo Darín**.

pages.statement: In El Eternauta, Juan Salvo saves Buenos Aires on his own, like a classic superhero.
pages.explain: The whole point is the group. That's why **nadie se salva solo** (nobody saves themselves alone) became a motto.

pages.prompt: Match the creation to its hook

pages.title: The author who disappeared
pages.body: Oesterheld was politically active with the **Montoneros**. During the dictatorship the military kidnapped him, and he was never seen again: one of the **desaparecidos**. His **four daughters** also disappeared, along with their partners and two grandchildren born in captivity. That's why the Eternauta's silhouette shows up on murals and at human-rights marches. It's a comic, and it's also memory.

pages.prompt: The motto of El Eternauta, painted on walls and carried at marches
pages.translation: Nobody saves themselves alone.
pages.explain: People quote it at marches, in politics, and when a neighbor needs a hand. It's the group, not the superhero.

example.en: The kids are watching cartoons.
Throw confetti!
Did you watch the Eternauta series?

vocabulary.en: indigenous chief; also a local political boss

classes.title: The writers
classes.summary: Borges, Cortázar, Alfonsina and the turtle from Pehuajó

pages.title: The man in the library
pages.body: The **escritor** (writer) every Argentine name-drops is **Jorge Luis Borges**. He wrote short, dizzying **cuentos** (short stories) about labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries. He went almost blind, and then became director of the **Biblioteca Nacional**: a man surrounded by books he couldn't read. He was nominated for the Nobel again and again, and never got it. Argentines still take that personally.
pages.fun_fact: He's said to have joked that not giving him the Nobel had become a Scandinavian tradition.

pages.statement: Borges ran Argentina's national library when he could barely see.
pages.explain: He called it an irony: all those books, and the eyes to read them gone. He kept writing by dictating.

pages.title: Rayuela: read it how you like
pages.body: **Julio Cortázar** published his **novela** (novel) **Rayuela** (*Hopscotch*) in 1963. You can read it straight through, or jump around chapters following a map he gives you, like a hopscotch game. It's set between Paris and Buenos Aires, and it made him an idol for students. His gloomier contemporary, **Ernesto Sabato**, wrote *El túnel*, a high-school classic.

pages.prompt: Recommending a book to a friend
pages.text: Leé ___, la podés leer en el orden que quieras.
pages.translation: Read Rayuela, you can read it in whatever order you want.
pages.explain: **Rayuela** is also the Argentine name of the hopscotch game kids draw in chalk on the sidewalk.

pages.title: Alfonsina and María Elena
pages.body: **Alfonsina Storni** was a feminist poet in the 1920s; she died in the sea at Mar del Plata, and the song **Alfonsina y el mar** keeps her alive. **María Elena Walsh** wrote the songs every Argentine kid sings: **Manuelita**, the **tortuga** (turtle) from **Pehuajó** who went to Paris, and **El Reino del Revés**, where everything is upside down.

pages.prompt: Match the writer to what you'll hear about them

pages.scenario: At a birthday party, a room full of adults suddenly starts singing "Manuelita vivía en Pehuajó…" with the kids.
pages.prompt: Who wrote what they're singing?
pages.explain: Walsh's songs cross generations. Parents learned them as kids and now sing them to theirs, word for word.

pages.statement: Alfonsina Storni wrote the children's song about Manuelita.
pages.explain: That's María Elena Walsh. Alfonsina was a poet, and she's the one the song is *about* in **Alfonsina y el mar**.

example.en: Borges wrote short stories, not novels.

classes.title: Inventions and Nobels
classes.summary: The birome, fingerprints, the bus, the bypass and salsa golf

pages.title: The birome
pages.body: In Argentina a ballpoint pen is a **birome**. **László Bíró**, a Hungarian journalist, patented it here in the 1940s with his partner **Juan Jorge Meyne**. **Bi**-ró + **Me**-yne = **birome**. Its first big customer was the British air force, because it didn't leak at altitude. Argentina is so proud of this **invento** (invention) that Bíró's birthday is the **Día del Inventor**.

pages.prompt: In class, you need a pen
pages.translation: Can you lend me a pen?
pages.explain: Hardly anyone in Argentina says *bolígrafo*. It's **birome** (or **lapicera**), a brand name turned into a word, like Kleenex.

pages.title: Fingerprints solve a murder
pages.body: In 1892, in the town of **Necochea**, two children were murdered, and their mother blamed a neighbor. The police compared a bloody **huella digital** (fingerprint) on a door with hers, using the new system of **Juan Vucetich**, a Croatian immigrant at the La Plata police. It matched, and she confessed: the first crime in the world solved with fingerprints. Argentina went on to identify people by fingerprints before almost anyone else.

pages.statement: The first crime in the world solved with fingerprints happened in Argentina.
pages.explain: Necochea, thanks to **Vucetich**. The system he built was copied all over the world, and the police school in Buenos Aires province carries his name.

pages.title: The colectivo
pages.body: In 1928, broke Buenos Aires taxi drivers had an idea: share the cab, charge each passenger a fixed fare, follow a route. The **taxi colectivo** was born, and soon they stretched the cars to fit more seats. Today the **colectivo** (or **bondi**) is the city bus. To ride one, pay with a **SUBE** card, and raise your hand at the stop, or it won't stop.

pages.scenario: You're at a bus stop in Palermo and your bondi is coming down the street.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Raise your hand so it stops
Wait, it stops at every stop
Get cash ready for the driver
pages.explain: No hand, no stop. And have your **SUBE** card ready: drivers don't take cash.

pages.title: Five Nobels and a sauce
pages.body: Argentina has five Nobel **premios** (prizes): two for peace and three in science. One scientist, **Luis Leloir**, won chemistry for work on how the body handles sugars. Legend says that, as a young man at a Mar del Plata golf club, he also mixed mayo with ketchup and invented **salsa golf**. You'll find it on every table with **papas fritas**.

pages.statement: Salsa golf is said to have been invented by a future Nobel winner.
pages.explain: Leloir, the story goes. Nobody can prove it, and Argentines love telling it anyway.

pages.title: Favaloro and the bypass
pages.body: **René Favaloro** was a country doctor in La Pampa for years, then went to the Cleveland Clinic. There he helped pioneer the coronary **bypass** with a leg vein, and the technique spread worldwide. Back home he built a famous heart foundation. In 2000, facing the foundation's debts, he took his own life. The country still mourns him.

pages.prompt: Match the name to what they gave the world
pages.explain: Favaloro's foundation still runs one of the country's top heart hospitals, in Buenos Aires.

example.en: Do you have a pen?
Can you lend me the pen?

classes.title: Modern icons
classes.summary: A Pope from Flores, the Generación Dorada, Las Leonas and two Oscars

pages.title: Francisco, from Flores
pages.body: **Jorge Mario Bergoglio** grew up in **Flores**, Buenos Aires. As archbishop he rode the subte and the colectivo. In 2013 he became **Pope Francis**, the first from the Americas. He loved tango and was a paying **socio** (member) of the football club **San Lorenzo**. At home he was divisive: many adored him, others disliked his politics, and he never came back as Pope.

pages.statement: Pope Francis made an official visit to Argentina as Pope.
pages.explain: He never did, and people still argue about why. Mention him at a dinner and you'll hear both sides.

pages.title: Manu and the Generación Dorada
pages.body: **Manu Ginóbili**, from **Bahía Blanca**, won four NBA titles with the San Antonio Spurs and made the eurostep famous. He led the **Generación Dorada** (Golden Generation), which beat the USA and took **Olympic gold** in basketball. Nobody expected that from a football country. For Argentines he's a **crack** on the court and a **capo** off it: humble, funny, brilliant.

pages.title: Las Leonas and Vilas
pages.body: The women's field hockey team became **Las Leonas** (the Lionesses) the day they first wore a lioness on their shirts, and Olympic medals followed. Before them, **Guillermo Vilas** made tennis popular here. In one magical season, 1977, he won almost everything, but the official ranking still put him No. 2. Argentines still feel robbed.

pages.scenario: At an asado, someone says: "Vilas fue número uno, lo que pasa es que el ranking estaba mal."
pages.prompt: What do they mean?
options: Vilas cheated his way to No. 1
Vilas was never a top player
pages.explain: The computer ranked him behind Connors, and plenty of Argentines never accepted it. A Netflix documentary retold the whole fight.

pages.title: Two Oscars and Darín
pages.body: Argentina has two Oscars for foreign-language film: **La historia oficial** and **El secreto de sus ojos**. The second stars **Ricardo Darín**, the face of Argentine cinema: *Nueve reinas*, *Relatos salvajes*, *Argentina, 1985*, El Eternauta. If a friend says **¿Vemos una peli de Darín?** (shall we watch a Darín movie?), say yes. You're in safe hands.

pages.statement: El secreto de sus ojos, starring Ricardo Darín, won an Oscar.
pages.explain: Best foreign-language film. It's a thriller, a love story and a very Argentine film about the past that won't let go.

pages.prompt: Praising someone who did something amazing
pages.text: Manu es un ___, lo más grande que hay.
pages.translation: Manu is a legend, the greatest there is.
pages.explain: **Capo** = legend, someone brilliant. A **chanta** is a con man, and a **socio** just pays the club fees.

example.en: You're the best, thanks.
Ginóbili was a star.
Did you see the Darín movie?

sections.title: Historia: el nacimiento de un país
sections.summary: From the first peoples to the tango: how Argentina came to be, up to 1930

classes.title: Before Buenos Aires
classes.summary: The first peoples, and a city that had to be founded twice

pages.title: They were here first
pages.body: Long before any Spaniard showed up, this land was full of peoples: the **guaraníes** in the humid northeast, the **diaguitas** farming the valleys of the northwest, the **mapuches** in the south by the Andes, the **tehuelches** across Patagonia, and the **querandíes**, hunters of the pampa right where Buenos Aires stands today. Argentines call them **pueblos originarios** (original peoples).
pages.fun_fact: Iguazú comes from Guaraní and means roughly 'big water'. Fair enough.

pages.prompt: Match each people to where they lived
pairs: the pampa, where Buenos Aires is now
pages.explain: The map was never empty, and many of these peoples' descendants still live there.

pages.title: Words that stayed
pages.body: You speak native languages every day here without noticing. From **quechua** (the Andean language of the Inca world): **cancha** (field, court), **choclo** (corn on the cob), **palta** (avocado) and even **mate**, which first meant the gourd. From **guaraní**: **ñandú** (the local ostrich-like bird) and **yaguareté** (jaguar). So when you ask for a **tostado con palta**, say thanks to the Andes.

pages.scenario: At a parrilla, your friend asks if you want a **choclo** on the grill.
pages.prompt: What are they offering you?
pages.explain: **Choclo** is corn on the cob, a word from quechua. The avocado is **palta**, also quechua, and never 'aguacate' here.

pages.title: Buenos Aires, take one
pages.body: In **1536** the Spaniard **Pedro de Mendoza** founded a settlement on the Río de la Plata and named it after the Virgin of the good winds, patron of sailors: **Santa María del Buen Ayre**. It went badly. Hunger, disease and fights with the **querandíes** crushed it, and a few years later the survivors abandoned it. Many sailed up the river to Asunción, in today's Paraguay.

pages.title: Take two
pages.body: Decades later, **Juan de Garay** came down from Asunción and founded the city again, this time for good. That's why you'll hear about **la primera fundación** and **la segunda fundación**. The old name stuck, and **Buen Ayre** became **Buenos Aires**. For two centuries it stayed a small, muddy port, famous mostly for smuggling. The real money was in the silver mines of **Potosí**, in today's Bolivia.

pages.statement: Buenos Aires had to be founded twice.
pages.explain: Mendoza's settlement (1536) was abandoned. The city that lasted is Garay's, from 1580.

pages.prompt: Where does the name Buenos Aires come from?
options: A Virgin of good sailing winds
The fresh air of the pampa
pages.explain: Sailors prayed to **Santa María del Buen Ayre** for good winds. The city kept the "good airs", and dropped the rest.

example.es: Los pueblos originarios vivían acá mucho antes.
example.en: Indigenous peoples lived here long before.

example.es: Un tostado con palta, por favor.
example.en: A toasted sandwich with avocado, please.

classes.title: A viceroyalty and two British invasions
classes.summary: How a sleepy port became a capital, and threw out the British twice

pages.title: The Virreinato
pages.body: In **1776** the Spanish crown created the **Virreinato del Río de la Plata** (Viceroyalty of the River Plate), with Buenos Aires as its capital. It covered today's Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia. Overnight the smuggling port became the boss, run by a **virrey** (viceroy) who answered to the king in Spain.

pages.statement: Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia were once governed from Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: All three were part of the Virreinato. It's one reason the neighbors share so much: mate, words, music, and a few old grudges.

pages.title: The Cabildo
pages.body: Every Spanish colonial city had a **cabildo**: the town council, and the building where it met. The one in Buenos Aires is still standing on **Plaza de Mayo**, white, with arches and a little tower. You can visit it: it's a museum now. Look closely: it's shorter than it used to be.
pages.fun_fact: It lost arches twice to make room for new avenues: from eleven down to five.

pages.title: The British are coming
pages.body: Argentines call them the **invasiones inglesas** (British invasions). In **1806** a British force took Buenos Aires. The viceroy ran away to Córdoba, not his finest hour. Locals organized under **Santiago de Liniers** and kicked the British out: the **Reconquista**. The next year the British came back, bigger. Porteños fought street by street, and won again: the **Defensa**.

pages.title: Hot water from the rooftops
pages.body: The story every Argentine kid learns: during the Defensa, neighbors threw boiling water and oil from the flat **techos** (rooftops) onto the British soldiers. Some of it is legend polished over time, but the street fighting was very real. And the lesson stuck: porteños had beaten an empire without Spain's help. Why keep obeying a viceroy?

pages.statement: When the British took Buenos Aires, the viceroy stayed and led the defense.
pages.explain: Viceroy Sobremonte fled toward Córdoba with the treasury, and the British caught up with the treasure anyway. The locals, led by Liniers, did the fighting.

pages.scenario: Walking downtown, you pass a street called **Reconquista**. Later, in San Telmo, you walk down **Defensa**.
pages.prompt: What do those street names remember?
pages.explain: **Reconquista** (1806) and **Defensa** (1807): the two times porteños beat the British. Buenos Aires names its streets after its history.

pages.prompt: An Argentine kid tells you the school version of the Defensa.
pages.text: Les tiraban agua hirviendo desde los ___.
pages.translation: They threw boiling water on them from the rooftops.
pages.explain: Flat **techos** and terraces are still everywhere in old Buenos Aires. Now you know what they were once used for.

vocabulary.en: the Spanish colony run from Buenos Aires
viceroy, the king's man in charge

example.en: Let's visit the Cabildo.

classes.title: May and July: the big dates
classes.summary: The Revolución de Mayo and independence, and why every town has those street names

pages.title: Spain in trouble
pages.body: In 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain and locked up its king. When news reached Buenos Aires that Spain had almost completely fallen, a big question landed: if there's no king, who's in charge here? The city held a **cabildo abierto**, an open town meeting of leading neighbors, and voted to remove the viceroy.

pages.title: 25 de mayo de 1810
pages.body: On **25 May 1810** a new local government took over: the **Primera Junta** (First Board), led by **Cornelio Saavedra**. It still ruled in the name of the Spanish king, at least on paper, so it wasn't independence yet. But it was the first government chosen here, by people from here. This is the **Revolución de Mayo**, and it's why the main square is called **Plaza de Mayo**.
pages.fun_fact: The classic school drawing shows the crowd with umbrellas. Historians argue about it: umbrellas existed, but they were an imported luxury, so that sea of umbrellas is probably exaggerated.

pages.title: 9 de julio de 1816
pages.body: Six years of war later, delegates from the provinces met in a house in **San Miguel de Tucumán**, in the northwest. On **9 July 1816** the **Congreso de Tucumán** declared **independencia** (independence) from Spain and from any foreign power. The house is now the **Casa Histórica**, a museum and a classic school-trip stop.

pages.statement: Argentina declared its independence in Buenos Aires, on the Plaza de Mayo.
pages.explain: Independence was declared far from the port, in Tucumán, on 9 July. The Plaza de Mayo is named after the 1810 revolution that started the process.

pages.title: Walk the calendar
pages.body: Both dates are **feriados** (public holidays), with escarapelas on chests and a patriotic menu: **locro** (a thick corn-and-meat stew) and **pastelitos** (fried pastries with quince). And the calendar is on the map. **Avenida 9 de Julio**, the huge one with the Obelisco, is named after independence day, and almost every town has a street called 25 de Mayo and another called 9 de Julio.

pages.scenario: It's the 25th of May and your friend offers you a bowl of locro and a plate of pastelitos.
pages.prompt: What are you celebrating?
options: The end of the British invasions
pages.explain: The 25th of May is the Revolución de Mayo. You'll get locro again on the 9th of July. Nobody complains.

pages.prompt: You're in a taxi and want the widest avenue in town. You say:
pages.text: Vamos a la avenida ___ de Julio, por favor.
pages.translation: Let's go to 9 de Julio Avenue, please.
pages.explain: **9 de Julio**: independence day, and the avenue with the Obelisco.

pages.statement: Drive through almost any Argentine town and you'll find a street called 25 de Mayo.
pages.explain: And one called 9 de Julio, usually a few blocks away. If you get lost, at least you'll know your history.

example.es: El 9 de julio se festeja la independencia.
example.en: Independence is celebrated on the 9th of July.
Tomorrow is a holiday, do you want to do something?

vocabulary.en: thick stew of corn, beans and meat
fried pastries filled with quince or sweet potato jam

classes.title: San Martín, Belgrano and the flag
classes.summary: The general who crossed the Andes and the man who made the flag

pages.title: Belgrano's flag
pages.body: **Manuel Belgrano** was a lawyer and economist who ended up a general in the independence wars. By the Paraná river in **Rosario**, he raised a light blue and white **bandera** (flag) for the first time. Buenos Aires wasn't thrilled: it looked a bit too independent. Belgrano died poor, and the day he died, **20 de junio**, is now **Día de la Bandera** (Flag Day).
pages.fun_fact: Rosario has a giant **Monumento a la Bandera** by the river, where he first raised it.

pages.title: Why celeste and white?
pages.body: Kids learn the **celeste** (light blue) and white come from the sky and its clouds. Some historians argue they come from the Spanish royal house of Borbón instead. Nobody can prove either one. Before the flag came the **escarapela**, a rosette people pin on their chest on patriotic days. The **sol de mayo** (May sun) in the middle came later.
pages.fun_fact: The 18th of May is Día de la Escarapela. Watch for the rosettes on kids' school uniforms.

pages.statement: Belgrano, the creator of the flag, died a poor man.
pages.explain: He gave much of what he had to the cause and died in Buenos Aires with almost nothing. His death day, 20 June, is Flag Day.

pages.title: San Martín crosses the Andes
pages.body: **José de San Martín**, born in **Yapeyú** (Corrientes) and trained as a soldier in Spain, had a bold plan: beat Spain in Peru by going through Chile. From **Mendoza** he built the **Ejército de los Andes** and crossed the **cordillera** (the Andes), with thousands of men, mules and horses, over passes more than 4,000 meters high. He helped free Chile, then Peru.

pages.title: Where you'll find him
pages.body: San Martín died in France, but his remains came home. His tomb is inside the **Catedral** on Plaza de Mayo, guarded by the **Granaderos**, the cavalry regiment he founded, in old blue uniforms. Argentines call him the **Padre de la Patria**, the greatest **prócer** (founding hero). Every town has a San Martín street, square or statue, usually on horseback.

pages.scenario: You step into the Catedral Metropolitana, next to Plaza de Mayo, and see soldiers in old blue uniforms guarding a tomb.
pages.prompt: Whose tomb is it?
pages.explain: San Martín's mausoleum. Step in quietly: for many Argentines this is the closest thing to a national shrine.

pages.prompt: Match what you'll see to what it's about
pairs: where the flag was first raised
pinned on your chest on patriotic days

pages.prompt: Argentines call San Martín the father of the nation:
pages.translation: He's the Father of the Homeland.
pages.explain: **Padre de la Patria**. His day is 17 August, the anniversary of his death, and another feriado.

classes.title: Unitarios, federales and gauchos
classes.summary: Decades of civil war, Rosas, and the horsemen of the pampa

pages.title: Independent... and now what?
pages.body: Winning independence was the easy part. Then came decades of civil wars between two camps. The **unitarios** wanted one strong central government run from Buenos Aires. The **federales** wanted the provinces to rule themselves, and each province had its **caudillo** (regional strongman) with his own followers. Behind it all: who keeps the money from the port? The provinces had a pretty good guess.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning
pairs: wanted a strong central government in Buenos Aires
wanted the provinces to govern themselves
a regional strongman with his own followers

pages.title: Rosas
pages.body: **Juan Manuel de Rosas**, a rich landowner and a federal, governed Buenos Aires for about two decades, with near-total power. Red was the federal color, and wearing it was all but required. His enforcers, the **Mazorca**, terrorized opponents. He also stood up to the British and French fleets. He fell at the battle of **Caseros**, and died in exile in England.

pages.title: Hero or tyrant?
pages.body: Argentines still argue about Rosas. For the liberals who came after him, like **Sarmiento**, he was a bloody tyrant. For the **revisionistas** (historians who rethought him in the 20th century), he defended national sovereignty. Today most academic historians step out of that duel and study why so many poor porteños and gauchos backed him. Don't bring it up at an asado unless you have time.
pages.fun_fact: The 20 November holiday, Día de la Soberanía Nacional, remembers a battle fought under Rosas against the Anglo-French fleet.

pages.scenario: At an asado, your host's uncle calls Rosas a great patriot. His cousin calls him a tyrant. Voices rise.
pages.prompt: What's your best move?
options: Let them argue; grab a chori
Take the British side of it
pages.explain: It's a debate that's been running for over 150 years. You won't settle it between the chorizo and the vacío.

pages.title: The gaucho
pages.body: Out on the **pampa** lived the **gauchos**: expert horsemen, often of mixed Spanish and native roots, who worked with cattle. Knife, **boleadoras** (throwing weights borrowed from native hunters), poncho, mate and guitar. Governments treated them as vagrants and forced many into the army on the frontier. Only later did they become national symbols.

pages.title: Martín Fierro
pages.body: What made them heroes was a book: **Martín Fierro**, a long poem by **José Hernández** about a gaucho dragged off to the frontier who ends up an outlaw. Every Argentine kid reads it at school. Hernández's birthday, 10 November, is the **Día de la Tradición**, when towns like **San Antonio de Areco** fill with horses, ponchos and folk music.

pages.statement: On the Día de la Tradición, San Antonio de Areco fills with gauchos on horseback.
pages.explain: Parades, asado, folk music and a lot of very proud horses. If you're near Buenos Aires in November, it's an easy day trip.

pages.prompt: The most quoted advice from Martín Fierro: brothers must stick together.
pages.translation: Brothers, be united.
pages.explain: 'Los hermanos sean unidos, porque esa es la ley primera.' Argentines quote it to this day, often at family fights.

example.en: Martín Fierro is a gaucho.

vocabulary.en: throwing weights joined by cords, for hunting

classes.title: The Campaña del Desierto
classes.summary: A constitution, a plan to fill the country, and a war still argued over

pages.title: A country on paper
pages.body: After Rosas fell, a **Constitución** was written in **1853** (Buenos Aires joined a few years later). The new leaders had a plan: bring in European immigrants, railways and investment, and take the land still held by the native peoples. The motto came from the thinker **Alberdi**: **gobernar es poblar**, to govern is to populate.

pages.title: The Campaña del Desierto
pages.body: In the late 1870s and 1880s, the army led by **Julio Argentino Roca** took the pampa and Patagonia from the **mapuche**, **ranquel**, **tehuelche** and other peoples. Official history called it the **desierto** (desert). Thousands were killed; thousands more were taken prisoner, families were split up, and many were forced to work on farms or as servants. The land went to a few big owners.

pages.statement: The 'desert' taken in the Campaña del Desierto was an empty land.
pages.explain: It was home to mapuche, ranquel, tehuelche and other peoples. 'Desierto' was the word the state used to justify taking it.

pages.title: Still debated
pages.body: For a long time schools taught it as a heroic **conquista** (conquest), and Roca was on the 100-peso bill. Today many historians and indigenous communities call it a **genocidio** (genocide); others reject that word and frame it as a war over territory. The debate is alive: many now write **Conquista del Desierto** in quotes, or avoid the name altogether.

pages.statement: Roca, who led the campaign, used to appear on Argentine banknotes.
pages.explain: On the old 100-peso bill. Who belongs on money, and on pedestals, is part of the same argument.

pages.scenario: In a town square you see a statue of Roca splashed with red paint. Nobody seems surprised.
pages.prompt: What's it most likely about?
options: A protest over a local tax
Paint left from a school trip
pages.explain: Roca's statues get painted, cleaned and painted again. Some want them gone, others want them kept. It's the same debate, in the street.

vocabulary.en: the founding law of the country
desert; the state's word for native land

vocabulary.note: A contested word for this campaign. Use it knowing it starts a debate.

classes.title: The boats: immigrants, conventillos, tango
classes.summary: Millions of Europeans, one room per family, and the music that came out of it

pages.title: The boats arrive
pages.body: From the 1870s on, **barcos** (ships) brought millions of Europeans, mostly **italianos** and **españoles**. For a while, around half of Buenos Aires was foreign-born. Porteños still call any Spaniard a **gallego**, since so many came from Galicia. The Italian mark is everywhere: pizza, **fainá**, talking with your hands, and **ñoquis del 29**, gnocchi at the end of the month, when money is short.
pages.fun_fact: The old Hotel de Inmigrantes, where newcomers slept their first nights, is now a museum in Retiro.

pages.statement: In Buenos Aires, a man from Madrid will often get called gallego.
pages.explain: Galicia sent so many people that gallego came to mean any Spaniard. It's usually affectionate. Usually.

pages.title: Life in the conventillo
pages.body: Many newcomers crammed into **conventillos**: old houses split into single rooms, one family per room, one shared patio and bathroom for dozens. Crowded, loud, mixed: Italians, Spaniards, Jews, Arabs and locals, all together. In 1907 the tenants went on a famous rent strike. La Boca's colorful **Caminito** is a tourist version of that world.

pages.scenario: You're in La Boca, walking down Caminito, between houses painted every color.
pages.prompt: What world does the street remember?
pages.explain: Workers painted their houses with leftover paint from the shipyards, the story goes. The colors are cheerful; the rooms were cramped.

pages.title: Laburo and tango
pages.body: From that mix came **lunfardo**, the street slang of Buenos Aires, full of Italian. The word you'll hear every day: **laburo** (job, from *lavoro*). And on the edges of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in the late 1800s, came **tango**, mixing habanera, milonga and African-rooted candombe. It started in humble places before it conquered Paris and the salons.

pages.prompt: It's Monday morning. Your friend groans:
pages.translation: Ugh, I'm off to work.
pages.explain: **Laburo** is work, straight from Italian *lavoro*. Nobody says trabajo when they're complaining.

pages.statement: Tango was born in the fancy salons of Buenos Aires, then spread to the poor barrios.
pages.explain: The other way round: it grew up in humble barrios and conventillos, and only got into the salons after Paris fell for it.

example.es: Mi bisabuelo era un inmigrante italiano.
example.en: My great-grandfather was an Italian immigrant.

vocabulary.en: tenement house, one family per room
a Galician; in Argentina, any Spaniard
vocabulary.note: Colloquial, usually affectionate.

classes.title: The granary of the world
classes.summary: 1880 to 1930: trains, wheat, the secret vote, and the coup that ended it

pages.title: El granero del mundo
pages.body: Around 1900 Argentina shipped wheat, corn and beef across the ocean, mostly to Britain. British money built the **trenes** (railways), which fan out from the port of Buenos Aires like the ribs of a hand fan: everything flowed to the port, so traveling between two provinces can still mean a long detour. **Frigoríficos** (meatpacking plants) sent chilled beef to Europe. The country called itself **el granero del mundo**, the world's granary.

pages.statement: Argentina's old railways were built mainly to carry grain and beef to the port.
pages.explain: Mostly British-built, they pointed at Buenos Aires to ship everything out. That's why, even today, going between two provinces can mean a long detour.

pages.title: Rich, but for whom?
pages.body: Around the **Centenario** of 1910, many Argentines felt they lived in one of the richest countries on earth, and some economic estimates agree. Buenos Aires got the Congreso and the **Teatro Colón**. But the best land was in a few hands, and many workers lived in crowded conventillos. That gap is why people still argue about how 'golden' those years were.

pages.title: Ley Sáenz Peña, 1912
pages.body: Before this law, elections were a show: people voted out loud, the **voto cantado** (sung vote), and fraud was routine. The **Ley Sáenz Peña** made the vote for men **secreto** and **obligatorio**: the **voto secreto** (secret ballot) had arrived. **Hipólito Yrigoyen**, of the Unión Cívica Radical, won the first presidential election held that way. Women had to wait decades more.

pages.scenario: It's 1905 and you walk into a polling station in Buenos Aires.
pages.prompt: How do you vote?
options: Out loud, in front of everyone
pages.explain: The **voto cantado**: you said your choice out loud, with the local boss listening. The secret ballot arrived in 1912.

pages.title: Los locos de la azotea
pages.body: In 1920, Enrique Susini and three friends climbed onto the roof of the Teatro Coliseo and broadcast Wagner's opera *Parsifal* to a few dozen homemade radio sets. They were nicknamed **los locos de la azotea**, the rooftop madmen. Argentina counts it among the world's first public radio broadcasts, and still celebrates the date as Broadcasting Day.

pages.prompt: What were the radio pioneers called?
pages.translation: The rooftop madmen.
pages.explain: **Azotea** is a flat roof terrace. In Buenos Aires they're everywhere, and now you know one made history.

pages.title: The dark side: the Semana Trágica
pages.body: Not everyone shared in the boom. In January 1919 a **huelga** (strike) at the Vasena metal works in Buenos Aires turned into the **Semana Trágica** (Tragic Week). Under Yrigoyen's government, police, soldiers and armed civilian groups crushed it. Hundreds died (the estimates vary a lot) and thousands were arrested. Gangs also attacked the Jewish neighborhood of **Once**.

pages.statement: During the Semana Trágica, the government sided with the striking workers.
pages.explain: Police, the army and armed civilian groups crushed the strike. It's remembered as one of the worst episodes of repression of the era, and as a pogrom against Once's Jewish community.

pages.title: 1930: the end of an era
pages.body: Then the world crashed. The 1929 crisis sank grain and beef prices, and Argentina's export boom stalled. In **1930** the army overthrew Yrigoyen, by then old and in his second term. It was the first of several military coups: for the next half century, elected governments and military ones would take turns. The granary years were over.

pages.prompt: Match what happened then to what you'll still notice today
pairs: Railways fanned out to the port

example.es: El tren va hasta el puerto.
example.en: The train goes to the port.
In Argentina voting is compulsory.

sections.title: Historia: el siglo XX y hoy
sections.summary: Coups, Perón, the dictatorship, Malvinas, 2001 and why everyone thinks in dollars

classes.title: Coups, Perón and Evita
classes.summary: From the 1930 coup to the man who still splits family asados

pages.title: A century of coups
pages.body: From 1930 on, the army overthrew governments again and again, most of them elected. A coup is a **golpe de Estado**, usually just **golpe**. The 1930s even got a nickname, the **Década Infame** (Infamous Decade), for its openly rigged elections. The good news: since **1983** Argentina has had uninterrupted democracy, its longest run ever, and most Argentines guard that fiercely.

pages.statement: Argentina's last military coup happened during the crisis of the 1990s.
pages.explain: The last one was in 1976. Democracy came back in 1983 and has held ever since, through hyperinflation, 2001 and everything else.

pages.title: Enter Perón
pages.body: **Juan Domingo Perón** was an army colonel in the government born of the 1943 coup. As labour secretary he backed unions and pushed new rights for workers: pensions, paid holidays, labour courts. Many workers felt they had never had a friend that high up. The army's old guard, the bosses and much of the middle class got nervous.
pages.fun_fact: The **aguinaldo**, an extra month's pay split into June and December, dates from those years. Argentines still count on it every year.

pages.title: 17 de octubre de 1945
pages.body: His rivals forced Perón out and locked him up on **Isla Martín García**. On **17 October 1945**, huge crowds of workers marched into Plaza de Mayo demanding his release. Some cooled their tired feet in the fountains, an image that became legend. That night Perón spoke from the balcony of the Casa Rosada. Peronists still celebrate it as the **Día de la Lealtad** (Loyalty Day).

pages.scenario: It's 17 October. Your Argentine friend posts a photo of Plaza de Mayo with 'Feliz Día de la Lealtad'.
pages.prompt: What are they celebrating?
pages.explain: The workers' loyalty to Perón, and his to them. Four months after that march he won the presidency.

pages.title: Evita
pages.body: **Eva Duarte**, a young actress from a small town in Buenos Aires province, married Perón. As **Evita** she ran a foundation that built hospitals, schools and homes, and gave aid directly to the poor. She pushed the law that gave women the vote. She died of cancer at just 33, and millions queued for days to say goodbye.
pages.fun_fact: When Madonna came to film *Evita*, plenty of Argentines were not amused. Peronist groups protested, and graffiti against her showed up in Buenos Aires.

pages.title: Los descamisados
pages.body: Opponents sneered at Perón's supporters as **descamisados**, 'the shirtless ones': poor, rough, not fit for politics. Perón and Evita flipped the insult and wore it with pride. Workers who had felt invisible suddenly felt that the country was theirs too. That feeling of **dignidad** is the heart of what Peronists love about Perón.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it means today
pairs: a proud label for poor workers
extra pay in June and December

pages.title: Why it still splits families
pages.body: After a coup in 1955, Peronism was banned for almost two decades. Perón came back, won again and died in office. For supporters, Peronism means social justice and workers' rights. Critics point to censorship, a personality cult, jailed opponents and costly economics. Peronists call their opponents **gorilas**. The divide is **la grieta**, 'the crack', and it often runs through the family asado.

pages.scenario: At a family asado, your girlfriend's tío grumbles that her new neighbour 'es un gorila'.
pages.prompt: What does he mean?
pages.explain: It's a jab, so keep it for when you know the room. Anti-Peronists have their own words for Peronists, too.

pages.prompt: Your friend explains why nobody talks politics at Sunday lunch.
pages.text: Es por la ___: mitad peronistas, mitad gorilas.
pages.translation: It's the divide: half Peronists, half gorilas.
pages.explain: **La grieta** runs through families, friendships and group chats. Many asados have a no-politics rule for a reason.

vocabulary.en: 'shirtless one': proud label of poor workers

example.es: Mi abuela es peronista de toda la vida.
example.en: My grandma has always been a Peronist.

vocabulary.note: A jab. Not a word for a first meeting.

classes.title: The last dictatorship
classes.summary: 1976–1983: the disappeared, the Madres and Abuelas, and 'Nunca Más'

pages.title: 24 de marzo de 1976
pages.body: After Perón died in 1974, his widow and vice-president, **Isabel Perón**, took over amid guerrilla attacks, killings by the far-right **Triple A** and economic chaos. On **24 March 1976** a military junta led by **Jorge Rafael Videla** seized power. It called itself the Proceso de Reorganización Nacional. Argentines just say **el Proceso**, or **la dictadura**.

pages.title: Los desaparecidos
pages.body: The regime hunted anyone it called 'subversive': guerrillas, but also union delegates, students, lawyers, priests, teenagers. People were kidnapped, taken to secret detention centres like the **ESMA**, tortured, and most were murdered, many thrown alive from planes into the sea. Families got no answers. The victims became **los desaparecidos**, the disappeared. Today you can visit the ESMA as a memory site.

pages.statement: In Argentina, 'los desaparecidos' refers to people who fled abroad during the dictatorship.
pages.explain: **Desaparecidos** are people the state kidnapped and made vanish, with no record, no body, no answer. Many others did go into exile, but they are called **exiliados**.

pages.title: How many?
pages.body: Human rights organisations speak of **30,000** desaparecidos, and '30.000' appears on banners every 24 March. It is an estimate: the regime destroyed its records, so a full count may never exist. Official records document close to 9,000 proven cases, disappeared or killed. The figure is contested, and when politicians question the 30,000 it sparks fierce public debate.

pages.title: Las Madres de Plaza de Mayo
pages.body: In 1977, a handful of mothers met in Plaza de Mayo to ask where their children were. Gatherings were banned, so when police told them to move along, they walked in pairs around the pyramid. They covered their heads with **pañuelos blancos**, white headscarves. They still walk there on Thursday afternoons, and the headscarf is painted on the ground around the **Pirámide de Mayo**.
pages.fun_fact: Their founder, **Azucena Villaflor**, was herself disappeared the same year.

pages.scenario: Thursday afternoon, Plaza de Mayo. A group of older women in white headscarves walk slowly around the monument in the middle.
pages.prompt: Who are they?
options: The Madres de Plaza de Mayo
pages.explain: The Madres have walked there every Thursday for decades. If you're there, stand back and watch in silence; many visitors do.

pages.title: Las Abuelas and the stolen babies
pages.body: Pregnant prisoners gave birth in captivity; their babies were handed to other families, often close to the regime, under false identities. The **Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo** (grandmothers) have searched for them ever since, helping pioneer DNA methods to prove kinship. Each **nieto restituido** (grandchild who got their identity back) makes the news: by 2025 there were 140, and the search goes on.

pages.prompt: Match the name to what it is
pairs: Mothers asking for their disappeared children
The white headscarf that became their symbol
Navy school used as a detention centre, now a memory site

pages.title: Nunca Más
pages.body: After democracy returned, a commission led by writer **Ernesto Sabato** published its report, **Nunca Más** ('Never Again'). Then civilian judges tried the juntas in the **Juicio a las Juntas**; prosecutor **Julio Strassera** closed with 'Señores jueces: nunca más.' Videla got life. Amnesty laws and pardons followed, but they were annulled or struck down in the 2000s and trials continue today. Every 24 March, the Day of Memory, crowds march for **Memoria, Verdad y Justicia**.
pages.fun_fact: The trial is the subject of the film *Argentina, 1985*, nominated for the Oscar for best international film.

pages.statement: The leaders of the junta were put on trial by civilian courts after democracy returned.
pages.explain: The Juicio a las Juntas, in 1985, was one of the first times a country tried its own former dictators in ordinary courts. Argentines are rightly proud of it.

pages.prompt: 24 March is the Day of Memory, a national holiday. Its motto is:
pages.translation: Memory, Truth and Justice.
pages.explain: Every **24 de marzo** hundreds of thousands march to Plaza de Mayo, with photos of the disappeared and the chant 'Nunca más'.

example.en: Her uncle is one of the disappeared.

Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo
stolen grandchild who recovered their identity

classes.title: Malvinas
classes.summary: The 1982 war, the veterans, and a claim nearly every Argentine shares

pages.title: The islands
pages.body: The **Islas Malvinas** sit in the South Atlantic, off the coast of Patagonia. Britain has held them since **1833**, when it expelled the Argentine authorities there, and Argentina has claimed them ever since. The British call them the Falklands. In Argentina, always say **Malvinas**: 'Falklands' lands very badly.

pages.title: 2 de abril de 1982
pages.body: The dictatorship, now led by **Leopoldo Galtieri**, faced a collapsing economy and growing protests. On **2 April 1982** Argentine troops landed on the islands, and crowds cheered in Plaza de Mayo. Margaret Thatcher's government sent a naval task force. Argentina surrendered in June. **649 Argentines** died, and British soldiers and islanders died too. The defeat sank the junta: democracy returned the next year.

pages.title: The soldiers
pages.body: Most who fought were **conscriptos**, 18- and 19-year-olds doing compulsory military service, known as **la colimba**. They were sent to freezing trenches, often underfed and badly equipped, and some later reported abuse from their own officers. When the cruiser **ARA General Belgrano** was sunk, 323 men died, about half of all Argentine deaths.

pages.statement: Most of the Argentine soldiers in Malvinas were career professionals.
pages.explain: Most were young conscripts, barely out of school, sent to fight in the South Atlantic winter.

pages.title: Ex combatientes y caídos
pages.body: Today the survivors are honoured as **ex combatientes** (veterans), and the dead as **los caídos**, the fallen. **2 April** is a national holiday: the Day of the Veterans and the Fallen in the Malvinas War. For years many veterans felt forgotten, and the war's wounds, physical and mental, are still an open subject.

pages.scenario: It's 2 April. Schools are closed, and there are flags and ceremonies all over the country.
pages.prompt: Who are people remembering?
pages.explain: The date the troops landed became the day for the people who were sent there. The victims of the dictatorship have their own day, 24 March.

pages.title: Las Malvinas son argentinas
pages.body: You'll see **'Las Malvinas son argentinas'** on road signs, murals and buses. The claim to **soberanía** (sovereignty) is written into the Constitution. It's one of the few things almost all Argentines agree on, across parties. The war is another matter: most see it as a doomed gamble by the dictatorship. The islanders voted in 2013 to stay British; Argentina does not accept that vote as deciding the question.

pages.scenario: Your taxi driver hears your English accent and says, half-smiling: 'Las Malvinas son argentinas, eh.'
pages.prompt: What's the best response?
options: Say 'Sí, lo sé' and ask him about it
pages.explain: It's usually a friendly-ish poke, not hostility. Listening goes a long way: many Argentines have a relative or neighbour who fought there.

pages.prompt: Complete the phrase you'll see all over the country
pages.translation: The Malvinas are Argentine.
pages.explain: Said as a permanent fact, and definitely not in the past tense.

pages.statement: Defeat in Malvinas helped bring down the dictatorship.
pages.explain: The defeat discredited the military. Galtieri was replaced within days, and elections were held in October 1983.

example.en: The Malvinas are Argentine.

vocabulary.note: Conscription ended in 1994, so older people use it most.

example.es: Reclamamos la soberanía sobre las islas.
example.en: We claim sovereignty over the islands.

classes.title: Democracy, hyperinflation and 2001
classes.summary: From Alfonsín to 'que se vayan todos'

pages.title: Vuelve la democracia
pages.body: In 1983 **Raúl Alfonsín**, of the Radical party (UCR), won the election and took office on **10 December**. He closed his rallies reciting the Preamble of the Constitution, and promised that 'con la democracia se come, se cura y se educa': with democracy, people eat, heal and learn. Every 10 December marks another year of democracy.

pages.title: Hiperinflación
pages.body: The economy didn't cooperate. Debt was huge, and a new currency, the **austral**, soon crumbled. In 1989 prices went wild: yearly inflation passed **3,000%**. Supermarkets relabelled prices several times a day, and there were **saqueos**, lootings. Alfonsín handed power to the Peronist **Carlos Menem** months early.

pages.scenario: It's 1989 and you just got paid in australes.
pages.prompt: What's the smart move?
options: Frame a note as a souvenir
pages.explain: With prices climbing by the day, money lost value in your pocket. People ran to the supermarket on payday, a reflex some Argentines still have.

pages.title: Convertibilidad: 1 peso = 1 dólar
pages.body: In 1991, Menem's economy minister **Domingo Cavallo** launched the **convertibilidad**: by law, one peso was worth one dollar, and you could swap them freely. Within a few years inflation fell to almost zero. The '90s brought privatisations, cheap imports and cheap trips abroad.
pages.fun_fact: Argentine shoppers abroad got the nickname **'deme dos'** ('give me two') in the cheap-dollar years around 1980, and it came right back in the '90s.

pages.title: The hangover
pages.body: Supporters remember the stability after years of chaos. Critics remember the rest: factories closed, unemployment passed 18%, and debt piled up to keep the peg alive. By the end of the decade the country was in recession, and the 1-to-1 dollar was getting hard to hold. Opinions on the '90s still split dinner tables.

pages.statement: Unemployment fell during the convertibilidad years.
pages.explain: Prices calmed down, but jobs didn't follow: many factories couldn't compete with cheap imports. That's the part critics remember.

pages.title: Diciembre de 2001
pages.body: Under President **Fernando de la Rúa**, people rushed to pull their money out. In December 2001 the government capped cash withdrawals: the **corralito**, 'little pen'. The middle class took to the streets banging pots: the **cacerolazo**. On 19 and 20 December protests and repression left dozens dead. De la Rúa resigned and left the Casa Rosada by helicopter.

pages.title: Que se vayan todos
pages.body: The chant was **'¡Que se vayan todos!'**: 'Out with all of them', every politician. Five presidents came and went in about twelve days. Then the 1-to-1 peso ended, and the **devaluación** (devaluation) wiped out much of people's savings. That's why many Argentines still don't trust banks, and why so many save in dollars.

pages.statement: After 2001, many Argentines stopped trusting banks with their savings.
pages.explain: Many still keep savings in dollars, and some in cash at home. The corralito taught a whole generation to be careful.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning
pairs: Limit on taking cash out of the bank

pages.prompt: Complete the chant of 2001
pages.translation: Out with all of them!
pages.explain: It's a demand: 'let them all go'. You'll still see it painted on walls and shouted at protests.

classes.title: Money today: thinking in dollars
classes.summary: Inflation, the dólar blue, arbolitos and cash under the mattress

pages.title: Pesos to spend, dollars to save
pages.body: After decades of inflation, devaluations and a corralito, Argentines learned one lesson: save in dollars. Flats and cars are priced in dollars (**U$S**). Pesos, the everyday **plata** (money), are for spending, fast. Plenty of savings sit at home in cash, **bajo el colchón**, under the mattress. Argentines are thought to hold more US banknotes per person than almost anyone outside the US.

pages.scenario: You're flat-hunting in Palermo. The listing says 'U$S 120.000'.
pages.prompt: How is a deal like this usually paid?
options: In US dollars, often in cash
pages.explain: Property is typically bought in dollars, and it's common for the notes to be counted on the spot at signing.

pages.title: Inflación, the national sport
pages.body: When the monthly inflation figure comes out, it's headline news. People **remarcan**, relabel prices, and everyone compares: '¿Viste lo que sale el café?' Yearly inflation passed 200% in 2023, then slowed sharply. Whether it stays low is a matter of hot debate. Either way, every Argentine is a part-time economist.

pages.title: El dólar blue
pages.body: For years, buying dollars legally was capped by currency controls, the **cepo**. So a parallel market boomed: the **dólar blue**, usually pricier than the official rate. Nobody fully agrees why it's called 'blue'. At one point there were over a dozen dollar rates, even a **dólar Coldplay**. Hence the small talk that rivals the weather: **¿A cuánto está el dólar?**

pages.scenario: Walking down calle Florida in Buenos Aires, a man on the corner mutters at you: 'Cambio, cambio, dólar, euro, real...'
pages.prompt: What is he offering?
options: To change money, off the books
pages.explain: He's an **arbolito**, a street money changer, offering the blue rate. They're a classic sight on Florida.

pages.title: Arbolitos y cuevas
pages.body: The **arbolito** ('little tree') stands on the pavement all day, like a tree, and takes you to a **cueva**, a 'cave': a back office where the swap happens. It's informal, and fake notes happen. Bring clean, newer US$100 bills: older **cara chica** (small face) notes often get a worse rate than **cara grande** ones. Since 2025 dollars can be bought freely again, but the habit of checking remains.

pages.statement: At a cueva, an older small-face $100 bill can get you fewer pesos than a newer one.
pages.explain: The **cara chica** discount is real. The newest bills, with a blue security ribbon, are the most welcome. Leave the old ones at home.

pages.title: Paying as a visitor
pages.body: Before you pay, ask. Many shops and restaurants give a discount for **efectivo** (cash) or bank transfer, and some quote prices in dollars too. Carry a mix: a card for big things, pesos for kioscos, small shops and tips. When someone asks **¿Efectivo o tarjeta?**, it's not small talk: the answer can change the price.

pages.explain: Argentines check the dollar the way others check the weather. Ask it and you'll sound like a local.
